title: SSE Generation Limited, per Gillespie Macandrew LLP , 5 Atholl Crescent, Edinburgh, EH3 8EJ Applicant against Crofters having rights in the common grazings of the townships of Strathy East, Strathy West and Baligill, per Brodies LLP , 58 Morrison Street, Edinburgh, EH3 8BP Respondents [2026] SLC 7
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2026] SLC 7,
Case reference: SLC/53/25

NOTE

Court members: Lord Minginish,
Tom Campbell

SSE Generation Limited, per Gillespie Macandrew LLP, 5 Atholl Crescent, Edinburgh, EH3 8EJ
Applicant
against
Crofters having rights in the common grazings of the townships of Strathy East, Strathy West and Baligill,per Brodies LLP, 58 Morrison Street, Edinburgh, EH3 8BP
Respondents

Section 19A

Strathy South Wind Farm Access

Act: Sutherland, advocate; Gillespie Macandrew  LLP

Alt: Ford, solicitor advocate; Brodies LLP

14 July 2026

Introduction

[1] This is an application under section 19A(1)(a) of the Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993 by SSE Generation Limited (“the applicants”) for consent to a Scheme for Development in connection with an access track which leads across part of the Strathy East, Strathy West and Baligill Common Grazing, which is part of the Armadale Estate, Sutherland, owned by the Scottish Ministers, to the site of a proposed wind farm on adjacent non‑croft land which is in third party ownership. The respondents are crofters holding shares in that common grazing. The dispute between the parties is confined to the question of whether the Scheme offers “fair recompense to each member of the crofting community in the area affected by the development” in terms of subsection (2)(c) of section 19A.

[2] It came before us for a debate on one aspect of that fair recompense dispute (identified below) on 27 May 2026, when the applicants were represented by Mr Robert Sutherland, advocate, and the respondents by Mr David Ford, solicitor advocate.

Context

[3] When built, this wind farm, to be known as Strathy South, will be one of three wind farms accessed by said track. The other two are Strathy North, which became operational in 2015, and Strathy Wood which is under construction.

[4] Entitlement to the current use of the track to access the other two wind farms is regulated by what is referred to in the pleadings as “The Existing Access Agreement” (EAA), which is in the form of a lease between the Scottish Ministers and the applicants registered in the Books of Council and Session on 8 November 2018 and in the Land Register of Scotland under Title Number STH4984. The tenant’s interest in that lease, originally held by the applicants, was subsequently assigned to Strathy Wind Farm Limited (SWFL) by assignation registered in the Books of Council and Session on 4 June 2021. SWFL is a member of the same group of companies as the applicants. The EAA is to run until the day preceding the 32nd anniversary of its date of entry, expiring on 10 December 2047.

[5] There is also to be taken into account a minute of agreement approved by this court in terms of section 5(3) of the 1993 Act on 19 December 2024, being an agreement amongst the Scottish Ministers, SWFL, RWE Renewables UK Onshore Wind Limited (the developers of Strathy Wood Wind Farm) and the shareholders having shares in said common grazing, in terms of which, in return for the adoption of certain obligations, the shareholders are to receive compensation of 50% of 75% of the rental and other monetary payments the landlords receive under each of their leases with (now) SWFL and RWE Ltd.

[6] Just as SWFL and RWE have entered into leases with the Scottish Ministers for their use of the access track, the applicants intend to enter into their own lease, or access agreement, giving them rights over said track. When that is done and Strathy South Wind Farm becomes operational, the Scheme provides for recompense to the shareholders comprised of two elements:

“Base Rent: £25,000 per annum payable from the date of commissioning of the wind farm until the date of commencement of de-commissioning.

Gross Revenue Rent: 0.375% of the gross income received per annum of the proposed [wind farm] from the date of commissioning … until the day immediately prior to the 15th anniversary of the date of commissioning, rising to 0.45% from the 15th anniversary until the day immediately prior to the 20th anniversary of the date of commissioning, whereupon gross income will rise further to 0.5% of the gross income received per annum until the date of commencement of decommissioning.”

[7] The Strathy South Wind Farm has a consented life of 50 years and the Scheme itself, if we grant our consent, will run for a period of 55 years to allow for construction, operation and decommissioning. Unless varied, recompense payments under the Scheme will end in or around 2080.

The issue debated

[8] The issue with which this decision is concerned is whether, if the Scheme proceeds, the respondents will be entitled to further payments under the EAA over and above those already being received in respect of Strathy North as well as what they are being offered in terms of the present Scheme. The respondents’ position is that, if that is so, then the Scheme does provide fair recompense to the respondents and that, if it is not, then the Scheme does not provide fair recompense. So, the question for us is whether the EAA is to be construed in such a way that the respondents will be entitled to further, additional payments under the existing agreement if the Scheme goes ahead.

Authorities cited

Muirhead & Turnbull v Dickson (1905) 7 F 686

Rainy Sky SA v Kookmin Bank [2011] UKSC 50

Arnold v Britton [2015] UKSC 36

@SIPP Pension Trustees v Insight Travel Services Ltd [2015] CSIH 91

Wood v Capita Insurance Services Ltd [2017] UKSC 24

Ashtead Plant Hire Co Ltd v Granton Central Developments Ltd [2020] CSIH 2

Network Rail Infrastructure v Fern Trustee 1 Ltd [2022] CSIH 32

Paterson v Angelline (Scotland) Ltd [2022] CSIH 33

Lagan Construction Group Ltd v Scot Roads Partnership Project Ltd [2023] CSIH 28

Trustees of Second Discretionary Trust v Bachelor 2023 SLT 1378

FES Ltd v HFD Construction Group [2024] CSIH 37

Glenfiddich Wind Ltd v Dorenell Windfarm Ltd [2025] CSOH 62

Submissions for respondents

[9] It is convenient to start with the submissions for the respondents since it is they who argue that whether the Scheme offers fair recompense depends on whether it will trigger additional payments under the EAA.

[10] Their starting point is the definition of “Wind Farm” contained in Clause 1 of the EAA, viz “the wind farm to be constructed by the Tenants on the Wind Farm Site”. The Wind Farm Site is delineated in red on a plan annexed to the agreement. That area covers the site of the two existing wind farms as well as the area of land on which Strathy South is to be built. The “Wind Farm” accordingly, say the objectors, includes all three wind farms, Strathy North, Strathy Wood and Strathy South.

[11] We are not, therefore, say the respondents, to construe the definition of “Wind Farm” as relating only to Strathy North; we are to construe it as including any wind farm built on the Wind Farm Site. Had the intention been to limit the definition of “Wind Farm” to Strathy North the EAA could easily have said so. The purpose of the agreement was to allow the applicants and their successors to develop the Wind Farm Site as a wind farm and to provide a means of access for doing so.

[12] The respondents also pray in aid the definition of “Gross Revenue” for the purpose of calculating the Gross Revenue Rent as:

“the aggregate income receivable by the Tenants from the sale or other commercial trading of electricity generated from the Wind Farm [their emphasis in Mr Ford’s Note of Argument].”

[13] The respondents go on to submit that, on a proper construction of the lease, if the tenants receive income from the generation of electricity on any part of the Wind Farm Site, that rent is to be factored into the rent payable under the lease. That means that income from Strathy South will fall to be “rentalised” in terms of the EAA. That was the bargain which had been struck in return for granting a means of access to the Wind Farm Site.

[14] Developing that argument, the existing agreement does not distinguish between different areas of the Wind Farm Site, nor in terms of when particular turbines forming part of the wind farm are constructed. It would make little sense to allow the tenant to avoid, or minimise, Gross Revenue Rent by restricting Gross Revenue Rent to the rent generated by the first part of the wind farm to be constructed. That would allow the tenant to build a wind farm comprising a single turbine, pay Gross Revenue Rent based on its revenue and then develop the rest of the site as another, different wind farm, free from Gross Revenue Rent.

[15] The applicants were looking at things from the wrong end of the telescope. They were concentrating on apparent restrictions in the EAA, rather than looking at the big picture. Yet they failed to identify words in the EAA which confined its application to Strathy North. There were no such restrictions. The reference to the planning permission which had been granted for Strathy North did not restrict matters to that development. Instead, the site, by reference to which the term “Wind Farm” fell to be determined, could be developed howsoever and whensoever the tenants wanted. It could be developed in phases, it could be expanded or contracted, but whatever income the applicants derived from the sale of electricity from the site fell to be rentalised.

[16] As to why an additional access agreement was required if the reference to a wind farm was to any turbines erected on the site and not just to Strathy North, that was simply because the existing access arrangements under the EAA had proved to be inadequate.

[17] Mr Ford then dealt with the effect of the assignation of the original lease to Strathy Wind Farm Limited. Assignation was allowed in terms of Clause 15 of the EAA but confined to a member of the applicants’ group. The intention was that the northern part of the site would be developed by SWFL and the southern area by the applicants. The EAA was to be construed as referring to the aggregate income from both entities. This was fortified by the provision, at Clause 2.2 of the EAA, to the effect that “references to the Tenants shall, where the context admits, include their employees, agents and contractors and also Related Entitiessharing possession of the Leased Subjects or any part of them and permitted sub-tenants (and their employees, agents and contractors)”. The applicants and SWFL were sharing the leased subjects in order to operate the Wind Farm Site and were therefore both embraced by references to “the Tenants” in the EAA. In circumstances in which both entities were making use of the leased subjects (i.e. the access track) the fact that two SSE Generation entities were operating the Wind Farm constructed on the Wind Farm Site did not allow the income from one part of the site to be rentalised whilst income from another part was not.

Submissions for applicants

[18] The motion for the applicants was that, having heard the objectors, we should dismiss their objections in respect of section 19A(2)(c), determine that the application satisfies the provisions of section 19A(2)(a) ‑ (d) and grant consent to the application under section 19A(10)(a).

[19] Mr Sutherland explained that the context in which the EAA had been entered into was that the Tenants (originally the applicants) had obtained consent for the development of Strathy North Wind Farm, referred to in the definition of “Planning Permission” in the EAA, whilst a separate wind farm was also anticipated at Strathy Wood, with a separate access lease to be entered into for that development. In those circumstances, it was reasonable to approach the interpretation of the EAA as making provisions which were specific to the tenants (i.e. the applicants’) in respect of the only wind farm that was being developed by them at that time (Strathy North). Had the parties anticipated that the EEA was to apply to any future development of a further wind farm on the site, it would have been reasonable to make express provision for that in the agreement.

[20] In any event the express terms of the EEA did not make any provision for payment otherwise than in relation to the development of Strathy North. The EAA created no liability to make payments from the proposed Strathy South development.

[21] Moreover, the fact that the lease had been assigned to SWFL meant that the applicants could not now be the tenants of the leased subjects and could not have the liabilities of the tenants under the lease. That was reinforced by the definition of “the Tenants” in the lease which expressly excluded joint and several liability with SWFL. Post‑assignation, only SWFL were liable for rent payments, both Base Rent and Gross Revenue Rent, not the applicants (Clauses 4.1.1 and 4.1.2 of the lease).

[22] In so far as the respondents were arguing that the applicants were caught by Clause 2.2 of the lease, which provides that references to “the Tenants” shall, where the context admits, include, inter alios, “Related Entities” sharing possession of the leased subjects, that argument was misconceived. Firstly, the reference to sharing possession was referrable to a sharing agreement as provided for in Clause 15.3 of the lease. There was no such sharing agreement between the applicants and SWFL. The applicants would be entering into their own lease with the Scottish Ministers thereby acquiring their own rights to use the leased subjects.

[23] Secondly, the obligation to pay rent was not shared. In terms of the lease the Base Rent was expressed as a single sum of money fixed by reference to the development of a single wind farm, Strathy North. There was no provision for the payment of more than one Base Rent.

[24] Thirdly, any sharing of possession permitted under Clause 15.3 was restricted to the “Permitted Use” of the subjects under the lease, which was use for the taking of access to the Wind Farm, which, in context, meant Strathy North Wind Farm. That was consistent with references in the lease to a separate access lease for Strathy Wood.

[25] The minute of agreement did not alter the provisions of the lease in any material way, but it did reinforce the applicants’ interpretation of the lease in that it expressly defined “Wind Farms” as “SWFL’S Strathy North Wind Farm and RWE’s Strathy Wood Wind Farm” at Clause 1. There was nothing in the minute of agreement which obliged payment to the respondents in relation to any wind farm other than Strathy North and Strathy Wood.

Relevant principles of statutory interpretation

[26] There being no dispute between parties as to what these principles are, they can be summarised as follows:

Construction of contracts is a unitary process. The whole terms of the contract require to be considered and the meaning of words in a particular part is to be assessed having regard to other relevant parts of the contract.

The court’s task was to ascertain the intention of the parties by determining what a reasonable person, having the background knowledge of the parties, would have understood from the language used.

The meaning of any provision is to be ascertained in the light of (a) the natural and ordinary meaning of the words used, (b) any other relevant provisions of the contract, (c) the overall purpose of the clause under consideration and the contract, (d) the facts and circumstances known or assumed by the parties at the time the contract was entered into, and (e) commercial commonsense, but disregarding parties’ subjective intentions; Arnold v Britton per Lord Neuberger of Abbotsbury at paragraph 15.

The court should identify what parties had agreed, not what it thinks commonsense would dictate.

If the contract contains no ambiguity, the court must apply it and should not rewrite what might seem to be a bad bargain for one side or the other.

Where, however, there are two possible constructions the court should prefer the one more consistent with business common sense; per Lord Hodge in Arnold v Britton at paragraph 76.

Contracts were made by what people say, not by what they think in their inmost minds; per Lord President Dunedin in Muirhead & Turnbull v Dickson at p 694.

Discussion of the principal issue

[27] When this debate was being fixed, we had reservations about two matters. One was that we were being asked to determine whether this Scheme offered fair recompense to the respondents by reference to another agreement, rather than what was being offered under the Scheme itself. However, if the respondents’ position is correct and the Scheme going ahead is going to trigger additional payments to the respondents under the EAA, we are satisfied that it can be said that this is part of the recompense which the respondents will stand to get by virtue of this Scheme.

[28] The second matter was a concern about being asked to interpret a contract (the EAA) when one party to the contract, the Scottish Ministers, was not represented. However, Mr Ford informed us that the Scottish Ministers had been advised, by his firm, that the debate was to take place and they had chosen not to seek to enter the case. Accordingly, we allowed the debate to proceed.

[29] Our starting point in resolving the primary issue is that neither the EAA nor the minute of agreement say anything about Strathy South Windfarm. That name simply does not appear in either of those documents.

[30] Secondly, while both documents expressly acknowledge that a second wind farm (ie one other than Strathy North) is going to be erected (i.e. Strathy Wood), nothing in the wording of the documents expressly contemplates the building of any other wind farm. Instead the natural meaning of these documents, read as a whole, conveys to the reasonable reader the impression that they have to do only with Strathy North and Strathy Wood Wind Farms.

[31] All of that being true, Mr Ford bases his case on necessary inferences. His starting point is the definition of “Wind Farm” as “the wind farm to be constructed by the Tenants on the Wind Farm Site”; Clause 1. Whereas the reader, absent reference to any other wind farm to be built by the tenants, would take that to mean Strathy North, certain inferences do arise from the size of the Wind Farm Site. The site, outlined in red on plan 2 annexed to the EAA, is a large one and comprises two main non‑contiguous areas, the northern one of which we take to be the site of Strathy North and the southern one the proposed site of Strathy South. It is therefore a reasonable inference that further development, on the southern part of the site, was in contemplation when the EAA was entered into.

[32] That does not, however, mean that development of the southern part of the site was to be dealt with, for rental purposes, under the EAA. There was always the possibility that such development could be dealt with by way of a separate access agreement, which, it seems to us, is exactly what the present application is about.

[33] Mr Ford also had an argument based on Clause 2.2 of the EAA to the effect that, notwithstanding the assignation of the EAA to SWFL, the applicants continued to be caught by the EAA because they and SWFL were “related entities sharing possession of the leased subjects or any part of them”. The rent provisions therefore continued to bind them.

[34] As against that, and as Mr Sutherland pointed out, the description of “the Tenants” in the instance of the EAA refers to:

“SSE Generation Limited … their permitted assignees and all persons who may succeed to the interest of the Tenants under this lease following a permitted assignation under Clause 15 (it being expressly declared that no joint and several liability shall arise among the several parties who may from time to time be successively in right of the Tenants part of this Lease following a permitted assignation thereof”.

That seems to us to close down any argument that the applicants have ongoing obligations under the EAA.

[35] As to Mr Ford’s argument based on Clause 2.2 of the EAA and the shared possession of the leased subjects by the applicants and SWFL, as Related Entities, we consider that this is a “catch all” provision intended to cover all emanations of the tenants for whom the tenants are to take responsibility, not a provision which transfers to the sharing occupants obligations which are, in terms of the rest of the EAA, those of the tenants alone. It is a parenthetic extension of the definition of tenant, not one which effects a major shift or extension of the tenants’ obligations under the lease.

[36] We also give some weight to Mr Sutherland’s submission that the fact that the EAA refers only to a single Base Rent suggests that only one wind farm was in contemplation.

[37] As far as the effect of the assignation of the lease by the applicants’ to SWFL is concerned, we see no reason to depart from the usual understanding that the benefits and obligations of the lease now pertain to SWFL and not to the applicants. As a consequence, the applicants no longer have rights of access to the site over the leased subjects by virtue of the EAA. These rights are now held by SWFL. That is why the lease proposed to be entered into in terms of the present Scheme is necessary. It is not intended to take the form of an amendment to the EAA, which would be all that would be required if it was simply a matter of making good the ways in which the EAA is said to be inadequate. It is a new and separate lease securing the access to the site which the applicants need, now that they are no longer the tenants under the EAA.

Decision on the principal issue

[38] We therefore conclude that the EAA does not govern the rental (and, consequently, the recompense payable to the respondents) in respect of Strathy South and that the present Scheme will not generate further payments to the respondents under the EAA.

Discussion of the secondary issue

[39] The secondary issue is whether the respondents’ pleadings give sufficient notice of the reasons for which it is being said that the payments offered under the Scheme do not constitute “fair recompense” in terms of section 19A(2)(c) of the 1993 Act. Mr Sutherland complained that there were no averments to support the bald proposition that the Scheme did not provide fair recompense. The applicants could not, therefore, prepare for proof on the question of fair recompense. They would not know what evidence the respondents might attempt to lead nor what evidence they themselves would need to lead in rebuttal. Accordingly, the foresaid bald averment should be deleted, and we should hold that the Scheme did provide fair recompense. That being the only contested issue in the case, its disposal allowed us to consent to the Scheme without further procedure and we should do so.

[40] In response, Mr Ford founded on the respondents’ following averments:

“Esto the Existing Access Agreement and Minute of Agreement provide no recompense whatsoever in respect of the Proposed Scheme (which is denied), the proposed Scheme does not provide fair recompense during any period, including from its commencement.”

(Answer 5.3) and the following averments from Answer 6:

“It is accepted by the Respondents that fair recompense is provided so long as the payments are received under both the Minute of Agreement and the proposed Lease for the duration of the Scheme. Accordingly, in the period 2048 to 2080 fair recompense will not be provided to the Respondents. Fair recompense is not provided by the Scheme, absent the payments under the Minute of Agreement/Existing Access Agreement continuing for the duration of the Scheme. To achieve fair recompense it is necessary for the payments up to and including the anticipated expiry of the Scheme in 2080 to reflect a payment with a value of approximately £1,688 per Mw per annum. At present, that is only achieved until December 2047, on the assumption that the terms of the Minute of Agreement and Existing Access Agreement are not varied and the Existing Access Agreement does not terminate prior to that date. Accordingly, the Scheme does not provide fair recompense having regard to the value of the development and to its effect on the members in question.”

Decision on the secondary issue

[41] Whilst those averments would benefit from an explanation as to why anything less than £1,688 per Mw does not represent fair recompense having regard to the value of the development and its effect on the individual respondents, we consider that fair notice is given of the respondents’ position and that the matter should go to proof in the knowledge that what evidence they are permitted to lead in support of it may be circumscribed by the absence of more detailed averments.

Disposal

[42] Accordingly, we have allowed a proof under deletion of the respondents’ averments relating to continuing liability on the part of the applicants to make payment of fair recompense to the respondents under the EAA.

title: Donald Norman MacLennan MacDonald Applicant against Finlay George Morrison Respondent [2026] SLC 6
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2026] SLC 6,
Case reference: SLC/16/24

NOTE

Court members: Lord Duthie,
Mr T Campbell

Donald Norman MacLennan MacDonald
Applicant
against
Finlay George Morrison
Respondent

Crofting Register: Challenge to first registration

Croft 1 Ardvourlie

22 April 2026

Introduction

[1] Further to our opinion dated 13 February 2026 in which we refused the applicant’s challenge to the first registration of Croft 1 Ardvourlie (other than in respect of the agreed removal of Kosiden from the registered extent on joint motion), the respondent moves the Court to award him the expenses of the whole cause, including preparation for and conduct of the opposed motion hearing in October 2024 (which was, in effect, a debate at which he unsuccessfully sought dismissal of the application without evidence) and the proof in October 2025, on the basis that he has achieved substantial success. He also seeks an additional charge of 85 percent under Rule 5(2) of the Taxation of Judicial Expenses Rules 2019, contending that factors including complexity, specialist knowledge, volume of documentation, travel requirements, importance of the proceedings to him, and efforts to limit or resolve matters justify an uplift. The applicant opposes that motion. Parties agree that the Court should determine the matter on the basis of written submissions, which, along with parties’ respective supplementary submissions, were duly lodged and considered by the Court. They are available in the Court process.

Submissions for the respondent

[2] The Court should award the respondent the expenses of the whole cause. The application has (other than in respect of Kosiden) been refused and the respondent has achieved substantial success. He had not resisted the removal of Kosiden from the registered extent. This could have been effected without the need for litigation. The applicant caused the procedure by bringing and maintaining the application and that, on the matters which truly required to be determined at proof, the respondent was wholly successful. In relation to the opposed motion procedure heard in October 2024, expenses should be assessed in the round, having regard to the ultimate outcome at proof and to the applicant’s lack of any live practical interest in the disputed areas as revealed by the evidence. It would be artificial to treat the debate as a discrete chapter for expenses purposes. Alternatively, the Court should make no award of expenses in respect of that procedure. The respondent seeks an additional charge of 85 percent in terms of Rule 5(2) of the Taxation of Judicial Expenses Rules 2019. The proceedings were relatively complex, required specialist knowledge of crofting law, involved a substantial body of productions and witness preparation, necessitated travel to Stornoway, were of significant importance to him both in practical and reputational terms, and he had taken reasonable steps to limit the issues in dispute and avoid proof, including in relation to Kosiden.

Submissions for the applicant

[3] The appropriate disposal is no expenses due to or by either party. The Court did not simply refuse the application but rather caused a modification of the Register by ordering the removal of Kosiden from the registered extent, with the consequence that the respondent could not properly be characterised as having achieved complete success. There had been a genuine and proper case to try, particularly in light of the absence of documentary or regulatory evidence of the alleged enlargement of the croft and the late emergence of certain averments on record. The respondent unsuccessfully insisted upon an opposed motion procedure on the issue of interest and title. The applicant was wholly successful at that stage. The expenses of the preparation for and conduct of that procedure should therefore be awarded in the applicant’s favour. In relation to the motion for an additional charge: the case was fact sensitive rather than legally complex; it did not require exceptional specialist skill; the volume of documentation was unremarkable; the location of the proof was not a special circumstance; no unusual financial or commercial importance had been demonstrated; and the respondent had not shown that any steps taken with a view to settlement were such as to justify an uplift.

[4] In a supplementary submission, the respondent advanced a further argument to the effect that, insofar as the applicant was assisted by a lay representative who was not charging for his services, any award of expenses in favour of the applicant should be restricted or excluded. Reference was made to Rule 92 of the Scottish Land Court Rules 2014 and to the principle that a party should not recover, by way of expenses, both for work done by himself and for work done by an unpaid representative.

Decision

[5] The respondent sought dismissal of the application at the opposed motion procedure heard in October 2024 on the basis that the applicant lacked the requisite interest to make the application. In our decision of 15 January 2025 we refused that motion and held that the applicant, as a person entitled to notification on account of the physical proximity of his croft, possessed sufficient statutory interest to proceed. The respondent now submits that our findings at proof demonstrate that the applicant did not, in reality, have a live practical interest in the disputed areas and that this should affect the allocation of expenses for that procedure. We do not accept that submission. The question debated in October 2024 was whether the applicant possessed the statutory capacity to advance the application. That issue was determined in his favour at that stage. While we make no criticism of the respondent or his solicitors for taking the point, our subsequent findings at proof do not retrospectively alter the outcome of the debate nor do they detract from the fact that the respondent caused that procedure, and its attendant expense. We find the applicant entitled to the expenses of the opposed motion procedure.

[6] Quoad ultra the respondent has been successful. The applicant’s challenge to the registered extent of the croft was not upheld, other than in respect of Kosiden, which was not resisted. The applicant’s case required a proof and the lodging of written submissions. The respondent resisted the application successfully. Again, the ordinary rule should apply and the applicant should bear the respondent’s expenses.

[7] Rule 92 of the Scottish Land Court Rules 2014 does not affect the appropriate disposal of expenses as a matter of principle or entitlement. The fact that a party has been assisted by a lay representative, whether remunerated or otherwise, does not of itself preclude an award of expenses in that party’s favour where such an award is otherwise justified. Questions as to the appropriate level of recovery, including the application of Rule 92(2) or (3), the identification of work properly attributable to the party litigant, and the exclusion of any possibility of double recovery, are matters for the Auditor of Court in the taxation of any account which may be lodged, all in accordance with the rules and established practice.

[8] The respondent moved for an additional charge in terms of Rule 5(2) of the Taxation of Judicial Expenses Rules 2019. We are not satisfied that any of the statutory heads relied upon have been made out. When set against cases routinely argued before this Court, this application was unexceptional in its factual scope, legal difficulty and procedural demands, and nothing in its conduct warrants the allowance of an uplift.

[9] In respect of head (a), we do not consider that the proceedings involved the degree of complexity, difficulty or novelty which would justify an uplift. The issues at proof turned on the evidence concerning whether an enlargement had occurred during the road realignment works. That was a fact sensitive inquiry of the kind routinely encountered in croft boundary disputes and did not involve complex statutory construction or novel legal argument. In respect of head (b), although crofting law is a specialised field and the respondent’s solicitor discharged his duties, if we may say so, with distinction, nothing in the work undertaken by him in this case required skill or knowledge beyond that ordinarily expected of a solicitor practising before this Court. The case did not require unusual expertise nor did it impose an exceptional burden of preparation. In respect of head (c), while the documentation lodged by parties was not insubstantial, it was not exceptional in the context of a boundary or first registration challenge. The volume and nature of the productions fell within the normal range for a proof of this kind and do not justify an uplift. In respect of head (d), the fact that the proof diet was held in Stornoway and required travel does not of itself warrant an additional charge. It is inherent to the work of this Court that it sits in remote locations throughout the crofting counties and we eschew firmly any suggestion that that fact should form any basis for making litigation more expensive for the paying party. Hearings remote from agents’ offices are commonplace in this forum and, while they may, in appropriate cases, entail additional recoverable outlays in terms of overnight accommodation and travel, they do not constitute a special circumstance for the purposes of Rule 5(2). In respect of head (e), although the proceedings were undoubtedly important to the respondent, particularly in relation to his reputation and long standing involvement in the croft, such personal significance does not elevate the case to the level of unusual importance contemplated by the rule. In respect of head (f), no evidence was led as to the financial value of the disputed areas and nothing suggests that the property interests at stake were of such magnitude as to justify an uplift: to the contrary, the disputed subjects were modest in extent and not obviously of significant monetary value. In respect of head (g), while the respondent submits that he took steps to limit the issues in dispute, we are not satisfied that the steps narrated were either unusual or such as to warrant an uplift.

[10] In all the circumstances, the appropriate disposal in respect of parties’ respective motions for expenses is that there be no expenses due to or by either party.
parties: Donald Norman MacLennan MacDonald Applicant against Finlay George Morrison Respondent

title: in the appeal of Graeme J Fraser Appellant against a decision of The Scottish Ministers Respondent [2026] SLC 5
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2026] SLC 5,
Case reference: SLC/8/26

OPINION OF LORD DUTHIE

Court member: Lord Duthie

in the appeal of
Graeme J Fraser
Appellant
against a decision of
The Scottish Ministers
Respondent

Applicant: Johnston, lay representative

Respondent: Young, advocate; Scottish Government Legal Directorate

13 March 2026

Introduction

[1] This is an appeal under the Rural Payment (Appeals) (Scotland) Regulations 2015 against a determination of the Scottish Ministers refusing Basic Payment Scheme eligibility for Region 3 land on the basis that the minimum activity requirement was not met. The decision challenged is contained in a letter of 19 August 2025 and in a review meeting report dated 11 December 2025.

[2] The appellant appeals on the basis that the Scottish Ministers erred in concluding that he had not met the statutory minimum activity requirement for Region 3 land, contending that the evidence he provided was sufficient to demonstrate that a lower stocking density was appropriate for the carrying capacity of the holding.

[3] The matter called for a procedural hearing in terms of Rule 59. The appellant was represented by Mr Thompson, lay representative, and the respondent by Mr Young, advocate.

The statutory framework

[4] The minimum activity requirement is set by Regulation 11 and Part 2 of Schedule 1 to the Common Agricultural Policy (Direct Payments etc.) (Scotland) Regulations 2015. For Region 2 and Region 3 land, minimum activity may be met only by one of the following routes:

stocking the land for periods totalling not less than 183 days at a stocking density of at least 0.05 livestock units per hectare; or

stocking at a density of less than 0.05 LU/ha, but only where the farmer demonstrates that such lower density is appropriate by reference to either historic records kept in respect of the carrying capacity of the holding or an environmental management agreement or agri‑environment commitment; or

carrying out an annual environmental assessment in accordance with the components specified in the Schedule.

The proposed grounds of appeal

[5] The appellant concedes that the Region 3 parcels were stocked at less than 0.05 LU/ha; that no flock or herd records exist for the hill unit prior to 2024, the land having historically been managed for sporting use; that he is not party to any relevant environmental management agreement; and that no annual environmental assessment was carried out. He contends, however, that other evidence establishes that a lower stocking density is appropriate for the land’s carrying capacity. He relies on wording in the Basic Payment Scheme guidance which states that a lower stocking density may be accepted where it is “justified by evidence … or other evidence in respect of the carrying capacity of the holding”. He submits that this permitted him to demonstrate appropriateness of a stocking rate below 0.05 LU/ha by reference to the inspection officer’s observations, photographs, land capability classifications, altitude and environmental description, and a 2012 stocking‑rate analysis carried out by the James Hutton Institute for comparable Land Capability for Agriculture classes and regions.

[6] The appellant also complains of procedural unfairness, noting that he was not asked for historic records and that the reason for deduction emerged late.

The respondent’s position

[7] Counsel for the respondent adopted his Note of Argument dated 23 February 2026. The court should refuse the application in terms of Rule 60 in respect that the proposed grounds disclose no realistic prospect that the decision could be changed or set aside. The 2015 Regulations prescribe the statutory requirements for eligibility. Taking the appellant’s case at its highest, none are here met. Guidance cannot alter the statutory eligibility requirements. The James Hutton Institute report is not an historic record kept in respect of the carrying capacity of this holding. The fairness points, taken at their highest, cannot convert ineligible land into eligible land where the statutory preconditions are not satisfied.

Decision

[8] This appeal turns on a short point. Did the appellant meet the statutory minimum activity test? The Ministers decided that he did not. He challenges that conclusion. At this stage I am concerned, not with determining the ultimate merits of the appeal, rather, with whether the grounds disclose a basis upon which the decision might realistically be expected to be changed or set aside. If I am not satisfied as to that sufficiency, I must refuse the appeal: Rule 60.

[9] It is not disputed that stocking was below 0.05 LU/ha, or that no annual environmental assessment was performed. No agri‑environment commitment or environmental management agreement exists in respect of these parcels, and none was suggested. Accordingly, the only route that remained open to the appellant was to demonstrate that the lower density was appropriate by reference to historic records kept in respect of the carrying capacity of the holding. That would require the materials relied upon to be habile to constitute historic records kept in respect of the carrying capacity of the holding.

[10] The materials relied on comprise inspection officer observations; photographs; land capability classifications; altitude and environmental description; and the 2012 James Hutton Institute stocking‑rate analysis. The photographs and the inspection officer’s observations may, taken at their highest, tend to confirm that the ground is of poor grazing quality. They are not, however, historic records of carrying capacity kept for this holding.

[11] The land capability classifications, altitude and habitat descriptions are descriptors of inherent land characteristics. They are not historic records of carrying capacity kept for this particular holding. They do not evidence what the holding has historically supported nor do they constitute a documented carrying‑capacity record maintained for the unit.

[12] The James Hutton Institute report is a national analytical study deriving area‑weighted average stocking rates by LCA class and region using IACS and census sources for 2009. It is not a record produced or kept by the appellant or his predecessors. It is not a record of the carrying capacity of this holding. It is an external, aggregated research output describing typical or average stocking patterns across classes and regions at a point in time.

[13] The appellant’s reliance on guidance language that mentions “other evidence” cannot assist him. The statutory eligibility criteria require demonstration by reference to historic carrying capacity records of the holding or to an environmental agreement. There is no freestanding “other evidence” route permitted by the Regulations. Guidance cannot amend, enlarge or dilute the statutory test. To the extent that guidance might ever be seen to use broader language, it must be read conform to the Regulations and cannot be taken to create a fourth route.

[14] The appellant complains that he was not asked for historic records and that reasons were given late. Even taking these complaints at their highest, they do not create a realistic prospect of reduction or remittal. Eligibility for payment turns on the substantive statutory criteria. These complaints concern administrative handling rather than the statutory test. Where, as here, the appellant does not say that qualifying historic carrying capacity records exist and were overlooked, and where no environmental agreement or annual assessment is suggested, such complaints cannot produce a different lawful outcome. No further procedure could supply evidence which the appellant himself says does not exist.

Disposal

[15] The grounds of appeal do not disclose any realistic prospect that the decision could be changed or set aside. The appeal is refused.

title: Colin Niall Kennedy Applicants against The Crofting Commission Respondent [2026] SLC 4
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2026] SLC 4,
Case reference: SLC/56/25

NOTE

Court member: Lord Duthie

Colin Niall Kennedy
Applicants
against
The Crofting Commission
Respondent

Subjects: 2 Arinagour

The Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993

Applicants: Sutherland, advocate; E Thornton & Co

Respondent: Thomson KC; The Crofting Commission

4 March 2026

Introduction

[1] This is an appeal under section 52A of the Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993 against the decision of the respondent dated 7 May 2025 to grant only in part the appellant’s application under sections 24(3) and 25(1)(a) of the 1993 Act for a decrofting direction in respect of 2.224 hectares of ground forming part of Croft 2, Arinagour. The respondent granted a decrofting direction only for a reduced area of 0.48 hectares.

[2] The appellant challenges the decision on the basis that the respondent (i) failed to take into account relevant and material considerations; (ii) erred in law; (iii) exercised its statutory discretion unreasonably or irrationally; (iv) failed to give proper and adequate reasons; and (v) acted under a procedure inconsistent with its standing orders and in a manner said to amount to procedural irregularity.

[3] The matter called for a hearing in terms of Rule 59 of the Rules of the Scottish Land Court 2014. Mr Sutherland, advocate appeared for the appellant and Mr Thomson KC for the respondent. Senior counsel for the respondent invited me to refuse the appeal in terms of Rule 60 on the basis that it discloses no colourable basis upon which the respondent’s decision of 7 May 2025 intimated on 4 June 2025 could reasonably be expected to be varied or set aside.

Submissions for the appellant

[4] Counsel for the appellant submitted that the decision is vitiated by error of law, failures in reasoning, failures to take into account relevant considerations, and unreasonableness. The respondent, it is said, failed properly to address the application before it which sought decrofting of land for a proposed development of five houses forming part of a wider Potential Development Area PDA 4/3. The respondent wrongly focused on a single house site associated with planning permission reference 22/00415/PPP rather than on the whole area and the purpose for which decrofting was sought. It failed to take into account (i) prior planning permissions in principle to the east and west of the site; (ii) the Masterplan Statement prepared at the direction of the planning authority; (iii) the planning authority’s designation of the land as PDA 4/3; and (iv) the fact that the Masterplan and the planning permission contemplate a coherent development of four or five units. It failed to give proper and adequate reasons for departing from the application as made, failed to assess the statutory factors in section 25(1)(a) in relation to the application for five houses and unreasonably restricted its reasoning to the merits of a single house site. No reasonable decision maker could have adopted this approach. The respondent has no policy requiring full planning permission before decrofting can be granted. The reasoning expressed in the decision letter is erroneous insofar as it suggests otherwise. The respondent failed to consider the statutory provisions governing reasonable purpose, public interest and the balancing exercise required by its own Policy Plan.

[5] The appellant also founded on Additional Condition 7, attached by the planning authority to permission 22/00415/PPP, requiring that not less than 25% of the dwellings identified in the approved Masterplan be affordable housing, submitting that this condition supported the coherence and public interest of the wider development and told against a piecemeal approach to decrofting. Counsel for the appellant also advanced an argument based on alleged procedural irregularity submitting that the respondent’s standing orders require minutes to be taken of Board meetings including regulatory decisions. The respondent failed to take any minute of the discussion or decision at the meeting of 7 May 2025. No detailed decision note or grounds were prepared, circulated or approved before issuing the decision letter of 4 June 2025. The decision letter appears to have been drafted by officials and possibly revised by the respondent’s solicitor without Board approval. Counsel founded on the respondent’s chief executive’s report of 14 May 2025, approved at a special meeting on 22 May 2025, which acknowledged that Tier 3 regulatory decisions are meetings of the Board that ought to be minuted and recommended amendments to the Scheme of Delegation, submitting that this demonstrated that the procedure employed on 7 May 2025 had already been recognised by the respondent itself as inconsistent with its standing orders. These matters were said to render the decision unlawful.

Submissions for the respondent

[6] Senior counsel for the respondent submitted that none of the grounds of appeal disclose any colourable basis for interfering with the decision and that the appeal should be refused in limine. The appellant advances two broad categories of ground: judicial review type criticisms of the merits and reasons of the decision and allegations of procedural irregularity. Neither has merit. The respondent addressed itself to the correct statutory test under section 25(1) of the 1993 Act. That test confers a broad discretion. The decision reached was one plainly open to the respondent. Its consideration of planning permission was lawful. There is no failure to take account of relevant matters or error of law. The appellant’s focus on standing orders and minute taking is misconceived. The decision under appeal was the decision taken by the full Board on 7 May 2025. The written decision letter of 4 June 2025 is merely the intimation of that decision. It is the act of intimation not the internal drafting process that engages appeal rights under Rule 58. Amendments to the Scheme of Delegation approved on 22 May 2025 founded upon by the appellant have no relevance to a decision taken on 7 May 2025. The appellant’s application, being one made by a commissioner, was necessarily determined by the full Board. There was no statutory or legal obligation to minute the decision in any particular manner nor any procedural requirement that was not met. The written reasons issued accurately reflect the respondent’s decision.

Decision

[7] At this stage the court’s task is not to determine the ultimate merits of the appeal but to decide whether the grounds advanced disclose a basis upon which the respondent’s decision may reasonably be expected to be changed or set aside: Rule 59. If after due consideration I am not satisfied as to the sufficiency of the grounds set out in the statement of grounds of appeal the appeal falls to be refused: Rule 60.

[8] The appellant contends that the respondent failed to take into account relevant planning history, the masterplan and the PDA designation and that it misunderstood the application as being for a single house. However, the decision letter records that the wider area is covered by the appellant’s masterplan and lies largely within a PDA and that planning permission exists for one plot within that larger area. The respondent decided to grant decrofting for that plot only and gave its reasons for doing so. That is a lawful exercise of the discretion conferred under section 25(1)(a) of the 1993 Act. Nothing in the statutory scheme requires the respondent to grant decrofting for all units at once. I note the respondent’s explicit statement that it remains open to the appellant to apply for decrofting of the remaining areas once planning applications for those individual sites are obtained. This makes plain that the respondent has not rejected the wider five house concept, rather, it has adopted a phased approach tied to planning progress. That explanation is a complete answer to the appellant’s criticisms of unreasonableness and failure to consider relevant matters. Further, Additional Condition 7 does not oblige the Commission to decroft the entirety of the land now, and it is consistent with the Commission’s stated position that any further decrofting can follow once the respective house sites advance to application stage.

[9] A decision maker must give reasons which leave the informed reader and the court in no real and substantial doubt as to the basis for the decision reached and the material considerations taken into account and which do not rest upon any error of law, misunderstanding of fact or failure to take account of a relevant matter: Wordie Property Co Ltd v Secretary of State for Scotland 1984 SLT 345 per Lord President Emslie at 348. The reasons given by the respondent centre on the existence of planning permission for one plot and the absence of planning applications for the remainder. They are intelligible and adequate for the purpose of explaining the decision appealed against. The appellant evidently disagrees with the weight assigned to particular factors, however, disagreement with weight does not of itself found a valid ground of appeal.

[10] The appellant also alleges procedural irregularity based on the absence of a minute of the Board’s discussion and on the preparation of the written decision by officials. I am satisfied that this complaint is without merit. The decision appealed against is the decision taken at the Board meeting on 7 May 2025. The letter of 4 June 2025 is merely the intimation of that decision. As at 7 May 2025 neither the 1993 Act nor the respondent’s procedures imposed any requirement that a particular form of minute be created as a condition of validity. Amendments to the Scheme of Delegation approved on 22 May 2025 were not retrospective in effect and cannot bear on the validity of a decision taken on 7 May 2025. In any event, the appellant identifies no prejudice arising from the form or absence of a minute and none is apparent.

[11] I am accordingly unable to identify any legal error, failure to take account of a material consideration, irrationality or procedural unfairness which could justify setting aside or altering the decision appealed against. The grounds advanced do not disclose a basis upon which the respondent’s decision may reasonably be expected to be changed or set aside. I refuse the appeal in terms of Rule 60.

title: Donald Norman MacLennan MacDonald Applicant against Finlay George Morrison Respondent [2026] SLC 3
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2026] SLC 3,
Case reference: SLC/16/24

OPINION OF THE COURT

Court members: Lord Duthie,
Mr T Campbell

Donald Norman MacLennan MacDonald
Applicant
against
Finlay George Morrison
Respondent

Crofting Register: Challenge to first registration

Croft 1 Ardvourlie

Applicant: Kermack, Lay Representative

Respondent: Rudd, Solicitor; Murchison Law

13 February 2026

Introduction

[1] Ardvourlie is a crofting township on the Isle of Harris, comprising two crofts and a common grazing. The applicant is the tenant of Croft 2, which does not appear on the Crofting Register. The respondent is the tenant of the neighbouring Croft 1 which is registered in the Crofting Register under number C770. Croft 1 was first registered in December 2014 on the application of the landlord, the North Harris Trust.

[2] The applicant seeks an order under section 14(4) of the Crofting Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 modifying the entry in the Crofting Register, contending that Croft 1 was registered with substantially enhanced boundaries so that it wrongly includes an area of land at the route of the former public road lying between the two crofts and the new A859 public road (land for which was resumed in 2004).

[3] By interlocutor dated 23 May 2024, the Court exercised its discretion in terms of section 12(5) of the 2010 Act, on cause shown, to allow this application to be dealt with as if it had been made before the end of the statutory 9 month period in respect that the applicant’s failure to make this application timeously - and lack of knowledge until 2023 of the fact of first registration of Croft 1 - was excusable in respect that he did not receive notification, either of the application for registration or of the registration itself.

[4] Other than in respect of one small area of ground, the respondent opposes the application.

[5] A diet of proof was held at Stornoway Sheriff Court in October 2025. The Court also took evidence of some witnesses at Ardvourlie and carried out a sight inspection. The applicant was represented by Mr Kermack, a retired solicitor acting on this occasion as a duly authorised lay representative. Mr Rudd, solicitor appeared for the respondent. Following the proof diet parties lodged supplementary written submissions.

[6] The plan which accompanied the 2014 application by the landlord for first registration of Croft 1 divides Croft 1 into three areas and shows the route of the new public road which was constructed in the period 2004 ‑ 2007 and runs between Areas 1 and 2 (on the east side of the road) and Area 3 (on the west side of the road). Area 3 denotes the apportionment to Croft 1 from the common grazings and is not controversial for present purposes. A detail of that plan appears below:

Figure 1 – Detail from plan from 2014 application for first registration of Croft 1

[7] A further plan was lodged by the applicant as his production 20 which is helpful in illustrating the areas in dispute. A detail of that plan is reproduced at Figure 2 below.

Figure 2 – Detail from applicant’s production 20

[8] Mr Kermack explained (and it was not disputed) that the areas outlined in red in Figure 2 are a projection of the boundaries contained on Figure 1, superimposed on the 1973 Ordnance Survey map for Ardvourlie, which map dates from some three decades before construction of the new road. Three areas are shaded blue on the Figure 2, two within the northern-most section outlined in red (which corresponds with Area 1 on Figure 1) and one in the southern-most section outlined in red (which corresponds with Area 2 on Figure 1). The applicant contends that the three areas shaded blue were wrongly included with the registered extent of Croft 1. The smallest of the blue shaded areas is within the northern-most section and is Kosiden house and garden (“Kosiden”). Parties agree that Kosiden was wrongly included within the registered extent of Croft 1, having previously been resumed from crofting in 1963, and accordingly should be removed from the Crofting Register. The dispute between parties relates to the two remaining areas shaded blue, referred to hereinafter respectively as the NDA (the Northernmost Disputed Area) and the SDA (the Southernmost Disputed Area) (together, the “Disputed Areas”).

[9] Parties disagree as to whether the registered boundaries of Croft 1 accurately reflect the current legal boundaries of Croft 1, including historic enlargements.

The applicant’s case in summary

[10] The applicant seeks removal of the NDA and the SDA from the registered extent of Croft 1 on the basis that the true extent of Croft 1 comprises only the following three areas:

The subjects shown on the Land Court order and plan dated 26 September 1922 (production number 1), which shows Croft 1 (then referred to as “1 Bowglass”) as a single yellow‑outlined enclosure extending to approximately 8 acres (the “Original Subjects”);

Figure 3 - Detail of plan referred to in Land Court order dated 26 September 1922

The 1965 enlargement (the “Reseedings”). (The applicant relies on correspondence dated between April and October 1965 between Douglas Kesting and the crofters commission, which records the landlord’s agreement to let to the then crofter “an area of ground adjoining the main public road extending to some 8.6 acres or thereby which has already been reseeded by Mr Morrison.” The applicant submits that this description corresponds precisely to the fenced enclosure shown on the 1973 Ordnance Survey map (production number 17), lying east of the pre‑2004 public road.); and

The 1995 Apportionment (Area 3 on Figure 1 above) which allocates 23.900 hectares of common grazing to Croft 1 (the “1995 Apportionment”); less the following two areas:

Kosiden, which was the subject of a 1963 resumption (see applicant's production number 4); and

the subjects decrofted in 1999 (the original croft house site) (see applicant's production number 6).

[11] The Court should accordingly modify the registration so that it reflects the Original Subjects, under exception of the 1963 resumption and the 1999 decrofting, together with the 1995 Apportionment, and the Reseedings. The Disputed Areas, which are associated with the former public road and its verges, are not part of Croft 1. There was no lawful enlargement of Croft 1 associated with the old roadway and the construction of a new roadway.

The respondent’s position in outline

[12] Kosiden and the original croft house site do not form part of Croft 1. Kosiden was erroneously wrongly included in the registered extent of Croft 1 at first registration and should be removed. Quoad ultra the registered boundaries are correct. Croft 1 comprises the Original Subjects, the Reseedings, the 1995 Apportionment plus the Disputed Areas which are the subjects of a further enlargement associated with the old roadway following the re‑routing of the Stornoway to Tarbert road during the period 2004 to 2007. Esto evidence of any element is deficient, the Court should declare the registered boundary to be the appropriate boundary in terms of section 14(6) having regard to long‑standing physical demarcation, occupation and subsequent administrative acts.

Statutory framework

[13] Section 14 of Crofting Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 empowers the Court, on an application challenging first registration, to make an order that the entry be removed or modified, or to make no order. Where an application raises a question as to the boundaries of a croft but the evidence is insufficient to enable any boundary to be clearly determined, section 14(5) and (6) require the Court, if making an order to modify, to declare the boundary to be that which, in all the circumstances, it considers appropriate.

[14] The Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993 governs how crofts are constituted and how they may be enlarged. Prior to 25 June 2007, section 4 provided that where the owner of land which was not itself a croft, and did not form part of a croft, agreed to let that land to a crofter, the land became part of the crofter’s existing croft on the date of entry if the parties agreed to that. However, if the combined area of the croft and the additional land was more than 30 hectares, and the combined rent was more than £100, the inclusion also required a direction from the Crofters Commission. The Commission could give such a direction only if the addition would benefit the croft and would not result in a croft substantially larger than 30 hectares or capable of being let at a rent substantially higher than £100 per year. After 25 June 2007, the rent threshold was removed, so that only the 30 hectare area threshold remained relevant to whether the Commission required to be involved.

Documents and plans

[15] The principal documents relevant to the boundaries and their evolution are:

The Land Court order of 26 September 1922 (County of Inverness RN3637) with plan, constituting the new holdings numbered 1 and 2.

The Land Court order of 27 May 1963 (County of Inverness RN10950) authorising resumption of 0.117 acres for the house site now known as Kosiden, with plan.

The decrofting direction dated 7 October 1999 in respect of the original croft house and garden.

The apportionment order of 15 June 1995 in favour of Croft 1.

Correspondence in 1965 between the landlord’s solicitor and the Crofters Commission relating to enlargement by addition of the reseeded land adjoining the then public road, giving an extent of about 8.6 acres and recording entry as at Martinmas 1965 and an increase in rent.

Ordnance Survey mapping from the early 1970s showing the route of the then public road and fenced enclosures.

The materials submitted at first registration in 2014, including the form A and plan prepared for the landlord.

Commission and landlord correspondence in 2013 to 2015 relating to the nomination and letting of Croft 1 to the respondent.

Witness evidence

[16] The Court heard evidence from the applicant and Mrs Macleod for the applicant; and from the respondent, Mr McSween, Ms Campbell, Mr Macleod, Mr Smith, Mr Maciver and Mrs Morrison for the respondent. All witnesses that gave evidence adopted the terms of their witness statements. No issues of credibility arise: we accept that all were seeking to give truthful evidence from their respective perspectives. Much of the evidence led was not ultimately significant to the question around which this dispute centres, that is to say, whether Croft 1 was enlarged during the period 2004-2007.

Evidence led for the applicant

[17] The applicant gave evidence and adduced evidence from Morag Macleod.

The applicant’s evidence

[18] The applicant inherited the tenancy of Croft 2 in 1999. A boundary dispute arose in 2023 when he proposed to replace perimeter fencing along the upper boundary of his croft adjacent to the disused former public road, which was superseded by a new road constructed around 2004. He believed neighbouring crofters had extended fencing into the disused road area and considered that he should be able to do likewise.

[19] In April and May 2023 he discussed boundaries with the respondent, who maintained that the two Disputed Areas formed part of Croft 1. He asked for supporting paperwork or maps but none were produced. At a site meeting the respondent showed a map which did not depict the Disputed Areas as part of Croft 1 and described the ground as “no man’s land”. He later discovered that Croft 1 had been registered in 2014, at a time when he had sublet Croft 2 to the respondent. He emphasised that he had received no notification of the application for registration or of the registration itself.

[20] The applicant spoke to a number of matters predating 2003 arising from his historical researches. Those events are not material to the question requiring determination, which is whether a landlord and crofter agreement occurred during the 2004 to 2007 road works. The boundaries of Croft 1 prior to that period are not in dispute

[21] The applicant obtained historic Ordnance Survey mapping and the Crofting Register extract and arranged for projection of the registered boundaries onto the 1973 map. He considered that this showed that Kosiden and the two Disputed Areas were wrongly included within the registered extent of Croft 1 and that the 1995 Apportionment was correctly plotted. He has identified no documentation in Crofting Commission files, correspondence or the Register of Crofts indicating any enlargement after 1995.

[22] During cross examination he accepted that he had never used, needed access to, or possessed the Disputed Areas. He regarded them as “no man’s land” that it “would be nice to have”. His interest is limited to the blue shaded area immediately above his croft. His application had initially challenged the inclusion of a larger area. He is unsure why he has restricted his position. He accepts that the 2014 registration materials show that the landlord proceeded on the basis of the boundaries as registered and that the Trust had not been asked to rectify or modify the entry.

[23] He observed what he believed to be boundary extensions or new fences erected by crofters at Bowglass up to the new road but did not discuss this with the respondent. He accepted there was a fence around the Reseedings and that he had had no discussions about it. The registered extent of Croft 1 does not affect his ability to move livestock, as he uses a trailer and his vehicular access is unaffected. He had been in communication with the Crofting Commission before applying to the Court but could not recall the details. His understanding of the boundaries developed over the course of the application as historical material came to light. He told North Harris Trust he would like the piece of land at the top of his croft and was told the matter was one for the Land Court.

Mrs Macleod’s evidence

[24] Mrs Macleod has lived in Ardvourlie all her life and now resides at Glenisle, a feu taken from Croft 2. She grew up in the croft house on Croft 2 and walked daily along what was then a single track public road. On the seaward side of that road there was a roadside fence which, in her recollection, ran from the corner of Mulag House towards a point just short of the culvert over the burn through Croft 2 and then tied into Croft 2 on the far side of the burn. That fence remained in the same position throughout her lifetime until the construction of the new road after the millennium. She spoke to various matters of local history, which are not material to the question requiring determination.

[25] Reseeding work on Croft 2 involved the spreading of sand (used as a conditioner and liming agent) on an old disused track near the croft entrance. This was carried out by family members with assistance from Donald John Morrison, the then crofter of Croft 1. The adjoining enclosure known locally as the Reseedings did not extend beyond the roadside fence and did not cross the burn or its culvert. Sand for that reseeding was deposited just inside a gate on the public roadside. Locally the Reseedings were not regarded as part of Croft 1.

[26] Peat cutting took place on land across the old public road and peats were stacked there before being transported home by hand. Movement between the croft house and the public road was not impeded because the roadside fence terminated at the far side of the burn. During the new road works, contractors removed the old fence and erected a new fence adjacent to the new road. In oral evidence she recalled that, when she was at school, the original fence lay on the south side of the watercourse and that the replacement fence did not follow the same line. She had no knowledge as to whether the Disputed Area had been added to Croft 1.

[27] The respondent gave evidence and adduced evidence from Ian McSween, Miranda Campbell, Alistair Macleod, Mark Smith, Alasdair Morrison, Michael Hunter, Colin Maciver and Catherine Morrison.

The respondent’s evidence

[28] The respondent was born in 1972. He is the tenant of Croft 1, having succeeded his uncle, Murdo Morrison, following Murdo’s death in 2010. His entry as tenant was recorded in the Register of Crofts in January 2015. Croft 1 comprises the Original Subjects, the roadside enclosure added in 1965 known as the Reseedings, the 1995 Apportionment and the Disputed Areas lying adjacent to the former public road.

[29] The Reseedings have formed part of Croft 1 since 1965, and their boundaries are reflected in long‑standing fences which, to the respondent’s knowledge, have not changed since at least the 1970s. During the period when Croft 2 was sublet to the respondent, neither he nor Murdo Morrison treated any part of the Reseedings as belonging to Croft 2.

[30] The Disputed Areas became part of Croft 1 when the public road was rerouted between about 2005 and 2007. Fences erected during the works enclosed those areas and remain in that position. The realignment works proceeded with the knowledge of Murdo Morrison and the landlord, and the enclosed areas have been possessed and worked with Croft 1 since at least 2007. Removal of the Disputed Areas would impede access to the Reseedings.

[31] The landlord submitted the 2014 application for first registration and relied on a plan prepared by SAC which followed the fences then present on the ground. The landlord accepted that fence based plan and used it for registration. The respondent understood the landlord and his predecessor as crofter to have proceeded on the shared basis that the fence lines represented the true extent of the croft. The inclusion of Kosiden was an unnoticed error.

[32] Public notice of registration was given by newspaper advertisement and a site notice. The applicant would, in any event, have been aware long before 2023 of the boundaries as physically occupied and of the extent later reflected in the Register.

[33] A decrofting direction in 2023 in respect of part of the former roadway area enabled the erection of the respondent’s house. The site was purchased from the landlord, and a dwellinghouse has now been constructed on the footing that the land formed part of Croft 1. The landlord continues to proceed on that basis. Were any part of the disputed ground held not to form part of Croft 1, the respondent would seek enlargement with the landlord’s support.

[34] Passages of the respondent’s evidence concerned fencing carried out in the 1990s by his uncle, family discussions about boundaries, and the limitations of historic plans. Those matters are peripheral and not relevant to the issue requiring determination.

[35] The respondent’s understanding of the current extent of Croft 1 derives from discussions within the family, including conversations with Murdo and Finlay Morrison, and from the fact that the fence lines present at the time of succession had long been treated by his predecessors as the operational boundaries. Maps were accepted as potentially imperfect, but the fences on the ground were regarded as determinative in practice. No fence lines have been moved during his tenure.

Ian McSween’s evidence

[36] Mr Ian McSween, born in 1949, is a lifelong resident of Scaladale and a crofter. He is familiar with both the old public road and the new one and has known successive crofters of Croft 1, including Murdo Morrison, Donald John Morrison and earlier members of the family.

[37] The respondent told him that he regarded the areas of the former roadway as having become part of Croft 1 following the rerouting of the public road. Mr McSween himself used the surface of the old roadway for loading sheep for transport because its condition made access straightforward.

[38] He recalled reseeding work at Scaladale in the early 1960s and understood that reseeding at Ardvourlie occurred around the same period. In his understanding, crofters affected by the realignment had taken in the additional areas lying between the old and new road fences, including parts of the former roadway. Murdo Morrison told him that Croft 1 had been enlarged as a consequence of the realignment.

[39] The applicant visited him in either 2023 or 2024, prior to the commencement of these proceedings, to ask about the boundary between the crofts. Mr McSween advised the applicant not to fall out with the respondent over the matter. He knows the applicant and the applicant’s family but has had no further involvement. He rejected any suggestion of “land grabbing”, describing such suggestions as “absolute rubbish”.

Miranda Campbell’s evidence

[40] Ms Campbell resides at Kosiden, now known as Seaforth, purchased with her late husband in 2000. She is the tenant crofter of croft 1 Bowglass, a tenancy previously held by her husband until his death in 2022.

[41] Between about 2003 and 2006 the widening and rerouting of the A859 caused significant disruption to croft 1 Bowglass, croft 1 North Bowglass and Croft 1 Ardvourlie. Comhairle nan Eilean Siar took land out of the Bowglass Common Grazings for the new road and embankments and, as a planning condition, fenced the common grazings from the new road. Rock spoil was deposited on croft 1 Bowglass and later covered with topsoil which subsequently washed off, altering drainage and leaving the lower part of the croft boggy. Rock spoil was also deposited on Croft 1 Ardvourlie in the area now occupied by the Norpower compound.

[42] A strip of land about the width of the old single track road was added to croft 1 Bowglass as compensation for disturbance.

[43] Her late husband dealt with all discussions with the Comhairle and she was not involved in detail. Her understanding is that an area of the old roadway was added to the Croft 1, although she does not know the detail of any discussions or agreements. Her only interest in the registered extent of Croft 1 Ardvourlie is that Kosiden, her house site, be removed from the registration. The respondent has not been a source of difficulty to her and she regards him and his wife as good neighbours. After this application commenced, the respondent informed her that her house had been included in the registered extent of his croft and undertook to have that error corrected.

Alistair Macleod’s evidence

[44] Mr Macleod was manager of North Harris Trust from 2013, having previously served as development officer from 2002. The respondent was ultimately nominated as tenant of Croft 1 after a period of vacancy following Murdo Morrison’s death.

[45] Mr Macleod submitted the registration application for Croft 1 in September 2014 on behalf of the landlord. The plan used for that application was prepared to follow the fences then present on the ground. In completing the application, he relied on information provided by the respondent as to boundaries. He did not investigate the historic evolution of the boundary, he did not scrutinise adjacent croft boundaries, and his working assumption was that crofters knew their own boundaries.

[46] The plan accompanying the application included areas of old roadway surface. Mr Macleod does not recall any discussion with the respondent about that particular feature, his understanding being that such operational matters would have been addressed during the road works between crofters and the Comhairle. He did not turn his mind to whether the inclusion of those areas reflected a prior legal enlargement.

[47] Kosiden should not have been included in the registration, it having been resumed in 1963. Mr Macleod did not know that at the time of submitting the application.

Mark Smith’s evidence

[48] Mr Mark Smith gave evidence by telephone from Madeira. He was formerly a resident engineer in the technical services department of Comhairle nan Eilean Siar and was involved throughout the project to reroute and upgrade the A859 between 2004 and 2007.

[49] When the new road was constructed, the Comhairle agreed to position the new fence line between the new road and the surface of the old single track roadway. Land that was not required for the scheme would ordinarily be returned, as the old roadway surface was of no use to the Comhairle. The fence line represented the minimum land take and was pegged out and agreed with crofters before erection. At Croft 1 Ardvourlie the old road surface was left unbroken at the request of Murdo Morrison, who had previously had a garage on the route of the then proposed new road which required to be demolished.

[50] Mr Smith had been shown a memorandum dated 9 May 2007, with an attached letter from the trust’s solicitor dated 8 May 2007, referring to the erection of the fence, together with a further memorandum concerning a meeting dated 25 June 2007. He accepted that although the memo was not issued on the same date as the meeting, it was possible that the meeting took place on 25 June and that the memo followed the usual practice of being sent out immediately.

[51] Land take plans were settled in advance with landlords and crofters, and amendments were made as required when the works were completed. Old road surfaces were normally broken up, reinstated with peat and returned to crofts or the estate once the Comhairle ceased occupation. Vacating the areas occupied depended on completion of reinstatement. Mr Smith did not know when, if at all, the old road was formally adopted.
