[52] Mr Smith is not a specialist in crofting law. Croft boundaries were, in his understanding, a matter for the Trust as landlord. The fence erected by the Comhairle served to indicate the minimum land required for the works. The final fence line was pegged out and agreed with crofters and could, depending on stage, reflect the outcome of a resumption process. In relation to landscaping, the usual reinstatement was to break up the old surface and cover it with peat, but at Croft 1 Ardvourlie the old surface was left at Murdo Morrison’s request. Any departure from the standard reinstatement practice would have been agreed with Scottish Natural Heritage.

Alasdair Morrison’s evidence

[53] Alasdair Morrison is the tenant crofter of - and resides at - Croft 2, Bowglass, which was previously his grandparents’ croft. He has lived there since the age of 12, apart from a short period living away.

[54] He recalls the rerouting of the A859 in around 2004 to 2007 but does not remember exact dates. At Bowglass the new road was built through the common grazings. The Comhairle deposited gravel onto his croft and used it to cover the old road surface, then covered the gravel to some degree with soil. The Comhairle’s fencers removed the old fence and moved it up to the new road. If the fence had not been moved there would have been a large unused space between the fence and the road. Something similar happened at Croft 1 Bowglass and Croft 1 Ardvourlie, which were similarly affected by the road works. Murdo Morrison was the crofter at Croft 1 Ardvourlie at the time. Murdo asked the Comhairle to deposit spoil where the Norpower installation now stands. Beyond that, he has no specific knowledge of the croft boundary at Croft 1 Ardvourlie.

[55] He regards the present dispute as “ridiculous” and disputes over small pieces of ground as “pointless”.

Michael Hunter’s evidence

[56] Mr Hunter was born in 1988 and became manager of North Harris Trust in March 2020. Croft 1 Ardvourlie was registered before his time as manager. He met with the crofters in 2023 prior to commencement of the present application, but that meeting did not resolve matters.

[57] He signed a letter on behalf of North Harris Trust to Finlay Morrison dated 14 August 2025 (respondent’s production 59), it having been tabled and agreed at the North Harris Trust board meeting on 11 August 2025. In it the Trust undertakes to the respondent that if for any reason the Court determines that the extent of Croft 1 has been incorrectly registered, the Trust will enlarge and re‑let the croft to the respondent, the extent of the croft to be the extent of Croft 1 as currently registered (with the exception of Kosiden).

Colin Maciver’s evidence

[58] Mr Maciver is a civil engineering manager with Comhairle nan Eilean Siar. The Comhairle’s involvement in the Aline to Ardvourlie road improvement was limited to defining the boundary of the newly constructed road. Initial land plans were prepared during the design stage to enable discussions with landowners and grazing committees. Following completion, as built fence lines were surveyed to update the plans, which revealed that sections of the old single track road lay outside the land conveyed to the Comhairle. Meetings were held with estate representatives and grazing clerks to address treatment of resumed land. Simon Fraser of Anderson Macarthur, acting for North Harris Trust, advised that a legal process existed to return resumed land to crofting tenure. It was understood that old road sections would be added to adjacent crofts, with responsibility for amending and registering croft boundaries resting with the Trust, Anderson Macarthur, the grazings committee, and croft tenants.

Catherine Morrison’s evidence

[59] Catherine Morrison resides at 1A Ardvourlie with her husband, the respondent. Existing fences on Croft 1 have remained unchanged since her husband became tenant, and are in the same position as when Murdo Morrison held the tenancy. Murdo Morrison intended to leave the croft to the respondent. Following Murdo’s death, the North Harris Trust nominated the respondent as tenant. She recalls that prior to this, the respondent sub‑let Mr MacDonald’s croft at 2 Ardvourlie to assist him when the Crofting Commission raised absenteeism concerns. The respondent acted in good faith and the fences have not moved during the period of his tenancy.

Submissions for the applicant

[60] Mr Kermack adopted his written submissions which are available in the Court process.

[61] In a section 14 application, the Court requires to determine whether the boundaries shown in the Crofting Register accurately reflect the legal boundaries of the unregistered croft, rather than boundaries of current occupation. Where the evidence allows a boundary to be clearly determined, the Court must recognise and give effect to that boundary; it has no discretion to substitute what it considers “appropriate”: Macaulay v Morrison, Scottish Land Court, unreported, 13 March 2017 at [28] and [29]. Only where section 14(6) applies, and the evidence is insufficient to allow any boundary to be identified, may the Court declare a boundary that it considers appropriate in the circumstances.

[62] In the instant case the Court should make an order under section 14(4)(b) of the 2010 Act modifying the Crofting Register entry for Croft 1 by removing the Disputed Areas so as to align the registration with the legal boundaries of Croft 1, under reference to:

the boundaries shown on the plan annexed to the Land Court order of 26 September 1922, subject to the area resumed by order of 27 May 1963 and the land decrofted by direction dated 7 October 1999;

the land apportioned by the apportionment order dated 15 June 1995; and

the fenced enclosure east of the former public road shown on the 1973 Ordnance Survey.

[63] The registered boundaries of the NDA do not reflect the legal boundaries of the unregistered croft. The correct extent of that northern section of Croft 1 is shown on the plan annexed to the Land Court order of 26 September 1922, which depicts a single enclosed holding of about 8 acres bisected by a track. The 1922 plan represents the original definitive boundary of the NDA.

[64] Correspondence dated 24 April 1957 from Stewart, Rule & Co., solicitors, to the Crofters Commission confirms that the rights of the tenants of 1 and 2 Bowglass were constituted by the final order of 26 September 1922 and that there had been no change to the extent of either croft between 1922 and 1957. That demonstrates that the registered extent of the NDA does not reflect the legal boundaries of Croft 1.

[65] The original croft house was decrofted by the direction dated 7 October 1999. The stated area of 0.304 hectares is plainly a decimal error; boundary measurements indicate an area of about 0.0304 hectares. The house site removed from crofting by this direction is wrongly included within the registered boundary of the NDA.

[66] The 1963 resumption of the Kosiden house site removed land from the NDA and did not add to it, yet the registration wrongly incorporates the entire Kosiden plot back into Croft 1.

[67] To the extent that the registered extent of the NDA includes land which was never part of Croft 1, its inclusion in the registration is an obvious error.

[68] The SDA adjoins an enlargement of Croft 1 made in 1965 of approximately 8.6 acres adjoining the then public road. The enlargement is evidenced by contemporaneous correspondence and corroborated by witness testimony regarding reseeding within a fenced enclosure.

[69] On 29 April 1965, Douglas Kesting, solicitor, wrote seeking procedural guidance on adding approximately 8 to 9 acres to Croft 1. On 28 May 1965 the Crofters Commission advised that an enlargement required intimation under section 2(2) of the 1961 Act, confirming the landlord’s agreement to let the land in enlargement of the holding. On 31 May 1965 Mr Kesting stated he would complete missives once a definitive plan was obtained and would then notify the Commission. The letter of 15 October 1965 records that an area of ground adjoining the then main public road, extending to about 8.6 acres, had been added to Croft 1 with entry at Martinmas 1965 and that the ground had already been reseeded by the crofter.

[70] Mrs Macleod’s evidence identifies the reseeding area as the fenced roadside enclosure long known locally as “the reseedings” and confirms that this was the only ground reseeded by Mr Morrison. Read as a whole, the sequence of correspondence establishes a single enlargement at the reseeding area now identified as Area 2, and this is corroborated by witness testimony.

[71] Area 3 corresponds to the 1995 Apportionment to Croft 1. Its boundaries are not disputed and the applicant seeks no order in respect of this area.

[72] There is no evidence of any enlargement of Croft 1 following construction of the new road from 2004. By 1995, the area of Croft 1 already exceeded 30 hectares (comprising the 8 acre original holding and the 8.6 acre 1965 enlargement together with the 23.9 hectare apportionment made in 1995, producing a total of approximately 30.62 hectares). Any subsequent enlargement could only take place under section 4(1)(b) of the 1993 Act, which required a joint application by landlord and crofter to the Crofting Commission and a direction from the Commission before the land could form part of the croft. No such application or direction exists and so no enlargement could have occurred during the period of the road realignment.

[73] The statutory framework required notice to the Crofting Commission of any such enlargement, or a joint application for enlargement. No such notice or record exists. The respondent’s case that there was an agreement with the landlord is unsupported and indicates, at best, tolerance rather than an implied agreement. Fencing erected during roadworks does not establish an enlargement under section 4 of the 1993 Act.

[74] In supplementary written submissions the applicant founded on section 1(9) of the Roads (Scotland) Act 1984 and on London Borough of Southwark v Transport for London [2018] UKSC 63, submitting that the former public road and its verges remained vested in the roads authority within the zone of ordinary use, and were inalienable for so long as that responsibility persisted; and accordingly, as at June 2007, the landlord had no power to agree an enlargement of Croft 1 into any part of the former roadway area.

Submissions for the respondent

[75] Mr Rudd adopted his written submissions which are available in the Court process.

[76] The onus lies on the applicant to prove that, on the balance of probabilities, the areas he seeks to remove should not form part of Croft 1. The task of the Court is to identify the status quo ante and follow it where the evidence is sufficient. Only where the evidence is insufficient does section 14(6) empower the Court to determine and impose what it considers to be an “appropriate” boundary.

[77] The only parts of the registered extent of Croft 1 now in dispute are those shaded blue on the applicant’s production 20, other than Kosiden, which parties are agreed should be removed. Quoad ultra the boundaries should remain as registered.

[78] The applicant lacks a practical interest to object to the registered boundaries of Croft 1, given that that he does not aver that the areas he seeks to have removed from Croft 1 form part of Croft 2 or of the common grazings.

[79] There is supporting evidence from multiple independent sources consistent with the respondent’s understanding of the boundary. The original holding was created in 1922. Its extent is shown in the plan appended to the Land Court order and the Board of Agriculture application.

[80] The 1995 Apportionment is uncontroversial and is properly included in Croft 1.

[81] The Reseeding Area was added to the croft in 1965. The only difference between parties in respect of this area relates to the northern extent of the reseeding area. The fenced and occupied extent of this area extends further north into part of the applicant’s blue-shaded area, and has done so since at least the 1970s and certainly since the 1990s. Esto any part of this ground does not form part of the 1965 enlargement, it was added during the later boundary adjustments associated with construction of the new road. IACS maps produced by the respondent show the areas the crofter claimed and worked, albeit these indicate usage rather than legal boundaries. With reference to the enlargement of Croft 1 during the period 2004 ‑ 2007 at the old roadway area, enlargement of a croft could occur by agreement between a landlord and a crofter in terms of section 4 of the 1993 Act as it then stood, without formal requirements for written form. The statutory notification requirement was administrative rather than constitutive. On the evidence, an agreement between landlord and crofter existed by 25 June 2007, and the croft as enlarged (excluding the common grazing) remained under 30 hectares and the rent remained under £100 per annum. The 30 hectare threshold in section 4(1)(b) of the 1993 Act as it then stood is not here engaged. The “area of the croft” for the purposes of that provision excludes any common grazing. The 23.9 hectare apportionment made in 1995 remains part of the common grazings and does not alter the extent of the in‑bye land.

[82] The fencing erected during the road re‑routing was done on the basis that the fenced area was being added to crofts in Ardvourlie and Bowglass. The evidence from their officers demonstrates that the Comhairle’s understanding was that the fenced land was being incorporated into the crofts and that the landlord’s factor participated in those discussions. Similar enlargements occurred at Bowglass. The applicant raised no issue with the fence lines before 2023 despite having been the crofter of Croft 2 since 1999.

[83] A number of outward actions evidence the existence of such an agreement, including: instructions given for fencing; what the respondent was told by Murdo Morrison; the absence of any separate occupancy arrangement; the landlord’s actions in relation to the 2014 letting, the first registration, the decrofting and disposition for the respondent’s house site, and later dealings with Norpower; and confirmation from the landlord that they understood the registered extent to be the correct extent. If, however, the Court finds that the evidence does not allow the boundaries of the alleged enlargement to be clearly determined, the Court should exercise its power under section 14(6) to declare the boundary which it considers most appropriate in all the circumstances. The current registered boundary represents the appropriate and pragmatic boundary, reflecting long‑standing de facto possession, decisions taken in reliance upon it, the concurrence of landlord and tenant and the absence of any practical benefit to the applicant from alteration.

[84] In supplementary written submissions, the respondent submitted that the Roads (Scotland) Act 1984 regulates the public management of roads and does not, by virtue of section 1(9), confer any heritable right of ownership on the roads authority. Once the new A859 was brought into use and the associated fencing was erected in 2004 and 2005, the former public road ceased to be used for its previous purpose. There is no competing title to the areas now in dispute, the North Harris Trust having acquired Title number INV29919 in 2003.

Decision and reasons

[85] In the particular circumstances of this case, determination of the precise legal boundaries of Croft 1 is, to a degree, a sterile exercise in respect that the landlord has undertaken to the respondent that, if for any reason the Court were to determine that the extent of Croft 1 had been incorrectly registered, the landlord will enlarge and re‑let the croft to the respondent at the currently registered extent (under exception of Kosiden). The practical outcome for the parties will be materially the same whether the matter is determined on the primary basis of enlargement or, failing that, on the respondent’s alternative case under section 14(6). The Court must nonetheless determine whether, as at the date of first registration in 2014, the legal boundary of Croft 1 includes the Disputed Areas.

[86] We find, on the evidence, that it does. We do so, not because of any constitutive effect of the fencing erected during the road realignment works (there is none), but rather on account of the crofter’s and landlord’s subsequent and consistent treatment of that fence line as the de facto boundary of the croft. In the context of section 4 of the 1993 Act as it then stood, enlargement did not require written form, nor any particular formality, provided that landlord and crofter reached consensus as to the subjects to be added. Such consensus may be inferred from their conduct. The sequence of outward acts (the pegging out of the fence line in consultation with the then crofter, the landlord’s engagement in the treatment of reinstated ground, the subsequent reliance on the same boundary at first registration in 2014 and the landlord’s use of that boundary in later decroftings) is consistent with a shared intention that the subjects enclosed by the fence formed part of the croft tenancy, and is inconsistent with mere tolerance or convenience.

[87] Events prior to the 21st century were ultimately uncontroversial. Croft 1 was constituted in 1922 in the terms of the Land Court’s order and plan. In 1963 Kosiden was resumed. Parties agree that Kosiden ought not to have been included at first registration and must now be removed. In 1965 there was an enlargement in favour of Croft 1 to the fenced roadside enclosure locally known as the Reseedings. In 1995 an apportionment of Area 3 was made in favour of Croft 1. The dispute between parties turns on whether there was a lawful enlargement associated with the road realignment. The Disputed Areas lie adjacent to the new A859 as defined on the ground by the fence erected during the 2004 to 2007 road works.

[88] On the evidence, and in particular the account given by Mr Smith of the pegging out and erection of the fence line during the road realignment project, we are satisfied that by the conclusion of the works in 2007 the physical boundary adjoining Croft 1 had been delineated in a manner known to, and not objected to by, the then crofter and the landlord.

[89] In assessing the competing accounts of the 2004 to 2007 period we place particular weight on the respondent’s evidence. He was a careful witness and we found him credible and reliable on the central matters. His evidence was consistent with that of the witnesses from the Trust and the Comhairle, which we also accept. We accept also the limited but consistent evidence of Mrs Morrison. By contrast, the applicant was not in a position to speak to Murdo Morrison’s dealings with the Comhairle or the landlord, and his understanding of the boundary does not derive from direct knowledge of those dealings. The available evidence, including circumstantial evidence, favours the respondent. The applicant’s lack of use of the Disputed Areas is not determinative of their legal status, but it is a further relevant adminicle when assessing the competing reconstructions of the post 2004 position, although not, for the avoidance of doubt, indicative of any diminution of rights through disuse.

[90] Section 4 of the 1993 Act, as it stood at the material time, permitted enlargement by agreement between owner and crofter, with effect from the agreed date of entry. No particular formality was prescribed where the 30 hectare threshold in section 4(1)(b) was not crossed, although notice to the Commission under section 4(4) was required thereafter. We infer from the available evidence the existence of an agreement between the landlord and the then crofter, Murdo Morrison, that the Disputed Areas would form part of Croft 1. The Trust and Murdo Morrison were evidently both content to proceed on that basis without demur. The sequence of outward acts is indicative of agreement: fence lines erected and thereafter adopted as the operational boundary; the landlord’s involvement in the 2007 discussions; the use of a fence based plan for first registration by the landlord in 2014; the nomination and letting at that extent; and subsequent transactions, including decrofting for the respondent’s house site and later dealings in which the landlord proceeded on the footing that the Disputed Areas formed part of Croft 1. The Trust’s later letter of August 2025 further vouches that understanding, (other than as regards Kosiden). We therefore hold that by 2007 at the latest the landlord and the then crofter had agreed that the Disputed Areas would form part of Croft 1 and that the enlargement took effect from that time. This consensus between landlord and crofter was reached during the period of the realignment works and, in any event, by their conclusion in 2007, at a time when the pre‑existing form of section 4 of the 1993 Act remained in force. For the purposes of section 4(1)(a), the effective date of entry for the added strip is the conclusion of the works in 2007. The subjects of enlargement are identified by reference to the as built fence and the adjacent former roadway, which landlord and crofter thereafter adopted in all dealings.

[91] In identifying the subjects by reference to the as built fence and the adjacent former roadway, we are not creating a new boundary but locating, on the balance of probabilities, the boundary adopted by landlord and crofter at the material time. The statutory requirement is one of consensus, not paperwork. Section 4(4) notice to the Commission is not constitutive: enlargement takes effect from the date of entry agreed between landlord and crofter. While the absence of contemporaneous notification or rent adjustment is a relevant consideration, it is not determinative. In this case, the landlord’s consistent treatment of the disputed subjects in the years following the works — including the first registration and subsequent decroftings — provides persuasive evidence that any omission to intimate was administrative rather than substantive. The Court therefore proceeds on the basis that the enlargement was effected through agreement and actings, rather than through formal documentation.

[92] The applicant founds on the absence of a Commission notice and on the lack of express missives or rent adjustment. Those are relevant considerations. Again, however, they are not determinative. Subsequent landlord conduct consistently proceeded on the basis that enlargement had occurred. In any event, the subsequent first registration in 2014, which proceeded upon the fence based plan adopted by the landlord, brought the extent to the attention of the Commission. On the whole evidence we do not regard the absence of earlier notification as displacing the inference of agreement. There was at no stage any separate licence or seasonal letting of the disputed strip, which is consistent with its being treated by landlord and crofter as part of the croft rather than as the subject of mere tolerance or permissive occupation.

[93] Section 4(1)(b) of the 1993 Act prior to 25 June 2007 requires the Court to assess the area of Croft 1 exclusive of any common pasture or grazing land held therewith. An apportionment is land within the common grazings allocated to a crofter’s exclusive use. It does not, however, alter the extent of the croft in-bye. It follows that the apportioned area is left out of account when applying the 30 hectare threshold. Whether a Commission direction under section 4(1)(b) was required turns on whether the area of the croft excluding any apportionment exceeds 30 hectares. It follows also that the applicant’s calculation of approximately 30.62 hectares, which treats the 23.9 hectare apportionment as being part of Croft 1, proceeds on a mistaken legal basis, and that the in‑bye area of Croft 1 remained well below the 30‑hectare threshold throughout.

[94] With reference to parties’ submissions anent the Roads (Scotland) Act 1984, vesting under section 1(9) is functional and expressly stated to confer no heritable title on the roads authority. The statutory vesting endures only for so long as land serves a road purpose. By the time the new A859 was brought into use, the former single track road at Ardvourlie had ceased to serve any road purpose. The Comhairle’s reinstatement decisions, including the agreement reached with Murdo Morrison as to the treatment of the old surface, are consistent with the authority no longer maintaining or requiring the land for road purposes. In those circumstances, nothing in the 1984 Act precluded the landlord and crofter from agreeing that the land contiguous to the croft would form part of Croft 1.

[95] Mr Kermack invited the Court to hold that no enlargement occurred and, esto the legal boundary could not be discerned, to determine an appropriate boundary under section 14(6). In our view, there is sufficient evidence for the boundaries - and the fact of enlargement - to be identified on the balance of probabilities. If, however, we are wrong about that and should instead have considered that the evidential picture at the locus of the former roadway to be insufficiently clear, we would, in that event, have declared, in terms of section 14(6), that the present registered fence line is, in all the circumstances, the most coherent, intelligible and administratively workable boundary. It has been visible and acted upon for almost two decades, has underpinned landlord and tenant decisions made in good faith, and has been reflected in subsequent transactions. We also take into account the landlord’s stated willingness to enlarge and re‑let Croft 1 so as to include the Disputed Areas if the registration were to be found inaccurate; and the absence of any better competing claim (or indeed, any claim at all) by the applicant to that ground.

[96] In the whole circumstances we shall modify the Crofting Register entry by removing Kosiden. Quoad ultra we shall refuse the application. All questions of expenses are reserved.
parties: Donald Norman MacLennan MacDonald Applicant against Finlay George Morrison Respondent

title: in the application by Stormont Trading LP Applicant against Claire Elizabeth Leslie Respondent [2026] SLC 2
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2026] SLC 2,
Case reference: SLC/1/25

DECISION OF THE COURT

Court members: Lord Minginish,
Mrs Lovell,
Mr Smith

in the application by
Stormont Trading LP
Applicant
against
Claire Elizabeth Leslie
Respondent

The Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1991

Applicant: Upton, advocate

Respondent: Sutherland, advocate

6 February 2026

Introduction

[1] By lease dated 18 and subsequent dates in January 2015, the then owners of Scones of Lethendy Farm, Perthshire, the Trustees of the Scones Lethendy Mortifications, entered into a limited duration tenancy of the farm with the present respondent, Claire Elizabeth Leslie. The lease was to run “from Martinmas (28 November 2014) to Martinmas 2034 inclusive”.

[2] On 26 June 2024 the foresaid trustees sold the farm to the present applicants, who are a limited partnership known as Stormont Trading LP. In this application they seek (one) declarator that they are not bound by the lease and (two) an order for the respondent’s removal from the farm.

[3] These craves are founded on the fact that the lease was not registered in the Land Register for Scotland in terms of the Registration of Leases (Scotland) Act 1857 (as amended by the Land Registration etc (Scotland) Act 2012), section 1(1) of which allowed registration in the Land Register of leases more than 20 years duration and section 2 of which made such registered leases valid and effective against singular successors.

[4] Accordingly, there are two questions in the case: (1) whether the lease was for a period in excess of 20 years, and (2) if so, whether it is valid and effective against the applicants as singular successors of the original landlords. We heard a debate on these issues in Edinburgh on 2 December 2025 when the applicants were represented by Mr Michael Upton, advocate, and the respondent by Mr Robert Sutherland, advocate.

[5] We deal with each of these issues in turn.

First issue: was the lease for a period in excess of 20 years?

[6] Counsel were agreed as to how computation of time in this area normally operates, which is that a lease with a date of entry in Martinmas of 1 year and running to Martinmas in another year excludes the day on which Martinmas falls at the commencement of the lease but includes the day on which it falls at the end of the lease. Wright v Cunningham 1802 Mor 15919, Rankine, Leases, (3rd edition) pp 338 ‑ 341 and Sickness and Accident Assurance Association v General Accident Assurance Corporation, (1892) 19R 977 were cited as authorities for that approach.

[7] The applicants argue that this approach does not apply in this case because of the use of the word “inclusive”: the lease is said to run “from Martinmas (28 November 2014) to Martinmas 2034 inclusive” [emphasis added]. The inclusion of Martinmas 2014 makes this, they say, a lease of 20 years and 1 day.

[8] We were referred to a number of cases on statutory interpretation; Muirhead & Turnbull v Dickson (1905) 7F 686 at page 694, Network Rail Infrastructure v Fern Trustee 1 Ltd, 2022 SLT 997 at paragraph 28; Trustees of Second Discretionary Trust v Batchelor, 2023 SLT 1378; Logan Construction Group (in Administration) v Scots Road Partnership Project Limited, [2023] at paragraph 10; and Glenfiddich Wind Limited v Dorenell Windfarm Limited, [2025] CSOH 62, 10 July 2025, paragraphs 53 ‑ 60.

[9] In the last‑mentioned case, Lord Sandison, conducted an extensive survey and analysis of leading cases on the interpretation of contracts and we gratefully adopt what he says at para [59] of his decision as a convenient summary of the approaches taken in the leading cases:

“The purpose of construction, if undertaken properly and responsibly, is rarely simple – at least in the kind of cases which are brought for adjudication of the senior courts. It is ‘essentially one unitary exercise’ (Rainy Sky at [21]), a ‘composite exercise, neither uncompromisingly literal nor unswervingly purposive’ (Arbuthnott v Fagan [1995] CLC 1396, per Lord Bingham of Cornhill at 1400). It is an ‘iterative process by which each suggested interpretation is checked against the provisions of the contract and its commercial consequences are investigated’: Wood at [12], citing Arnold at [77] and In re Sigma Finance Corp [2009] UKSC 2, [2010] BCC 40 at [12], and it matters little whether one commences the exercise with an examination of the ‘factual background and the implications of rival constructions or a close examination of the relevant language in the contract’, so long as the indications furnished by each are balanced in the final analysis. It is not necessarily the case that the language of the contract falls to be favoured in that balance when the product of professional drafters, as is made clear when Wood at [13] is read as a whole. The circumstances in which a contract was produced, insofar as they are truly known in any particular case, constitute no more than one element in the mix of factors which a proper process of construction requires to consider delicately in order to come to the legally correct conclusion. Unfortunately, because of the deceptive simplicity of concentration on the ‘natural and ordinary’ meaning of the language used in a contract, there is a constantly‑present temptation to overlook, or pay insufficient attention to, the context which the language in question appears and the purpose which it was intended to serve. That is a temptation which, it might be thought, not all of the Scottish cases cited to me have entirely succeeded in avoiding. The risk of a lapse into what was called in Ashtead at [16] a ‘brutal literalism’ must always be recognised, not only because it is an approach apt to produce arbitrary results but because it represents, inherently, an inadequate discharge of the judicial responsibilities requisite in carrying out the task of contractual construction.”

[10] Opting to start the exercise of interpretation by looking at the ordinary meaning of the word “inclusive”, it seems plain to us that it means including both 28 November 2014 and 28 November 2034 which would indeed make this a lease of 20 years and a day. Mr Sutherland submitted that that the word itself was ambiguous, but we fail to see the ambiguity. If we ask ourselves the question whether the tenant was entitled to occupy the farm on 28 November 2014 as well as on 28 November 2034 the answer, on the plain and only meaning of the word “inclusive”, would have been an unequivocal yes.

[11] Turning to the context, we have heard no evidence as to the circumstances in which the contract was made but what we do have, as a specialist agricultural court, is the judicial knowledge that agricultural leases are customarily entered into for a period of years and that a lease for a period of years plus a day would, to say the least, be a novelty. We think it highly unlikely that that is what the parties intended and nothing in the rest of the lease suggests otherwise. On the contrary, Mr Sutherland pointed out that there was nothing in the lease to explain how the rent for the additional day was to be calculated and paid. That, he submitted, was an indicator that a lease for a term of 20 years only was intended.

[12] On the other hand, although highly unusual and lacking any explanation as to why parties would have wanted a lease of 20 years and a day, such a lease is not an impossibility nor is there anything about it which does not make sense or makes the lease unworkable. In the abstract, one reason for such a lease would be to make it registrable in the Land Register but clearly that was not the reason here, or, if it was, it was never followed through. The unusual duration has no bearing on the business efficacy of the lease. It is a choice which was open to parties and, on the face of it, they made it although we strongly suspect that what happened was that neither the drafter of the lease nor any lawyer who revised the draft realised the significance of the word “inclusive”.

[13] Balancing these considerations, and bearing in mind Lord President Dunedin’s dictum to the effect that contracts are made by what people say, not what they think in their inmost minds in Muirhead & Turnbull v Dickson, supra, we have come to the conclusion that this is a lease for 20 years and a day.

Second issue: Given that this is a limited duration tenancy of over 20 years’ duration which was not registered in the Land Register, is it valid and effective against singular successors?

Legislation

[14] Leases Act 1449

“Item it is ordanit and statute that for the saueritie and favor of the pure pupil that laubouris the grunde that thai and al uthiris that has takyn or sal tak landis in tym to cum fra lordis and has termes and yeris tharof, that suppose the lordis sel or analy thai landis, that the takaris sall remain with thare takis one to the ische of thare termez quhais handis at ever thai landis cum to for sic lik male as than i tuk theim of before.”

[15] Registration of Leases (Scotland) Act 1857 as amended by the Land Registration etc (Scotland) Act 2012:

“1(1): It shall be lawful to register in the Land Register of Scotland or as the case may be record in the general register of sasines in Scotland, probative leases, whether executed before or after the passing of this Act, for a period exceeding twenty years, of lands and heritages in Scotland and to register or record assignations and translations of such leases, all herein-after mentioned.

…

2.  Leases registerable under this Act, and valid and binding as in a question with the granters thereof, which shall have been duly registered or recorded, as herein provided, shall, by virtue of such registration, be effectual against any singular successor in the lands and heritages thereby let, whose title is completed after the date of such registration.

…

20B(1): Registration in the Land Register of Scotland has the effect of –

(a) vesting in the person registered as entitled to the lease a real right in and to the lease and in and to any right or pertinent, express or implied, forming part of the lease, subject only to the effect of any matter entered in that register so far as adverse to the entitlement.

(b) making any registered right or obligation relating to the registered lease a real right or obligation, and

(c) affecting any registered real right or obligation relating to the registered lease, in so far as the right or obligation is capable, under any enactment or rule of law, of being vested as a real right, of being made real or (as the case may be) of being affected as a real right.”

(2) Registration in the Land Register of Scotland is the only means –

(a) whereby rights and obligations relating to a registered lease become real rights or obligations, or

(b) of affecting such real right or obligations.

…

20C: The Leases Act 1449 (c. 6) does not apply to a lease registrable under this Act and granted on or after the date on which –

(a) the land to which the lease relates, or any part of that land, became land within an operational area (that is to say within an area in respect of which the provisions of the Land Registration (Scotland) Act 1979 (c. 33) had come into operation, or

(b) section 52 of the Land Registration etc (Scotland) Act 1857 (c. 26) comes into force.”

Applicant’s submissions

[16] Mr Upton’s fundamental submission on this head was that the Agricultural Holdings Acts which give a tenant security against the land‑owner’s rights depend upon the premise that the tenant has either a personal contract with the landowner or else a real right under the lease.

[17] The Leases Act 1449 was foundational to the regime which gives security of tenure to agricultural tenants; Gill, Agricultural Tenancies, 4th edition, 2‑03, where the learned author says:

“This Act is the source of the tenant’s right in rem under a lease of heritable property. The existence of this right is a fundamental assumption underlying the entire agricultural holdings legislation.”

However, the 1449 Act did not apply to leases registrable under the Registration of Leases (Scotland) Act 1857; section 20C of the Act as amended.

[18] Limited Duration Tenancies (LDTs) were a creature of the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 2003 (“the 2003 Act”). It contained no express provision nor any necessary implication disapplying the principles which govern the constitution of real rights. The principles that a real right requires possession in the case of a lease up to 20 years and otherwise registration under the 1857 Act were long‑established and fundamental. There is a presumption of statutory interpretation against alteration of long-established and fundamental principles; Bennion, Statutory Interpretation (7th edition), section 26.7, Craies, Legislation (13th edition) section 14‑010; Lord Atkinson in Leach v R [1912] AC 305, AT P 311; cf Lord Reid in Geo. Wimpey & Co. Ltd v British Overseas Airways Corp [1955] AC 169, at p 191.

[19] In addition to the statutory provisions set out above, he prayed in aid Rennie et al on Leases, at paragraph 6‑09, where the authors say:

“… although an unregistered lease for a period of more than 20 years was still a binding contract between the original parties, it was not binding on singular successors nor available as a security. So far as the Land Registration etc. (Scotland) Act 2012 is concerned, s. 52(2) adds a new s. 20B to the 1857 Act which provides again that registration of the lease is the only way in which a real right can be obtained.”

[20] Moreover, Explanatory Note 48 to the 2003 Act stated in terms that the provisions of section 1 of the 1857 Act continued to apply:

“The 2003 Act does not require that SLDTs or LDTs be entered into in writing. The general law on the constitution of leases and specific statutory provisions, for instance section 1 of the Registration of Leases (Scotland) Act 1857 (c. 26) as amended, which requires that long leases for terms exceeding 20 years are required for certain purposes to be entered into in writing and registered in the property registers, continue to apply.”

[21] The chief protections provided by the 2003 Act to a tenant of an LDT against removal during the currency of the lease were the restrictions on irritancy in sections 12 and 18. The primary rule was, however, that stated at section 18(1), that “it is for the landlord and tenant to provide in the lease constituting a short limited duration tenancy or a limited duration tenancy what grounds there are for irritancy of the lease.” This preserved the general law of contract and property and the principal provision about early termination of the tenant’s rights contained in the legislation did not alter but gave primacy to the general law.

[22] It followed that, in terms of the 1857 Act, as amended by the 2012 Act, the respondent did not have a real right under this unregistered lease. The applicants, as purchaser from the granters of the lease, were singular successors (Erskine, II, 7, 1 and III, 8,‑1, Lady Taylor v Brunton 1998 SLT (Sh Ct) 72, per Sheriff Principal Nicholson at p 75J‑L and where a tenant’s right under a lease was not a real right it did not bind a singular successor of the granter (Stair, I, 15, 4 and II, 9, 1-2), Rankine, Leases, (3rd edition), pp 132‑3.

[23] The applicants’ plea to the relevancy should, therefore, be upheld.

For the respondent

[24] In response to Mr Upton’s reliance on Lord Gill’s comment on the foundational significance of the 1449 Act, Mr Sutherland submitted that all that the learned author was doing there was giving an account of the legislative history of the agricultural tenant’s security of tenure. He was not discussing the application of the 1857 Act to agricultural tenancies, in fact the 4th edition of Agricultural Holdings contained only a single reference to that Act and that was to do with charges against a registered lease under section 75 of the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1991; Gill, Agricultural Tenancies, 4th edition., paragraphs 4‑06, 39‑28 and 39‑29. By contrast, the text contained extensive coverage of how the tenancies of agricultural holdings might be ended but nowhere was it suggested that a tenancy in excess of 20 years required to be registered under the 1875 Act.

[25] LDTs were a creature of statute and, whilst the 1857 Act provided a means for creating a real right for leases in excess of 20 years generally, the agricultural holdings legislation created specific legislative schemes which gave rise to security of tenure for agricultural tenants who were in occupation under a qualifying lease.

[26] In terms of section 93 of the 2003 Act, defining “landlord”, the applicants had automatically become entitled to the rent payable under the lease in place of their predecessors.

[27] There was no maximum term for an LDT, so it must have been foreseeable that LDTs might be created for longer than 20 years without being registered in the Land Register. That might not create a real right but that did not matter because tenants would be protected against eviction by the security of tenure conferred by the statutory regime governing LDTs.

[28] It was also significant that section 2(2) of the 2003 Act, which allows the conversion of a 1991 Act tenancy to an LDT of a minimum duration of 25 years did not suggest that such leases would not be valid and effective against singular successors of the original landlord without registration under the 1857 Act. Had the Scottish Parliament, foreseeing the likelihood of a change of landlord in leases of that duration, wanted to restrict the protection of such leases to ones registered under the 1857 Act it could have said so, but it had not. It was extremely unlikely that they had intended that the protection of an LDT tenant could be lost so easily. The result was that a new landlord under an LDT could not serve notice bringing the lease to an end in a manner different from section 8 of the 2003 Act.

Discussion of this issue

[29] Over the years successive governments have found it necessary to regulate certain sectors of the leasehold economy in Scotland, the most obvious examples being residential and agricultural leases. In the latter case the process can, as we have seen, be traced back as far as the Leases Act 1449 with the pace picking up markedly in the second half of the 19th century followed by sporadic bursts in the century which followed and a veritable onslaught in what has passed of the present century. The Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1883, the Crofters Holdings (Scotland) Act 1886, the Agricultural Holdings Act 1900, the Agricultural Holdings Act 1906, the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1908, the Agriculture Act 1920, the Agriculture Scotland Act 1948, the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1949, The Crofters (Scotland) Act 1955, the Crofting Reform (Scotland) Act 1976, the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1991, the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 2003, the Crofting Reform etc Act 2007, the Crofting Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 and the Land Reform (Scotland) Act 2016 are merely the principal milestones along what is a continuing journey.

[30] That process has been driven by two considerations; the social need to protect rural and agricultural tenants and the public interest in maximising and maintaining the efficiency of agricultural production. (See the speech of Lord Salmon in Johnson v Moreton [1980] AC 37.)

[31] One result of these reforms has been to create security of tenure for crofters and tenants of agricultural holdings capable of lasting for generations without any need for recording or registration under the 1857 Act. Of course, most of these leases would not be eligible for recording in the Register of Sasines or registration in the Land Register, whether because they were not probative or because they were leases from year to year or for some other reason, but the point is that security of tenure in agricultural leases extending over long periods of time is no novelty.

[32] It is likewise instructive, as Mr Sutherland pointed out, that in providing for the transition of existing 1991 Act tenancies into LDTs, the 2003 Act (at section 2(2)) required that the term of the new lease be not less than 25 years, without any requirement for registration of the lease under the 1857 Act.

[33] Given such an overlay of legislation on the common law of leases, it is neither necessary nor helpful to talk about real rights: the protection for the tenant, if it exists, is in the legislation.

[34] Turning then to LDTs, they are, of course, leases like any others, in that they have a landlord, a tenant, defined subjects and an agreed rent and duration, the requirements laid down in Gray v University of Edinburgh 1962 SC 157, but they are governed by the 2003 Act. They are leases of agricultural land for a term, originally, of not less than 15 years, now 10 years (Public Services Reform (Agricultural Holdings) (Scotland) Order 2011), which do not constitute 1991 Act tenancies; section 5(1) of the 2003 Act. No maximum length is prescribed. In terms of section 8(1), (3), (4), (5), 8C, 17, 18 and 22 of the 2003 Act they are terminable by (i) written agreement of the parties (subject to making provision for compensation as between them), (ii) the landlord giving the tenant a notice of intention to terminate the tenancy at its expiry followed by a notice to quit effective from the date of expiry or the date of expiry of any statutory continuation of the lease, (iii) the tenant giving to the landlord a notice of intention to quit, (iv) resumption of the entire subjects of let, (v) irritancy on any of the grounds specified in the lease and (vi) failure of succession to the tenant’s interest. If not terminated in any of these ways they go into a cycle of renewals, firstly of two short continuations of 3 years and then a long continuation of 10 years, with the cycle repeating itself until one of the events capable of terminating the lease occurs; section 8(6). Clearly, therefore, an LDT is capable of being in subsistence for a period well in excess of 20 years. They are assignable subject to the landlord’s consent; section 7(1) of the 2003 Act.

[35] The purpose of setting all of these matters out is to show how the 2003 Act provides a code for the operation of LDTs. We consider that to be a self‑contained code, with no need to go beyond it and not susceptible to qualification by any unspoken requirement for registration under the 1857 Act.

[36] Mr Upton drew our attention to Explanatory Note 48 to the 2003 Act which says that “the general law on the constitution of leases and specific statutory provisions, for instance section 1 of the Registration of Leases (Scotland) Act 1857, … continue to apply”. Undoubtedly that is so. Here there is no issue as to the constitution of the lease. So far as the applicability of section 1 of the 1857 Act is concerned, it is permissive, not prescriptive. It permits the registration of leases of over 20 years to be registered in the Land Register. One reason for doing so would be to enable the tenant to use it as security. But the tenant’s security of tenure does not depend on registration. The Scottish Parliament, imposed no maximum duration on LDTs and, on the contrary, provided a mechanism for the extension of such leases (and be it noted that these are extensions of the original lease, not the creation of new leases) for successive periods which could extend them beyond 20 years. As such, it could not have intended that failure to register the lease, for which there is no requirement in the 2003 Act, would defeat the tenant’s security of tenure against a singular successor of the landlord.

[37] The definition of “landlord” in section 93 of the Act is also indicative of the Parliament’s intention to entrench the tenant’s security against singular successors. It reads:

“‘landlord’ means any person for the time being entitled to receive the rents under a lease constituting a tenancy and includes the executor assignee, legatee, disponee, guardian or legal representative (within the meaning of Part I of the Children (Scotland) Act 1995 (c. 36) of a landlord or the trustee or interim trustee in the sequestration , under the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 2016, of a landlord’s estate”.

[38] Had this been a lease for 20 years there is no dispute that the tenant could not be removed by a singular successor of the landlord within that term. To lose that protection because it is a lease for a day more than 20 years would be a perverse result. Hard cases no doubt make bad law but we do not consider that the law leads to that result.

[39] As to the 1449 Act, it is expressly disapplied by section 20C of the 2003 Act as amended. Mr Upton prayed in aid of his position what Lord Gill says about the 1449 Act being the source of the tenant’s right in rem under a lease of heritable property and the existence of that right being a fundamental assumption underlying the entire agricultural holdings legislation. That bedrock, so to speak, having been removed in the case of LDTs, his argument was that the only way a right in rem could be created in an LDT of over 20 years was by registration under the 1857 Act. But that overlooks the protection with which the 2003 Act replaces it. It is true that the 2003 Act does not expressly exclude the 1857 Act but nor does it say that LDTs of over 20 years are in a different category from other LDTs, one which makes the tenant vulnerable to a change of ownership even within the 20 year term. Were that the intention of the Scottish Parliament, given that all the other ways of terminating LDTs are specified, it is a surprising omission.

[40] Not all leases of agricultural land have statutory protection. Mountain’s Trustees v Mountain 2023 SC 202 is an example of one which did not and there is no doubt that the creation of a right good against singular successors in such cases would require registration under the 1857 Act. But where a lease is governed by one of the statutory regimes, parties’ rights are governed by that regime, as well, of course, as the terms of the lease itself and, in the case of leases in excess of 20 years, the tenant’s security is not dependent on registration under the 1857 Act.

Decision

[41] The result is that the application fails and we have, therefore, sustained the respondent’s plea‑in‑law, repelled the plea‑in‑law for the applicants and dismissed the application.
parties: in the application by Stormont Trading LP Applicant against Claire Elizabeth Leslie Respondent

title: in the application by The Executors of Major John Carmichael Kirkpatrick Young Applicants against James Stewart Miller Respondent [2026] SLC 1
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2026] SLC 1,
Case reference: SLC/104/06

OPINION OF THE COURT

Court members: Lord Duthie,
Mr John Smith

in the application by
The Executors of Major John Carmichael Kirkpatrick Young
Applicants
against
James Stewart Miller
Respondent

The Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1991

Applicants: Sutherland, advocate; Gillespie Macandrew LLP

Respondent: Upton, advocate; Holmes Mackillop

22 January 2026

Introduction

[1] This is an application by the landlord applicants under the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1991 for an order declaring that the lease of Burnside and Flenders Farm, Clarkston, Glasgow, was validly terminated by a notice to quit dated 26 May 2006. The notice specifies termination at Martinmas 2007 in respect of the lands ploughed for crop and the lands in hay for that crop, and termination at Whitsunday 2008 in respect of the houses, yards and pastures. The application is opposed.

[2] The original tenant was Matthew Miller, who died on 29 May 2007. His son, James Stewart Miller, who is named as respondent in the instance, intimated acceptance of transfer of the tenant’s interest under section 12(1) of the 1991 Act. The applicants served a counter‑notice objecting to receiving him as tenant.

[3] The respondent invites the court, in light of the procedural history of this matter outlined below, to dismiss the application on the ground of inordinate, inexcusable and unfairly prejudicial delay by the applicants in progressing the application. The matter called for a debate on the respondent’s preliminary plea.

Procedural history

[4] The application was commenced in 2006. Following the death of Matthew Miller, James Stewart Miller gave the landlord notice on 21 May 2008 of his inheritance of the lease under section 12(1) of the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1991. The landlord sent a counter‑notice but did not apply to this court for an order terminating the lease under section 12(2). After sundry procedure a proof was fixed. However, that proof was discharged and on 15 and 17 February 2010 parties executed a Minute of Agreement, which was registered in the Books of Council and Session on 18 February 2010. The agreement provides for dismissal of the application in consideration of surrender of the lease, sale of part of the holding to the tenant, grant of a limited‑duration tenancy over other parts, and provision for possible development. Clause 13 makes the agreement conditional on the obtaining of the consent of Mactaggart & Mickel as holder of an option and a standard security over the subjects. In the event, no agreement was reached with Mactaggart & Mickel. The application was sisted. No steps were taken to progress the application between January 2009 and December 2022.

[5] On 13 December 2022 the court ordained parties to lodge proposals for further procedure. Sundry procedure followed. Major Young died on 14 November 2024. His executors obtained confirmation on 7 July 2025, following which the court fixed a diet of debate.

Submissions for the respondent

[6] Counsel adopted his note of argument. Rule 1(4) of the Scottish Land Court Rules 2014 directs the court to have regard to practice in the sheriff court in making any order in relation to a matter not expressly provided for in those rules. The practice of the sheriff court and the Court of Session is to dismiss where there has been both inordinate and inexcusable delay together with an added element of unfairness in the relevant factual and procedural context: Macphail, Sheriff Court Practice, paragraphs 2-10; Newman Shopfitters Ltd v M.J. Gleeson Group plc 2003 SLT (Sh Ct) 83. Reference was also made to decisions of the Court of Session (which, counsel commented, follow the lead of the sheriff court in respect of the courts’ inherent, common‑law powers) as stated in Tonner v Reiach & Hall [2007] CSIH 48 and Hepburn v Royal Alexandra NHS Trust [2010] CSIH 71. Dismissal is justified only if the element of unfairness is such that there is a substantial risk that a fair trial is no longer possible: Hepburn, supra per Lord President Hamilton at [39] and Lord Reed at [51]. Whether there is such a risk is partly a function of the survival of evidence: Hepburn, supra per Lord President Hamilton at [42], [43]. In addition, a respondent has the right, in terms of Article 6(1) of the European Convention on Human Rights, to have his civil rights and obligations determined by the court “within a reasonable time”.

[7] The delay is inordinate. Nineteen years have passed since the application was lodged and 12 years since the conditional settlement agreement was entered into. No steps were taken to progress the application between January 2009 and December 2022. The prospect of further delay in the future is also relevant, particularly given defects in the landlord’s pleadings. If or when the application is admitted to proof, that could only be after a further period of time for amendment or adjustment of the pleadings. A proof would presumably take much of a week, after which there would be a period of avizandum and possibly a subsequent appeal, which would defer determination of the application until more than two decades after it was commenced.

[8] The delay is inexcusable. The applicants found on the late Major Young’s deteriorating health as meaning that he was not in a position to pursue the application. However, a power of attorney was in place since September 1996. By the time that the Minute of Agreement was entered into in February 2010, it recorded that James Alister Aitkenhead was acting as his attorney. It is no answer to a plea of inordinate, inexcusable and unfairly prejudicial delay that the respondent could have taken steps to progress matters. A respondent is subject to no such positive responsibility: Tonner, supra at [128]. Inexcusable delay remains inexcusable though caused by a pursuer’s solicitor: Wilson v Drake & Scull Scotland Ltd, 2005 SLT (Sh Ct) 35, at [20].

[9] There is a substantial risk that a fair trial is no longer possible. The pleadings refer to numerous oral discussions between 1986 and 2006. Five of the eight participants in those discussions have since passed on. The whereabouts of a sixth individual, Mr Alan Beckett, the contractor with whom the Millers discussed repairs in 1998, are unknown. The memories of the three surviving witnesses of conversations dating from 2006 back to 1986 will have deteriorated.

[10] Documentary evidence is absent for issues including rent reviews, repair costs and correspondence. There are several matters in respect of which it is either manifest or could reasonably be inferred that relevant documents existed between 1984 and 2007 but which have not been produced and are not available to the respondent, including documents pertaining to the respondent’s participation in rent reviews, complaints, the cost of storm damage repairs, and a letter written by the tenant in December 2005. The absence of such documents creates a substantial risk of unfairness and is, of itself, sufficient to justify dismissal.

[11] The applicants’ argument that the respondent has had the benefit of occupation without paying rent is irrelevant to the determinative issues of whether, in circumstances where there has been inordinate and inexcusable delay, there is a substantial risk that a fair trial is not possible. In any event, the respondent tendered rent, which was refused. Further, esto the landlord has been wrongly prejudiced by the respondent’s occupation of the farm (which is denied), that is because of his own failure to progress this case. Moreover, any claim for rent older than 5 years is extinguished by prescription.

[12] Dismissal accords with parties’ underlying, substantive rights. The application seeks to enforce a right to terminate for non-payment of rent in 2003. A right of rescission must be exercised within a reasonable time. Eighteen years is manifestly unreasonable.

Submissions for the applicants

[13] Counsel adopted his note of argument and supplementary note. Dismissal is a course of last resort and is not justified on the circumstances of the present case.

[14] Two applications between the same parties are in dependence before the court. The present application concerns the validity of termination of the tenancy. Application SLC/39/21 (raised by the tenant in 2021, and which seeks approval of tenant’s improvements in respect of the same subjects as the present proceedings) is sisted to await the outcome of this application. There is a substantial overlap between the two applications.

[15] In the present application a proof was fixed in 2010 but negotiations resulted in the 2010 Minute of Agreement. The respondent failed to implement its terms. The agreed sale of land and the creation of a limited duration tenancy did not proceed, nor were the associated option and security arrangements regularised. The respondent has remained in occupation throughout and no rent has been paid.

[16] Delay, even where substantial, is not of itself determinative of whether dismissal should be granted. Each case turns on its own circumstances. Dismissal requires a substantial risk that a fair trial cannot be held. Reference was made to Tonner, supra, Hepburn, supra, Abram v British International Helicopters Ltd 2015 SCLR 95 and Mannas v Chief Constable of Police Scotland 2019 SCLR 909. In the present case the delay is at least partly excusable and does not give rise to such unfairness. Any relevant delay should be assessed from late 2010, when it became apparent that the Minute of Agreement would not be implemented, until the death of Major Young in November 2024. From around 2014 onwards, Major Young’s deteriorating health and constrained financial position rendered him unable, in practical terms, to advance the litigation or to raise further proceedings.

[17] Despite the passage of time, a fair hearing remains possible. Determination of the issues is neither impossible nor impractical. Although some witnesses are no longer available, contemporaneous documentary records exist. Evidence is available from the former law agent and from Savills, whose directors have dealt with the estate for many years. James Stewart Miller has been directly involved throughout the relevant period and remains available to give evidence. Any disadvantage arising from the absence of witnesses falls more heavily on the applicants, who bear the onus of justifying the notices to quit.

[18] The applicants would suffer prejudice if the application were dismissed. The respondent has remained in occupation without paying rent and now advances claims for historic tenant’s improvements under a separate application. Dismissal would expose the applicants to potential liability for improvements which would not arise if the tenancy had been validly terminated. Any prejudice to the respondent arising from the delay is not so great as to justify dismissal. Application SLC/104/06 should be permitted to proceed to determination.

Decision

[19] We are satisfied that the delay in this application has been inordinate, inexcusable and has resulted in a substantial risk that a fair trial is no longer possible.

[20] The delay is inordinate. The application was raised in 2006. No procedural steps were taken between January 2009 and December 2022. More than 19 years have elapsed since commencement. More than a decade passed after the execution of the 2010 conditional Minute of Agreement during which no progress was made. If the application were now to proceed to proof, final determination will occur more than 20 years after proceedings were raised. Delay of that magnitude goes well beyond what is tolerable in civil litigation.

[21] The delay is inexcusable. A continuing power of attorney was in place since 1996. By February 2010 it was expressly recorded that Major Young was acting through an attorney. There was no legal impediment to procedural steps being taken on his behalf. Nor does the failure of the 2010 Minute of Agreement excuse subsequent inaction. It was apparent by late 2010 at the latest that the conditions for its implementation would not be met. No steps were taken thereafter for more than 12 years, and then only as a result of intervention by the court.

[22] The fact that the respondent did not seek to force progress does not render the delay excusable. A respondent is under no obligation to advance proceedings raised by another party. Delay remains inexcusable even where attributable to the actions of a party’s agents. Responsibility for progressing the application lay with the applicants.

[23] The delay has resulted in unfairness of such a degree that there is now a substantial risk that a fair hearing is no longer possible. Central issues in the application depend upon factual disputes concerning events spanning many years, including alleged oral discussions, rent reviews, repairs, set off arrangements and the circumstances said to justify termination for non‑payment of rent. Five of the eight individuals who participated in relevant discussions are now deceased. The whereabouts of a sixth individual are unknown. The remaining two witnesses would be required to recall conversations dating back as far as 1986. The inevitable deterioration of recollection over such a period materially undermines the reliability of any evidence now capable of being led.

[24] The position is not materially improved by reference to documentary evidence. There are significant gaps. Documents which one would reasonably expect to have existed, relating for example to rent reviews, repair costs, complaints, storm damage and correspondence in December 2005, are absent and appear no longer to be available. In circumstances where the application depends upon proof of historical facts, the loss of such material increases the risk of unfairness.

[25] The applicants’ submission that a fair trial remains possible because some witnesses and professional advisers are still available is unpersuasive. The question is not whether it is possible to hold a hearing, rather, whether there is a substantial risk that the court would be unable to determine the issues fairly. In our view that risk is now considerable. Any disadvantage arising from the absence of evidence may fall on either party, but that does not mitigate the unfairness inherent in requiring the respondent to resist these proceedings after such an excessive and unexplained delay.

[26] We have had regard to the prejudice said to arise if the application were dismissed, including the respondent’s continued occupation and the existence of a separate application for approval of improvements. Those matters do not outweigh the fundamental difficulty that the present proceedings can no longer be resolved fairly. The prejudice to the applicants is the result of the landlord’s own failure to bring matters to determination timeously.

[27] We will grant the respondent’s motion and dismiss the application. We appoint parties to submit any motions for expenses within 21 days of intimation of this decision.
