title: in the application by The North Harris Trust Applicant against Donald N M MacDonald Respondent [2025] SLC 11
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2025] SLC 11,
Case reference: SLC/47/24

OPINION OF THE COURT

Court members: Lord Duthie,
Mr John Smith

in the application by
The North Harris Trust
Applicant
against
Donald N M MacDonald
Respondent

Subjects: Common Grazings, Township of Ardvourlie, Harris

26 September 2025

Introduction

[1] The applicant seeks to resume 3,180 square metres of common grazing at Ardvourlie, Harris in term of sections 20 and 21 of the Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993. The stated purpose of the resumption is to develop an Outdoor Hub, including a facilities building with café and retail space to support mountain biking and improve visitor infrastructure. Planning permission has been granted and preliminary works have commenced.

[2] The application is opposed by the respondent who is one of only two shareholders in the common grazing. Parties agreed that the court should determine the matter on the basis of written submissions.

The Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993

[3] The 1993 Act provides, inter alia, as follows:

“20 Resumption of croft or part of croft by landlord.

(1) The Land Court may, on the application of the landlord and on being satisfied that he desires to resume the croft, or part thereof, for some reasonable purpose having relation to the good of the croft or of the estate or to the public interest or the interests of the crofting community in the locality of the croft, authorise the resumption thereof by the landlord upon such terms and conditions as it may think fit, and may require the crofter to surrender his croft, in whole or in part, to the landlord accordingly, upon the landlord making adequate compensation to the crofter either by letting to him other land of equivalent value in the neighbourhood or by compensation in money or by way of an adjustment of rent or in such other manner as the Land Court may determine.

…

21 Crofter’s right to share in value of land resumed by landlord.

(1) Where the Land Court authorises the resumption of a croft or a part thereof under section 20 of this Act, the crofter shall be entitled to receive from the landlord, in addition to any compensation payable to him under that section, a share in the value of the land so resumed the amount whereof shall be one half of the difference between, subject to subsection (5) below, the market value of the land (on the date on which resumption thereof is so authorised) as determined by the Land Court in accordance with subsections (2) and (3) below (less any compensation payable as aforesaid) and the crofting value thereof.”

Submissions for the applicant

[4] The proposed development is for a reasonable purpose. The development will enhance the visitor experience, benefit the wider community and economy and encourage responsible use of designated paths, thereby protecting the common pasture. Planning consent has been obtained. Initial works commenced in early 2023, maintaining the validity of the consent. These works include installation of services and an electric vehicle charge point, as well as ground preparation.

[5] The land is not actively grazed. Sufficient alternative grazing is available.

[6] Compensation of £250 was previously agreed with the respondent, reflecting the limited impact on grazing and the anticipated community benefit. The respondent, however, has since withdrawn consent and obtained a higher valuation, which the applicants dispute as being inappropriate for the nature of the proposed development. No further compensation is due under the Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993. No fencing condition is required.

[7] The court is invited to determine whether the statutory criteria for resumption are met and to fix any compensation or share of value due.

Submissions for the respondent

[8] The respondent raised a number of objections, some of which were inconsistent. They are as follows.

[9] The planning permission relied upon by the applicants expired in July 2024. No valid development has commenced. Alternatively, if development has commenced, the application is retrospective, contrary to the Court’s Practice Note No 1.

[10] The application is premature. There is uncertainty over funding and timescales for completion. The applicants have failed to disclose who will operate the Outdoor Hub.

[11] The proposed resumption and facilities are unnecessary. Previous resumptions have already provided facilities in the area, including the Scaladale Centre, which remains underutilised.

[12] The proposed mountain bike trails may extend beyond the resumption site into common grazings and crofter forestry without proper authority. The applicant is not respectful of the rights of the shareholders. One of the applicant’s directors grazed his cattle on the common grazing (contrary to the applicable woodland scheme).

[13] The proposed compensation is inadequate. The subjects, assuming planning permission, have a market value of £65,000. Reference is made to a valuation of the subjects commissioned by the respondent. The respondent is entitled to a share of that value: section 21 of the Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993.

Decision

[14] We are satisfied on the basis of the material before us that the statutory criteria for resumption are met. We authorise resumption in principle. Planning permission has been obtained and, permissibly, initial works have been carried out to preserve the validity of the consent. We are satisfied that these works constitute a valid commencement of development, and accordingly, the planning permission remains extant. The application is not retrospective. The proposed development constitutes a reasonable purpose having relation to the good of the estate or public interest. The development is likely to enhance visitor infrastructure and support responsible outdoor recreation. While other facilities exist in the area, we do not consider these vitiate the reasonableness of the proposed development. The land identified for resumption is not actively grazed, and adequate alternative grazing is available. The development will not prejudice the crofting interests of the respondents and will contribute positively to the local economy (potentially improving employment opportunities) and visitor infrastructure.

[15] While there is no fixed timescale for completion, the applicants have secured initial funding and are actively seeking further support for the main building works. The absence of a definitive completion date does not, in our view, render the application premature.

[16] Turning to the respondent’s complaint that the applicant has failed to disclose who will operate the facilities, the applicant has indicated that it will operate the facilities building and lease the café and retail units to third parties. That is sufficient for present purposes. The applicant is a community‑controlled trust. If the applicant were subsequently to sell the subjects, profits would be reinvested in the community.

[17] The respondent expressed concerns regarding the potential extension of mountain bike trails beyond the resumption site. However, the application relates solely to the delineated area. Any development beyond that boundary is not before the court and would require separate authorisation.

[18] Allegations of unauthorised grazing by a director of the applicant are not directly relevant to the merits of the present application.

[19] We have insufficient information before us to allow us to determine the question of what compensation should be payable. Similarly, we are currently unable to assess the value of the land to be resumed and therefore any share the respondent should receive. The valuation commissioned by the respondent places a market value of £65,000 on the land, assuming residential or commercial use. However, that valuation is no guide to the value of the land taking account of the purpose of the resumption and the planning permission actually obtained and is accordingly irrelevant to the matter at hand.

[20] We shall fix a hearing at which parties can address the court on how compensation and the respondent’s share of the value of the subjects should be assessed. All questions of expenses are reserved.
parties: in the application by The North Harris Trust Applicant against Donald N M MacDonald Respondent

title: in the appeal by INEOS FPS Limited Applicant against a decision of The Scottish Environmental Protection Agency Respondent [2025] SLC 10
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2025] SLC 10,
Case reference: SLC/85/24

OPINION OF THE COURT

Court members: Lord Duthie,
Mr Tom Campbell

in the appeal by
INEOS FPS Limited
Applicant
against a decision of
The Scottish Environmental Protection Agency
Respondent

Subjects: Forties Pipeline System, Kinneil

10 September 2025

Introduction

[1] This is an appeal against the imposition of two civil penalties totalling £68,960 by the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (“SEPA”) under Article 52 of the Greenhouse Gas Emissions Trading Scheme Order 2020 (the “Order”). The penalties relate to a failure to surrender sufficient allowances to cover verified emissions for the scheme years 2021 and 2022.

[2] The appellant operates the Forties Pipeline System, a key component of the North Sea oil and gas infrastructure. The non‑compliance concerns a specific source stream at the Kinneil site known as the F7 Propane Flare, which emits small volumes of propane during the regeneration cycle of product driers. This part of the process is unmetered. The volume of flared propane was calculated using a design value for the void space in the drier. That void space value (“0.05” or 5%) was provided by the equipment manufacturer and was communicated to the previous operator in 2013. The value continued to be used by the appellant following its acquisition of the asset in 2017. In 2023, during a separate engineering project, the appellant’s engineers contacted the manufacturer again and were advised that the void space was in fact larger (“0.37” or 37%). Upon learning of the discrepancy, the appellant voluntarily recalculated its emissions and surrendered the additional allowances in April 2024.

[3] Parties agreed that the matter could be determined on the basis of written submissions, which were duly submitted.

The legal framework

[4] The Order provides, inter alia, as follows:

“47.—(1) Where the regulator considers that a person is liable to a civil penalty under any of articles 50 to 68 the regulator may impose a civil penalty on the person.

…

52(4) This paragraph applies where—

(a) the regulator becomes aware that an installation’s reportable emissions (as determined by the regulator under article 45) in a scheme year exceed the installation’s verified reportable emissions for that year; and

(b) the operator of the installation failed to surrender allowances equal to the difference—

(i)  on or before 30th April in the year following the scheme year referred to in sub-paragraph (a); or

(ii) where the end date set out in a surrender notice under paragraph 11 of Schedule 6 or a revocation notice under paragraph 12 of that Schedule falls in the scheme year referred to in sub-paragraph (a), on or before the date set out in the notice for the surrender of allowances.

…

(10) The civil penalty is £20 multiplied by the inflation factor for each allowance that the operator or the aircraft operator failed to surrender.”

SEPA’s decision

[5] SEPA’s reasons for imposing the penalties appealed against are contained in its decision letter dated 26 September 2024 which should be referred to for its full terms. The relative penalty notices are dated 20 November 2024. The penalty imposed in respect of 2021 is £39,270, discounted from a headline penalty of £78,540 in respect of 2021. The penalty imposed in respect of 2022 is £29,690, discounted from a headline penalty of £59,380. The reasons stated in the decision letter are consistent with the submissions for SEPA advanced in this appeal, summarised below.

Submissions for the appellant

[6] Article 47(1) of the Order gives SEPA the power to impose a penalty. It does not create a mandatory obligation. SEPA’s own enforcement guidance recognises this discretion, and states that the imposition of penalties must be fair, proportionate, and appropriate in the circumstances. Article 52(10) sets the formula for calculating the maximum penalty, but does not preclude SEPA from applying a reduction or waiving the penalty entirely where justified.

[7] The under-surrender arose from an inadvertent error in the emissions calculation methodology applied. The void space value used in the relevant formula was inherited from the previous operator and manufacturer and was accepted in good faith. The error was identified in 2023. The breach was unintentional, non‑systemic, and promptly remedied: the appellant voluntarily recalculated the emissions and surrendered the additional allowances in April 2024, without any enforcement action having been initiated.

[8] The extent of the under-surrender was de minimis, amounting to 1.539% of total emissions in 2021 and 1.255% in 2022. No financial benefit or competitive advantage was obtained: the surrendered allowances were acquired at cost and not traded. The breaches caused no environmental harm.

[9] SEPA failed to exercise its discretion under Article 52 of the Order in a manner that was fair, proportionate, or consistent with its own enforcement guidance. SEPA failed to provide adequate reasons for imposing a flat‑rate 50% penalty in each year. SEPA failed to take into account the mitigating circumstances. SEPA did not undertake a proper investigation prior to the imposition of the penalties, and failed to seek clarification or further evidence from the appellant before reaching its decision. The penalties do not serve the regulatory objectives of deterrence or compliance, particularly in circumstances where the breach was promptly remedied and voluntarily disclosed. SEPA’s approach risks creating a de facto strict liability regime.

[10] The appellant is committed to environmental compliance and improvement. Since acquiring the Forties Pipeline System, it has achieved a 45% reduction in emissions. The court should quash the penalties in their entirety, or alternatively substantially reduce them, having regard to the nature of the breach, the conduct of the appellant, and the principles of fairness, proportionality, and regulatory discretion.

Submissions for SEPA

[11] The penalties were lawfully imposed, reasonably calculated, and appropriately reduced in light of the circumstances. The appellant breached conditions 2 and 4 of its greenhouse gas emissions permit. The error persisted for 6 years and resulted in an underreporting of nearly 7,000 tonnes of CO2 equivalent. That figure is significant both in absolute terms and in relation to the integrity of the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (the “UK ETS”). Reliance on manufacturer data, while done in good faith, does not absolve the appellant of its responsibility to ensure accuracy.

[12] While the appellant did act transparently upon discovering the error and voluntarily surrendered the correct allowances, the obligation to report accurate emissions is continuous and fundamental to the operation of the UK ETS. The surrender of additional allowances following the identification of an under-report was not voluntary, but a legal obligation. The appellant, a large commercial operator, bore the responsibility to verify inherited data and ensure its accuracy from the outset of its participation in the scheme.

[13] The decision was procedurally fair. SEPA issued a Notice of Intent, gave an opportunity for representations, and engaged in correspondence with the appellant. The penalties were calculated in accordance with the statutory formula and SEPA’s internal guidance, which was updated in 2023. The reductions applied were the maximum available under SEPA’s methodology, and were based on engagement with the appellant, the absence of aggravating factors, and the mitigatory information provided. SEPA’S methodology for determining penalties is designed to ensure consistency across cases. SEPA applied discretionary reductions of 25% for both attitude and gravity, resulting in a total reduction of 50% from the maximum penalty. The £20,000 penalty for breach of the reporting condition was waived entirely.

[14] The penalties are neither excessive nor unjustified. They serve the regulatory objectives of maintaining scheme integrity, deterring future non-compliance, and ensuring a level playing field. The court should dismiss the appeal.

Decision

[15] No issue is taken by the appellant with SEPA’s calculation of headline penalties (£78,540 in respect of 2021 and £59,380 in respect of 2022). Rather, it is the discounted penalties which are challenged. The task of this court is to consider whether the penalties applied are proportionate to the breach and whether the relative decisions take account of mitigating circumstances; are fair and reasonable in light of the operator’s conduct; are vitiated by procedural unfairness; and comply with natural justice.

[16] No question of procedural unfairness or breach of natural justice is made out.

[17] Article 52 of the Order allows SEPA to impose civil penalties where an operator fails to surrender sufficient allowances. The penalty regime supports deterrence and scheme integrity. The appellant under-surrendered allowances for 2021 and 2022, albeit unintentionally.

[18] We accept that operators are responsible for verifying inherited data. Participation in the UK ETS entails a continuous duty of accuracy. That duty entails ensuring data is and remains accurate. In that one respect the appellants failed, for a time. The breaches in question persisted for six years.

[19] Against that, the incorrect void space value which resulted in under reporting was inherited from the previous operator, who in turn was provided it by the equipment manufacturer. That is a very technical error: an engineering consultant was required to order for the appellant to ascertain the error. On identifying the error, the appellant promptly and voluntarily corrected the error and surrendered allowances without the need for enforcement proceedings. The appellant did not profit from the breach. The breach did not cause environmental harm.

[20] Penalties should be proportionate and reflect the actual impact of any given breach. SEPA followed its internal procedures and applied discretionary reductions in respect of various mitigating factors. The Court is mindful of SEPA’s regulatory objectives, including deterrence and scheme integrity. However, where an operator self‑reports, cooperates, and remedies the breach, the deterrent effect may, depending on the case, be achieved through means other than penalties. The imposition of overly severe penalties in respect of breaches that are unintentional, technical, non‑systemic and non‑culpable and where the operator self‑reports runs the risk of a cooling effect, discouraging self‑reporting when breaches are discovered. That would not further the regulatory objectives.

[21] We find that, in all the circumstances, the penalties imposed, even having regard to the reductions already applied by SEPA and SEPA’s internal guidance, are disproportionate to the breach. This decision should not be taken to set a precedent and is entirely contingent on the particular circumstances of this case. While the imposition of financial penalties was appropriate for the reasons set out by SEPA, insufficient weight was given to the appellant’s mitigating conduct, their lack of culpability, the minor nature of the breach, the lack of environmental impact and the fact the appellant did not profit from the error. The regulatory objectives can be met by a substantially reduced penalty that better reflects the nature of the breach and the appellant’s proactive and transparent conduct in self‑reporting. While the imposition of a penalty was lawful, the quantum of the penalty imposed was disproportionate. The appeal is allowed in part. The penalties imposed by SEPA are varied. Applying the judicial blunt axe, a more appropriate discount to both penalties is 80%. We reduce the penalty imposed in respect of 2021 to £15,708 (discounted from a headline penalty of £78,540). We reduce the penalty imposed in respect of 2022 to £11,876 (discounted from a headline penalty of £59,380).
parties: in the appeal by INEOS FPS Limited Applicant against a decision of The Scottish Environmental Protection Agency Respondent

title: in the appeal under section 25(11) of the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 2003 by Comrie Development Company Limited Appellant against John Keddie Respondent [2025] SLC 9
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2025] SLC 9,
Case reference: SLC/35/24

OPINION OF THE COURT

Court members: Lord Duthie,
Mr T Campbell

in the appeal under section 25(11) of the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 2003 by
Comrie Development Company Limited
Appellant
against
John Keddie
Respondent

Subjects: 4.27 hectares of land at Overton Farm land (entry number AT1700 in the Register of Community Interests in Land

Appellant: Lean, solicitor; Shepherd and Wedderburn LLP

Respondent: Colquhoun, advocate; rradar (Scotland) Limited

22 August 2025

Introduction

[1] This is an appeal under section 25(11) of the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 2003 against the decision of the Keeper of the Registers of Scotland, dated 3 May 2024, to reject the appellant’s challenge to the registration of the respondent’s notice under section 25(1) of the 2003 Act. The notice concerns an interest in acquiring 4.27 hectares of land at Overton Farm (the “Subjects”), recorded as entry number AT1700 in the Register of Community Interests in Land (“RCIL”). The effect of the entry is to give the respondent a pre-emptive right to buy the Subjects should the appellant seek to sell them. The appellant argues that the respondent does not hold a qualifying tenancy under the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1991 (a requirement for the registration of such a notice) and, therefore, the registration should not have been permitted. The respondent maintains that he is the tenant of the Subjects under a 1991 Act tenancy, and that the Keeper was correct in rejecting the appellant’s challenge.

Events giving rise to these proceedings

[2] The Subjects form part of Muirside Estate, near Oakley in Fife. From at least the mid‑1970s until in or around 1996, Overton Farm (and therefore the Subjects) were owned by the National Coal Board (“NCB”), at which point they were sold to Land Regeneration and Development Limited (“LRD”). In 2006, the respondent bought three parcels of Overton Farm from LRD and in 2008 bought three further parcels. Following those purchases, the only remaining areas still owned by LRD and farmed by the respondent were fields immediately to the south of Blairhall Village, and the Subjects. LRD entered administration on 17 July 2015, creditors voluntary liquidation on 11 July 2016 and were dissolved on 23 September 2023. The respondent surrendered his occupation of the fields immediately to the south of Blairhall Village in October 2017, leaving the respondent in occupation only of the Subjects.

[3] In 2021, the appellant bought the Subjects from LRD’s administrators. The respondent remained in occupation of the Subjects. The respondent attempted to make payments of rent to the appellant, who refused payment on the basis that the respondent was not a tenant. In or around September 2022, the appellant fenced off the Subjects. In Spring 2023 the respondent removed part of the fence in order to sow crops on the Subjects.

[4] Against the background of this emerging dispute, on advice the respondent registered his interest in the Subjects in the RCIL. That application was accepted by the Keeper and the Subjects were registered with reference AT1700. The appellant challenged that registration on 21 March 2024.

[5] The Keeper’s decision letter dated 3 May 2024 states that she has received conflicting evidence from parties as to the existence or otherwise of a 1991 Act tenancy; that the Keeper can only rescind an entry in the Register where it is clear there is material inaccuracy in the Register; that the evidence provided is not sufficient to allow her to determine whether there is a material inaccuracy in the Register; and that the entry under AT1700 will therefore remain on the Register unamended. The appellant appeals against that refusal.

The 2003 Act

[6] Section 25 of the 2003 Act provides, inter alia, as follows:

“(1) a tenant of a 1991 Act tenancy may apply to have registered an interest in acquiring the land comprised in the lease by sending a notice (in this Section referred to as a “notice of interest”) to the Keeper.

…

(5) On receipt of the notice of interest, the Keeper must—

(a) register—

(i) the tenant’s interest in acquiring the land;

(ii) the details specified in the notice of interest; and

(iii) the date of registration; and

(b) send an extract of the registration to the tenant and the owner of the land.

…

(8) If the owner of the land disputes any matter contained in the extract of registration, the owner may, by notice in writing to the Keeper, challenge the registration of the tenant’s interest in acquiring the land on the grounds that any matter contained in the extract is inaccurate.

(9) On receipt of notice under subsection (8), the Keeper is to make such enquiry in connection with the tenant’s interest in acquiring the land as the Keeper considers appropriate; and following such an enquiry, if the Keeper considers that the notice of interest is inaccurate, the Keeper—

(a) must, if the inaccuracy is material, rescind the registration of the tenant’s interest; and

(b) may, if the inaccuracy is not material, amend that registration.

…

(11) The tenant or the owner of the land may appeal to the Land Court against any decision made, following notice under subsection (8), by the Keeper in respect of the registration of the tenant’s interest in acquiring the land; and in an appeal under this subsection the Court may make such order as it considers appropriate.”

Witness evidence

[7] At the appeal hearing the appellant led evidence from Robert Haugh, Callum Carmichael and Alan Kenney. The respondent gave evidence himself and led evidence from Lynsey Pender, Edward Henderson and Luke Devine. All witnesses had signed witness statements containing their evidence which were lodged in advance of the proof diet, are available in the Court Process and should be referred to for their full terms. With the exception of Mr Devine (who was unable to attend the proof diet due to illness) all witnesses attended court and adopted under oath their respective statements as their evidence. On the respondent’s unopposed motion, the court allowed Mr Devine’s evidence to be received without the need for him to attend or be cross examined. The remaining witnesses were all subject to cross examination. We do not consider any real issues of credibility arise, however, in the context of this dispute there are clear limits as to the matters to which some witnesses, particularly those led on behalf of the appellant, could speak.

The appellant’s witnesses

Robert Haugh’s evidence

[8] Mr Haugh is a director of the appellant. The appellant purchased the Subjects in January 2021 for non-agricultural development, with planning permission already in place. At the time of purchase, he was unaware of any agricultural use or tenancy claims by the respondent. No rent has been accepted from the respondent since the appellant acquired the Subjects. Mr Haugh firmly believes that the respondent does not hold tenancy rights over the Subjects and accordingly challenged the respondent’s attempt to register a pre-emptive right to buy, leading to the current proceedings.

[9] We accept Mr Haugh’s evidence, quantum valeat. However, this witnesses’ evidence does not assist the court on the critical issues, that is to say, the existence or otherwise of a tenancy and the respondent’s use and occupation of the Subjects prior to the appellants’ purchase of the same, for the simple reason that he has no knowledge of the Subjects prior to the appellant’s acquisition of the Subjects in 2021.

Callum Carmichael’s evidence

[10] Mr Carmichael is an insolvency practitioner and partner at FRP Advisory Trading Limited. He gave evidence regarding the administration and liquidation of LRD. During LRD’s insolvency processes, the respondent sought to purchase agricultural land, claiming tenancy rights. However, the respondent was never accepted as being a rent-paying tenant during the administration or liquidation period.

[11] While Mr Carmichael’s belief that the respondent is not a tenant may well be sincerely held, this witness is not in a position to speak to agreements entered into before the insolvency process and accordingly his evidence does not assist the court.

Alan Kenney’s evidence

[12] Mr Kenney is a development liaison consultant and former member of Fife Council. He spoke to his long-standing involvement with the Comrie site, including its transition from mining operations to land development. He worked with LRD during its planning and restoration efforts and assisted insolvency practitioners during LRD’s liquidation. He is unaware of any agricultural use or tenancy agreement involving the respondent on the disputed land. A comprehensive search during the liquidation process revealed no tenancy rights held by third parties. The respondent did not assert any such rights or make rent payments at that time.

[13] We consider Mr Kenney was attempting to assist the court, however, he is not in a position to dispute the respondent’s evidence. He cannot speak to the agreement between LRD and the respondent, nor to whether rent was tendered.

The respondent’s witnesses

The respondent’s evidence

[14] The respondent has farmed the Subjects for around 50 years. Overton Farm was initially tenanted by the respondent’s father and uncle in partnership (the firm of J&J Keddie). The respondent joined the partnership in or around 1975 and has farmed there ever since. The area of land farmed under the tenancy was originally far larger than the Subjects: over the years various parcels of land have been sold, in some cases to him. The partnership paid rent to the landlord, who until 1996 were NCB. The respondent's uncle retired from the partnership in 1988. His father retired in “about 1993” and not 1988 as stated in his witness statement (this point was clarified during cross examination). The original partnership came to an end and he became the sole tenant, farming under the same trading name: accounts prepared for the year to Martinmas 1994 lodged with the court show him as “John Keddie T/A J, D & J Keddie”. Subsequent accounts lodged with the court for 1996, 1998, 1999, 2000, 2003, 2005, 2006, and 2008, show rent payments in respect of the Subjects being made by the partnership he subsequently formed with his wife. He has been in partnership with his son since 2008 and his daughter since c.2020.

[15] Sales particulars prepared on behalf of the then landlord, LRD, in 1996 record the respondent as being the tenant, paying £11,750 annually (see page 10 of the respondent’s production number 2). He is unaware whether there was ever a written lease: if there ever was, it has been lost. In 2008 the respondent requested documentation from LRD to vouch the existence of a lease in order to demonstrate to the Scottish Government Rural Payments and Inspections Directorate (SGRPID) his eligibility to claim agricultural support payments for farming the subjects. In response, LRD provided the undated document lodged as Item 4 on the respondent’s first inventory of productions. This document records the respondent rather than any partnership as tenant.

[16] LRD entered insolvency proceedings in 2015. (Note: the respondent refers to LRD being in receivership, however, it is not understood to be disputed that in fact LRD entered administration on 17 July 2015 and a creditors voluntary liquidation on 11 July 2016; and were dissolved on 23 September 2023). The respondent wrote to Mr Carmichael, the insolvency practitioner dealing, offering to pay rent in respect of the Subjects but received no response. He was, however, invited to attend and did attend a meeting with the insolvency practitioners and other stakeholders on the basis of his tenancy. Mr Kenney, who was acting for the insolvency practitioner, also attended that meeting. At that meeting it was accepted that the respondent had a secure agricultural tenancy over, inter alia, the Subjects. The respondent agreed to release some land (but not the Subjects) from the tenancy. Thereafter the respondent calculated that the rent due in respect of the Subjects, being the only part of Overton Farm still subject to the tenancy, was £160 per annum. However, the insolvency practitioner never responded with details of how to pay the rent. Following the appellant’s purchase of the subjects, the respondent’s solicitors sent the applicants a cheque covering rental payments due for 2021, 2022 and 2023, however, this was returned along with a denial as to the existence of any tenancy.

[17] The respondent claimed agricultural support payments in the name of the partnership under the IACS scheme. Such payments were made not to him personally, rather, to the partnership. He did not have a personal bank account until he turned 65 and so made use of his business account with such payments being made to the partnership. He did not distinguish in his own mind between himself and the family partnership of which he is the principal. He was farming the Subjects but using the partnership as a vehicle for his finances.

[18] We found the respondent to be a straightforward, credible witness who was trying his best to give truthful evidence. We do not consider that the various inconsistencies brought out during cross examination as against the contents of his witness statement and his pleadings (for example, in respect of the year during which his father retired from the partnership and when his wife became a partner) impugn his credibility. He was prepared to be corrected on points of detail, to his credit. He plainly takes more interest in farming the Subjects than spending time thinking about what are to him arcane legal niceties (eg which juristic entity holds the tenancy; the finer points of partnership law), however, that is hardly unusual for witnesses appearing in this court, still less a basis to impugn his credibility.

Lynsey Pender’s evidence

[19] Ms Pender is a solicitor who was instructed by the respondent in respect of his acquisition of land from LRD’s liquidators in 2017. She speaks to the partial renunciation by the respondent of the respondent’s interest in the lease in 2017. When she previously worked at Stevenson and Marshall LLP, she was instructed by the respondent in connection with his proposal to acquire land forming part of Muirside Estate from LRD’s liquidators. She was instructed to bid for land which the respondent advised he had been farming. Her instructions came from the respondent who was lead partner for the partnership, the Firm of J & D Keddie. The land which is the subject matter of this dispute is not the same as the transaction she was involved in. However, the respondent asserted that he had a tenancy over land which other parties wanted to buy and this alleged tendency became relevant when a global bid was being submitted.

Luke Devine’s evidence

[20] Mr Devine is a former director of LRD. LRD bought Muirside Estate, of which the subjects form part, from NCB in or around 1997/98. When LRD acquired the Estate there were a number of tenant farmers on the Estate, including the respondent who was the tenant of Overton Farm. For a time, the respondent continued to pay LRD the rent he had previously paid to NCB. In due course he purchased most of the land he had been tenant of (all of the holding other than the Subjects which he wanted to carry on working as a tenant) from LRD. Thereafter he consistently paid a reduced rent of £1,000 per annumfor the then remaining pockets of land which are the subject of this appeal.

Eddie Henderson’s evidence

[21] Mr Henderson is a chartered surveyor and managing partner of Hendersons Chartered Surveyors. He has provided professional services to the respondent for over 30 years. Bogside Farm is the respondent’s principal farming base although he rents neighbouring land at Overton Farm. A partial renunciation agreement, signed in 2017, references the earlier lease, reinforcing its existence. Beyond that Mr Henderson’s evidence appeared to be derived from what he was told by the respondent and, while we have no reason to doubt his credibility, we set it aside for present purposes.

Submissions for the appellant

[22] Mr Lean adopted his written submission. Although the application is described as an appeal against the Keeper’s decision, it does not follow the usual format of an appeal, as no findings of fact have yet been made. It is for the respondent to demonstrate that he is a tenant of a 1991 Act tenancy and accordingly eligible to register a pre-emptive right to buy. If the tenancy is held by the partnership rather than by the respondent personally, the appeal should be allowed. The respondent has failed to demonstrate the existence of a qualifying tenancy regulated by the 1991 Act. He is accordingly not entitled to register an interest in acquiring the subjects and the appeal should be allowed. The court should uphold the appellants’ first and second pleas-in-law and grant an order rescinding the registration.

[23] The respondent’s occupation of the subjects was only ever as a partner in the family firm. Any tenancy which may once have existed was held by the partnership, not by the respondent personally. Rent was paid by the partnership. Agricultural support payments were received by the partnership. The respondent has difficulty distinguishing between actions taken as an individual and those taken as a partner in the family business. This was evident in the inconsistencies between his oral evidence, his written statement and the pleadings lodged on his behalf. He ultimately accepted that the partnership had been responsible for paying rent over a number of years and had received agricultural support payments, not him personally.

[24] The only documentary evidence of sole trading is a single balance sheet from 1994. This is inconsistent with the broader history of the partnership. The only document which might be construed as a lease – the respondent’s Production 4 - is undated and informal. If it constitutes a lease at all, it commenced in 2008 and would therefore be regulated by the 2003 Act, not the 1991 Act.

[25] A lease to a partnership terminates upon a change in its composition. A lease held by a partnership cannot survive changes in its constitution unless it is a lease to a continuing house: Moray Estates Development v Butler 1999 SLT 1338. Here, the unwritten nature of the arrangement precludes it from being a lease to a house. The new partnership which came into existence on the assumption of the respondent’s daughter and the death of his wife has not been accepted as a tenant by the applicants. No tenancy exists in favour of any newly constituted partnership.

[26] The evidence of the respondent’s witnesses, including Ms Pender and Mr Henderson, are of limited value. Ms Pender acted on instructions from the partnership and Mr Henderson’s knowledge is derived from the respondent. The appellants’ own witnesses, while not directly involved in tenancy arrangements, confirm that no rent was accepted from the respondent following their acquisition of the land.

Submissions for the respondent

[27] Counsel adopted his written submissions. An appeal under section 25(11) is a de novo hearing, not a review of the Keeper’s decision: Gunn v Luyken 2018 SLCR 10. The burden lies on the Applicant to prove the averments made in support of the appeal. The appellant fails to aver facts supporting the contentions either that no lease exists over the Subjects, or that the entry in the Register of Crofts and Agricultural Land is materially inaccurate. The appeal is irrelevant.

[28] A lease entered into prior to 27 November 2003 need not be in writing: Morrison‑Low v Paterson 1985 S.C. (H.L.) 49. Evidence of parties’ actings may prove the existence of an unwritten lease: Andert Ltd v J & J Johnston 1987 SLT 268. Where rent is agreed and occupation taken, the law implies a term of one year: Shetland Islands Council v BP Petroleum Development Ltd 1990 SLT 82. Consensus in idem as to Subjects, rent, and duration is required: Gray v Edinburgh University 1962 SC 157. The continued occupation and payment of rent may give rise to an inescapable inference of a lease, even where the parties were unaware of its legal effect: Morrison-Low v Paterson 1985 SC (HL) 49per Lord Keith of Kinkel at 78.

[29] A 1991 Act tenancy may only be terminated in accordance with the 1991 Act or by operation of law: see the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1991, sections 3, 20, 21, and 23. The appellant has not produced any notice to quit, decree of removing, or other evidence of termination. The burden of proving termination lies with the party asserting it: Inland Revenue v Graham’s Trustees 1971 SLT 46.

[30] The respondent is, and has for many years been, the tenant of the Subjects under a secure tenancy governed by the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1991. He has occupied the Subjects continuously since the 1970s, initially as part of a family farming partnership and subsequently in his own right. Occupation was with the agreement of the landowner (first NCB and subsequently LRD). Rent was paid annually. The respondent’s own evidence to that effect is supported by the evidence of Mr Devine who confirms both that rent was accepted from the respondent and that his occupation of the Subjects was permitted. Partnership accounts spanning several years record rental payments for the Subjects. The existence of a lease is vouched by the deed signed by Mr Devine in 2008 for the purposes of the respondent’s subsidy application which, although not properly executed, is spoken to by both the respondent and Ms Pender, identifies the respondent as the tenant and is consistent with the evidence of Mr Devine. The 2017 renunciation also vouches the existence of a lease.

[31] Even if the original tenancy was granted to a partnership, the respondent continued in occupation and paid rent after the dissolution of the original firm. A new tenancy may arise in such circumstances. The respondent’s use of partnership funds to pay rent is immaterial.

[32] Such evidence as was adduced by the appellants’ witnesses is of limited assistance. Mr Haugh can speak only to the period following the appellant’s purchase of the land. He does not dispute the respondent’s prior occupation. Similarly, neither Mr Kenney nor Mr Carmichael have direct knowledge of the respondent’s tenancy. Mr Carmichael’s actions in executing the renunciation tend to contradict his denial of the lease.

Decision

[33] We find, on the basis of the respondent’s evidence, which we accept (and which is supported by that of Mr Devine) as follows. Following dissolution of the family partnership on the retirement of his father in 1993, the respondent continued to occupy the Subjects. He did so with the consent of NCB and subsequently LRD. He paid rent annually. Following the appellant’s purchase of the Subjects, he continued to tender rental payments, albeit they were refused by the appellant. We infer from these primary facts the existence of a new, unwritten lease in respect of which the respondent was tenant. This new lease came into being in or around 1993 and in any event prior to 27 November 2003. The lease is of ground used for agriculture. It is accordingly a 1991 Act tenancy. The respondent is the tenant in his own right of the Subjects under a secure tenancy governed by the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1991.

[34] We are reinforced in this view having regard to the available contemporaneous documentation, including (i) the accounts prepared for the year to Martinmas 1994 lodged with the court showing him as “John Keddie T/A J, D & J Keddie; (ii) sales particulars prepared on behalf of LRD in 1996 recording the respondent as being tenant in his own right; and (iii) subsequent partnership accounts for the firm he formed with his wife spanning several years which record rental payments for the Subjects. The respondent’s use of partnership funds to pay rent is unremarkable, particularly in circumstances where he did not have a personal bank account and standing his obvious tendency not to distinguish in his own mind between his own business interests and those of various family partnerships. The unsigned deed signed by Mr Devine in 2008 for the purposes of subsidy application, while not itself a lease, is further evidence of a pre-existing lease in respect of which the respondent is tenant, as is the 2017 renunciation running in the name of the respondent. The Keeper was correct to refuse the appellant’s challenge to the registration of the respondent’s notice under section 25(1) of the 2003 Act as entry number AT1700 in the RCIL.

Disposal

[35] We refuse the appeal. We appoint parties to enrol any motions in respect of the question of expenses within 21 days of the date of intimation of this decision. In the event of any such motion being opposed, parties should advise the court whether they wish a hearing or are content for the question of expenses to be determined on the basis of written submissions.
parties: in the appeal under section 25(11) of the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 2003 by Comrie Development Company Limited Appellant against John Keddie Respondent

title: George Ross Applicant against Robert Stuart Franklin and Helen Jane Franklin Respondents And Robert Stuart Franklin and Helen Jane Franklin Applicants against George Ross Respondent [2025] SLC 8
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2025] SLC 8,
Case reference: SLC/1/21 and SLC/36/21

OPINION OF THE COURT

Court members: Mrs Deborah Lovell,
Mr John A Smith

George Ross
Applicant
against
Robert Stuart Franklin and Helen Jane Franklin
Respondents
And
Robert Stuart Franklin and Helen Jane Franklin
Applicants
against
George Ross
Respondent

Subjects: Land at West Gruinards

The Crofters (Scotland) Act, 1993

SLC/1/21

Applicants: Ross; Inkster

Respondent: Franklin; Murchison

SLC/36/21

Applicants: Franklin; Murchison

Respondent: Ross; Inkster

7 August 2025

Introduction

[1] This decision relates to two applications in respect of the same croft, collectively known as West Gruinards in the County of Sutherland, registered with the Crofting Commission and extending in total to 316.57 ha or thereby.

The croft

[2] The croft subject to the applications comprises a number of separate and constituent areas. As a reference point we include a copy of a plan produced by Galbraith (lodged as part of the landlords’ expert’s independent report dated 13 June 2023 referred to later in this decision as “the Galbraith report”) which shows these constituent areas. This plan forms part 1A of the schedule to this decision (the “Galbraith plan”).

[3] The constituent areas are:

the croft with Crofting Commission number R2124 (C169) comprising an area of 17.4 hectares or thereby (measured by Galbraith as 18.18 hectares) shown outlined in red on the Galbraith plan;

the croft with Crofting Commission number R2125 (C170) comprising an area of 15.37 hectares or thereby (measured by Galbraith as 13.59 hectares) shown outlined in blue on the Galbraith plan; and

the croft with Crofting Commission number R2126 (C179). It should be noted here that the original application referred to this as comprising an area of 82.07 hectares or thereby and including two apportionments per the plan at schedule part 1B(3)(i) (“plan B3(i)”) which was the plan included with the crofter’s application. During the course of the application in 2022 the crofter acquired a further apportionment (in two parts) extending to 3.6 hectares as part of R2126. The crofter’s application was amended by February 2024 to make reference to this third apportionment. That apportionment is approximately the areas shown shaded red and blue on the Galbraith plan. The plan included at part 1B(3)(iii) of the schedule (“plan B3(iii)”) (which is the plan from the order on the Crofting Commission’s website) shows the extent of the third apportionment in darker blue on that plan. It can been seen more clearly from plan B3(iii) that this apportionment is in two parts (separated by another apportioned area, shaded purple, which does not pertain to this case). The Crofting Register has since been updated to the plan included as part 1B(3)(ii) of the schedule (“plan B3(ii)”) which shows the apportionment marked “Area 4” and “Area 5”. The Galbraith plan defines croft R2126 as measuring 282.57 hectares outlined in purple and the Galbraith report (at paragraph 3.1) further describes R2126 as:

“incorporating 4 areas of permanently apportioned land, which are all delineated separately on the plan, and which I understand are included in the application to purchase.”

We will refer to the darker blue shaded area on plan B3(iii) as the “western apportionment”.

[4] Within the purple outlined area on the Galbraith plan are various parts which are referred to in this decision as follows:

the areas shaded green being the original in-bye croft;

the area shaded pink comprising a previously apportioned area and what we refer to in this decision as the “northern apportionment” (and labelled as such on the plan). This is also shown on plan B3(ii) as “Area 3”; and

the area shaded purple also comprising a previously apportioned area and what we refer to in this decision as the “southern apportionment” (also labelled as such on the plan). This is also shown on plan B3(ii) as “Area 2”.

[5] We have noted the following additional point from the Galbraith report (at paragraph 3.1 supra):

“The total area of the croft land under consideration is therefore 314.34 Ha (776.73 acres). Please note the areas quoted in this section differ to those recorded in the Register of Crofts, but are based on the registered croft boundaries and are therefore considered to be more accurate than what shows on the Register of Crofts.”

We make no further comment on the area measurements. This was not raised as an issue by either party.

[6] For the purposes of this decision we will treat the crofter’s application to purchase to be in respect of the three areas shown on the plans collectively forming part 1B(1), 1B(2) and 1B(3)(ii) of the schedule to this decision (plans 1B(1) and 1B(2) of which formed the productions referred to in the original application to us). We will refer to those areas, collectively in this decision, as “the croft”.

The apportionments and the lochs

[7] The two parts of the western apportionment are adjacent to the northern apportionment (in each case, on its west). The southern apportionment is adjacent to the northern apportionment (on its south). The southern apportionment is also adjacent to a loch known as Loch a’ Bhaid-bheithe (and referred to as “Loch BB” for the purposes of this decision). Loch BB and Loch Amat can be seen on the extract part of the plan of the registered extent of the landlords’ estate (registered in the Land Register for Scotland under title number ROS10488). A section of the title plan included at schedule part 1C of the schedule to this decision (“plan 1C”) shows the extent of the landlords’ ownership (in each case shaded pink) of each loch.

The applications

[8] The first application, application SLC/1/21, was brought by the crofter, Mr Ross, to purchase his croft in terms of the provisions of section 12 of the Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993. The crofter’s application SLC/1/21 was received by the court on 5 January 2021. The application is opposed by the landlords, Mr and Mrs Franklin, under section 13(2)(b) of the 1993 Act on the basis that to grant the application would cause a substantial degree of hardship to the landlords.

[9] The second application, application SLC/36/21 was brought by the landlords, Mr and Mrs Franklin, for resumption of part of the croft under the provisions of section 20 of the 1993 Act. The resumption area is shown on a plan by Galbraith lodged as a production and forming part 1D of the schedule to this decision. The landlords’ application was received by the court on 24 March 2021. It is opposed by the crofter, Mr Ross, on the basis that the requisite tests set out in section 20 of the 1993 Act have not been met by the landlords.

[10] For the purposes of this decision we will refer to Mr Ross as the “crofter” and to Mr and Mrs Franklin as the ‘landlords’ for their respective interests in each application.

The landlords’ estate

[11] The croft forms part and portion of all and whole the lands and Estate of Gruinards, registered in the Land Register under title number ROS10488 and owned in common by the landlords. The landlords acquired the estate on 30 September 2016 (with registration on 10 October 2016).

[12] The landlords’ estate includes other crofted land held by two other crofters, namely Mr Brian Ross (Mid Gruinards, Ardgay, Sutherland) and Mr Derek Matheson (Creag Mhor, Wester Gruinards, Ardgay, Sutherland). By Order dated 12 April 2023 (SLC/90/22) the Land court authorised the landlords’ resumption of two areas of ground extending to 50.03 hectares in total or thereby, forming part of Mr Brian Ross’ croft at Mid Gruinards, under section 20 of the 1993 Act, for the purposes of forestry creation.

Procedure

[13] By order dated 27 October 2023 the court appointed both applications to be heard concurrently. It was decided that the substantive issues for both would best be resolved by hearing a full proof on both applications together.

[14] We heard evidence on 5, 6 and 7 November 2024 at a diet of proof conducted in Inverness Justice Centre. We heard submissions at Edinburgh on 26 November 2024. Mr Inkster of Inksters Solicitors appeared on behalf of the crofter. Mr Murchison of Murchison Law appeared on behalf of the landlords. The court carried out a site inspection on 16 April 2025.

[15] At the proof and in advance of witness evidence being led, the court dealt with a number of preliminary matters at the request of the parties. At the request of Mr Murchison, the court agreed to issue specific directions to all witnesses to refrain from discussing or disclosing evidence, including on social media, until conclusion of the proceedings. Further productions were lodged (including a copy of a joint minute between the experts, referred to later) and some minor referencing errors in the lists of authorities and productions were corrected. It was noted that certain productions had been lodged separately in both cases and accordingly parties would require to be clear with the referencing when directing witnesses to productions. At the request of Mr Inkster the court agreed to source and provide copies of certain past cases which had not been published.

[16] The court subsequently asked the parties for further submissions on the case of Kennedy v Smith SLC/81/15 which had not been previously cited by either party. Written submissions were received on 10 July 2025 for consideration by the court.

Authorities

[17] The parties lodged and referenced a large number of authorities. We noted that some decisions referred to by the parties in their submissions were not within the list of authorities lodged and vice versa. Some cases were cited or referred to by party but using different (from the other party and also from the version lodged) reports of the decision. For ease of reference, we have reproduced a list of authorities, including the main statutory provisions referred to in this decision, in part 2 of the schedule to this decision.

Evidence

Expert reports, joint minute and evidence

[18] In advance of the proof reports and valuations of experts appointed by each of the parties, Mr Atholl Newlands (crofter) and Ms Clare Acheson (landlords), were lodged along with a joint minute from both (referred to later). The expert evidence is critical to a number of matters in this decision. Accordingly, for ease, we have summarised the evidence presented by each expert across their reports, joint minute and evidence led at the proof in the following paragraphs.

Report of expert witness for the crofter: Mr Atholl Newlands, partner, Bowlts chartered surveyors, Member, RICS

[19] Mr Newlands was appointed on behalf of the crofter to prepare a rental assessment of crofts R2124, R2125 and R2126 and a valuation of the resumption site (as two house sites). This croft rental assessment was produced in his report dated 14 February 2024 and the house site valuations in his report dated 26 February 2024 (both lodged as productions). The basis and methodology of valuation of the croft were set out in part 9 of his report and the croft value was assessed on a market rental value of £565 per annum. The basis of valuation of the house sites was set out in part 7 of his report (being open market value of the two existing buildings and land) and each site assessed as having a value of £55,000.

Report of expert witness for the landlords: Ms Clare Acheson, partner, Galbraith, Member, RICS

[20] Ms Acheson produced the Gabraith report referred to earlier relative to her assessment of the fair rent payable in respect of the croft. In this report, Ms Acheson provided two fair rent valuations: the first based on current agricultural use only (paragraph 4 of her report) and the second being an ‘alternative purposeful use’ (paragraph 5 of her report). In doing so, she had used published data and an applied average. She had visited the croft once. She had not seen any farm accounts. Her value of the fair rent assessed on an agricultural basis was £2,238 per annum and assessed on an alternative purposeful use basis was £3,881.23 per annum.

Joint minute of the experts

[21] As ordained by the court, Mr Newlands and Ms Acheson met to prepare a joint minute setting out points of agreement and disagreement, to be read alongside their reports. That joint minute, dated 30 August 2024, set out the position of each expert under the following headings:

Purchase application: (1) (i) “Fair rent for West Gruinards Croft – agricultural basis” and (ii) “Fair Rent – Consideration of alternative purposeful use”; and (2) “Valuation of Reserved Timber”; and

Application to resume: (1) “Valuation of buildings for resumption on basis that redevelopment is within permitted development. Valuation with and without planning permission”; and (2) “Requirements (including access and duration) and likely cost of surveys related to birds, bats etc”.

Joint minute: Purchase application

[22] In respect of the “fair rent – agricultural basis” the experts agreed to follow the methodology set out in Ms Acheson’s report. They agreed that the stocking level for the croft should be 210 ewes but after that they applied differing calculations to come to their individual conclusions. Ms Acheson’s assessed rent was £2,143.82 while Mr Newlands’ was £1,530.22.The valuation of reserved timber was agreed at £8,500.

[23] On the “fair rent – alternative purposeful use basis” the experts were not agreed with the approach. Mr Newlands was not instructed to deal with the question of the hypothetical tenant and has never seen this test before. His concerns around the use of this approach had been raised and discussed with Ms Acheson at the meeting to agree the joint minute and were recorded as comments in the joint minute.

Joint minute: Resumption application

[24] In respect of the valuation of the buildings for resumption the assessment of the experts in the joint minute was:

“The market value of the buildings without planning permission is likely to be c.£25,000-£30,000 per site. The market value of the buildings with planning permission in place might be £55,000-£60,000 per site.”

Evidence of experts at the hearing

[25] The court heard from both experts on the second day of the evidential hearing. The court agreed to allow the evidence of Ms Acheson to be heard ‘out of order’ in order to accommodate a prior commitment on her part. Ms Acheson’s evidence was therefore heard before that of Mr Newlands as expert witness for the crofter. In the course of Mr Newlands giving evidence it was noted by the landlords’ agent that it was not possible for certain comments and concerns raised by Mr Newlands on the proposed “fair rent – alternative purposeful use basis” to be put to Ms Acheson, Ms Acheson already having been discharged as a witness by that time. Given that Mr Newlands had not been instructed to deal with such methodology but, by his own evidence, had expressed his concerns at the meeting of the experts (which concerns were summarised in the joint minute), it is our view that Ms Acheson had had fair notice of the points of concern ahead of her appearance. She was given the opportunity to respond to and comment on such. Accordingly the court does not consider that this has had any bearing on the decision reached as set out below.

Ms Acheson

Purchase application

[26] With regard to the agricultural use fair rent valuation, she and Mr Newlands were agreed on the amount attributable to the sheep margin but not on the subsidies. There was a question between them over whether the fair rent should be based on current or future rent. As the levels 2 years away are not known and the position is speculative a 30% discount had been applied.

[27] The alternative purposeful use approach was not an agreed position with Mr Newlands and she had not used this method of valuation before. It has not been done on this basis before to her knowledge. She had undertaken a desktop survey only. She was proposing a combined use for planting or forestry (native woodland rather than commercial) and agriculture. She had rejected tourism as a prospective use on the basis of the capital outlay required and the lack of demand.

[28] She acknowledged that there were risks with the approach. Unless carbon units were sold (after year 5), it would take 6 years to get to a profit basis. A party doing this would, therefore, need some way to finance themselves until then. There are risks to selling units. A unit can only be sold once and only when it is validated. The main risks for a landowner is that they may have no valid claim for any subsidy (which needs to come from an accredited scheme) and there is a liability to the party to whom the unit is sold if the expected value is not delivered. Presently there are two more years guaranteed at the current rates. The impact on rents is unclear: this is a capital income stream and involves a degree of long‑term commitment.

[29] She was not aware of the proposed windfarm development on the common grazing. She acknowledged this may impact on her proposal with potential issues around the planting of trees affecting any proposed development. On the other hand, the developer may carry out a compensatory planting scheme as part of the development and that could deliver benefit to the croft. She agreed that there is usually an exclusion zone but that native woodland is likely to be less disruptive than commercial.

Resumption application

[30] Valuation ranges were given in the joint minute for the buildings with and without planning permission. The valuation with the benefit of planning is higher as it reflects additional time and costs to get planning due to the presence of wildlife. She was not aware of the Franklins’ proposals to demolish the existing buildings and rebuild these for use as holiday lets. In her view there was a lack of demand for such use. The capital expenditure involved was unlikely to be readily recovered through the likely levels of holiday rental income.

Mr Newlands

Purchase application

[31] He has concerns around the “alternative purposeful use” test advanced by the landlords and set out in the Galbraith report. He has never seen the “alternative purposeful use” test used before. He accepts that Ms Acheson’s approach is reasonable and balanced and he has no issues with her methodology or assumptions nor any reason to doubt her desktop analysis or integrity. However in his view there are a number of costs, risks and limitations associated with proposed scheme as set out that means it is not viable.

[32] In his view the scheme would not be viable without addressing fundamental issues in the approach. The first is that an application for any woodland creation scheme must be made and approved. Surveys will then determine the suitability for such a scheme. There are then significant start up costs to implement the scheme and risks associated with it once built. The second issue is that the approach relies on an income stream from carbon credits which carry inherent risks in actual realisation and the current rates for which are only guaranteed for another 2 years. As a tenant crofter cannot get the carbon without the landlords consent, both the landlords and the tenant need to sign up. It was not clear that the scheme binds successors, even where the crofter is the owner rather than tenant. Ms Acheson’s indicative scheme showed that it could take up to 6 years to get to a profit basis. A party doing this would, therefore, need some way to fina.nce themselves until then. In Mr Newland’s view, the risks with the approach are so high, no hypothetical tenant would take them.

Resumption application

[33] He was not previously aware of the landlords’ proposed demolition and rebuild of the two derelict buildings for use as holiday lets. He had discounted tourism as a viable purposeful use by a crofter in his report and confirmed the same comments would apply to the landlords’ proposals. He and Ms Acheson are in agreement in discounting tourism as a viable use though he did accept that he has no direct experience in what he referred to as a difficult area.

Other witness evidence

[34] In advance of the hearing, witness statements and productions were lodged by each of the parties. As the two applications were being heard concurrently, all witnesses gave evidence on relevant matters for both applications. Each witness adopted their statements and spoke to those statements and the productions, all of which had been lodged into process. As the application to purchase was received first, the crofter led their witness evidence first (other than the evidence of Ms Acheson, taken out of turn, as referred to above). We do not attempt to summarise all the evidence given by witnesses or established by the documentary productions. Although all evidence led has been considered thoroughly we will set out the main issues of fact upon which our decision is based and, where appropriate, make reference to the evidence bearing on these issues.

[35] We took note of the fact that Dr Ross’ witness statements (presented as an affidavit and then supplementary witness statement), in each case, states that she has read the witness statement and supplementary witness statement of her husband, the crofter and “can confirm and agree with everything stated in that Witness Statement”. Neither statement set relevant matters out in her own words. Each of Mr and Mrs Franklin’s supplementary witness statements also, in part, made reference to agreeing with or endorsing the other’s supplementary statement. Such statements are not statements made in the witnesses own words setting out their personal knowledge and observations. In each case we therefore gave weight to the direct evidence heard from each witness over such statements. While Dr Ross is not a party to the application and should have provided her own statement, we do not consider this impacted on Dr Ross’s credibility.

[36] As a general observation, we found all witnesses to be credible and reliable in their accounts. It was evident that the crofter and the landlords held differing views on several key matters, and the tone of prior communications and the overall dispute has obviously at times been acrimonious. However, even where we preferred one account over another, we did not consider differences in any account to be the result of any dishonesty on the part of any witness. Rather, they appeared to reflect genuine divergences in perspective, shaped by each party’s individual experiences and understanding. Where possible, we assessed their positions against independent evidence. Having been appointed by the court to confer on certain relevant issues, we gave the opinions of the expert witnesses appropriate and considered weight. For the present purposes, we simply give an indication of the broad scope of the evidence given by each witness in the following paragraphs.

Submissions

[79] The court received very detailed notes of argument and written submissions from each of the parties in advance of the hearing on 5, 6 and 7 November 2024. The parties respectively adopted these positions in the hearing. The position of each of the parties in respect of each application is summarised in the following paragraphs. In each case the court was invited by each of the parties to find a considerable number of facts as set out in the submissions to be proven. Given that considerable number, we see no merit in listing each fact and instead have referred to what we consider to be the relevant facts supported by the evidence led in our discussion below.

Application to purchase - arguments led for the crofter

[80] On the basis of the court finding the (73) facts as stated, the landlords are not able to demonstrate the requirements of section 13(2) of the 1993 Act, namely either or both a substantial degree of hardship would be caused to the landlords or it would be substantially detrimental to the interests of sound management of the landlords’ estate if the application was granted.

[81] The landlords put forward the position that substantial hardship will be caused to the landlords in two core ways should the crofter’s application be granted, namely: (1) material risk to a proposed windfarm development proceeding and (2) loss of access to or use of the western side of the landlords’ estate, in particular Loch BB. Submissions in respect of the first issue (the windfarm development) were only introduced by the landlords and were introduced by them at a later stage (16 June 2023) than the original application (30 March 2021).

[82] The hardship to the landlord or detriment to the estate requires to be of a substantial nature for any objection to succeed (Mackay v Trustees of Miss S N Barr 1981 SLCR App 76 and Geddes v Martin 1987 SLCR 104). The test is a high test (Waugh v Thrumster Estate Limited (Brickigoe) (Application RN SLC/156/05 – 18 August 2006)). Cases cannot be decided on speculation but on the evidence led and submissions made (Rodenhurst v Thrumster Estate Limited (Application RN SLC/26/11 – 17 July 2015 referred to).

[83] In response to a suggestion by the landlords that, in establishing hardship, the court is to have regard to the proportion of the land to be purchased as it bears to the size of the estate (the higher the proportion, the greater the risk of hardship), the cases of Geddes v Martin (supra) and Rodenhurst v Thrumster Estate Limited (supra) are relevant. Geddes can be distinguished as here, proportionately, the croft to be acquired compared to the estate is much smaller than in Geddes. In any event, the landlords have led no evidence of any significant attempt at management that would be affected should the application be granted (Rodenhurst v Thrumster Estate Limited (supra)).

First core way: windfarm development

[84] Any information presented to the court has been sketchy at best. No heads of terms were produced to the court and the exclusivity agreement produced incorrectly defines the crofter’s apportionments as being part of the common grazing. The draft option agreement produced excludes the apportionments from the option site. Any current plans to develop a windfarm are in respect of 10 turbines on the common grazing and not on the apportionments, in particular the southern apportionment.

[85] No evidence has been led by the landlords, the windfarm developer or any independent windfarm developer of any impact on the proposed development by the grant of the crofter’s application. No evidence has been led by the landlords that the landlords would have any greater degree of control over activities on the crofter’s land that might affect the proposed development if the application was refused than they would have should it be granted. Indeed evidence to the contrary has been led. When making a determination of whether a landlord would be caused a substantial degree of hardship, a comparison of the positions with or without the order is required (Fraser v MacKintosh 1995 SLCR 91 and Waugh v Thrumster Estate Ltd (South Yarrows) Application RN SLC/157/05 – 18 August 2006).

[86] No detailed financial breakdown has been provided by the landlords as to any financial hardship that might occur. At most, the hardship would equate to a speculative 50% of the rental income of one turbine that may possibly be located on the southern apportionment. If the application was granted it would not preclude the developer seeking the consent of the crofter to an 11th turbine on the southern apportionment. The landlords would benefit from 50% of the rental income during the subsisting 10 year clawback security period, part of any acquisition order.

[87] The onus is on the landlords to present evidence to support their case (Macaskill v Basil Baird & Sons Ltd and Another 1986 SLCR 133). The cases of MacDonald v Hilleary 1992 SLCR 51, Mackay v Trustees of Miss S N Barr 1981 (supra), Geddes v Martin (supra), Rodenhurst v Thrumster Estate Limited (supra), Fraser v MacKintosh (supra) and Waugh v Thrumster Estate Ltd (South Yarrows) (supra) are all authority that, when applied to the found facts, the landlords have not met the high test required.

[88] Macaskill v Basil Baird & Sons Limited and Another (supra) and MacDonald v Hilleary (supra) are cases where not enough detail was presented to allow the court to make a decision based on hardship or detriment to sound estate management. This is the case here. On the contrary evidence points to there being no such hardship or detriment to sound estate management.

[89] Instead of being able to decide based on evidence led and submissions made, the court has been invited by the landlords to consider what might happen with a windfarm development on the estate on an anticipated or speculative basis. Any comparison of the position of the landlords with or without the order being granted would essentially show no difference. If anything it would show the landlords in a better position with the order granted given the sale price receipt.

Second core way – Loch BB

[90] On the second core way, namely access to and use of the western side of the estate, in particular Loch BB, no evidence was led relative to the western side. The only issue of real concern would appear to be access to and use of Loch BB. Loch BB is not used by the landlords for estate purposes but rather for private leisure purposes only. The loss of Loch BB would not impact financially but emotionally. Waugh v Thrumster Estate Ltd (South Yarrows) 2006 SLCR (2) 53 considered emotional hardship and concluded that, as the party in that case was a limited company, it was not capable of suffering emotional hardship. However the court had not been referred to Mackenzie v Hardy and Another 1998 SLCR 49 which dealt with emotional hardship.

[91] The loss of Loch BB does not provide anywhere near the degree of hardship necessary to warrant refusal of the application. There is a question of whether emotional hardship can be established on the basis of the comparison test in Fraser v MacKintosh. Following the reasoning in Waugh v Thrumster Estate Ltd (South Yarrows) (supra) it is irrelevant that the business is not held in the name of a limited company given that the estate is owned by the landlords as a business. Granting the application will not deprive the landlords of the right to access and use Loch BB as they will have the right to roam for recreational purposes. A sporting lease will be granted for a right to fish for trout for 21 years: this despite the fact that they have never fished for estate purposes.

Inclusion of lochs in application

[92] The landlords’ position is that, as the two lochs are not included in the Crofting Register they cannot form part of the purchase application. This ignores the law relating to ownership of lochs as set out in Rankine, Reid, Gloag & Henderson, Robbie, Gordon and Stair, which textbooks refer to a number of relevant case authorities to support their stated propositions. The result is that if the application is granted, the lochs in so far as bounded by the croft will be included as a pertinent of the grant.

[93] It would be anomalous to exclude the lochs and leave these in estate ownership lying within owner/occupied crofts. It would also negate the need for sporting leases for trout fishing which exist for the reason that lochs and rivers will pass into the ownership of crofters exercising their rights to buy when these crofts have lochs or rivers on their boundaries. On the estate when Derek Matheson purchased his croft the adjacent river was not excluded from his title and a sporting lease was granted for brown trout fishing for 21 years.

Southern apportionment

[94] The landlords have suggested that the southern apportionment is not contiguous or adjacent to the croft and therefore should be excluded from the crofter’s acquisition. The meaning of “adjacent or contiguous” was considered by the case of Gillies v Countess of Sutherland’s Trs 1978 SLT (Land Ct) 2 and Ross v Trustees of Miss S N Barr 1994 SLCR 60 at 71. All apportionments including the southern apportionment are contiguous or adjacent to any other part of the croft. The crofts and apportionments together form one complete unit with no separation between them.

[95] The landlords have suggested that the southern apportionment is not used by the crofter and, to the extent that it is used, it is not worked in conjunction with his croft. It is grazed throughout the year and used overnight by sheep in the summer. The sheep are free to roam as the crofter is managing the croft for the benefit of biodiversity, namely breeding waders.

Area also subject to application to resume

[96] This should be included with the acquisition and the resumption refused for the reasons submitted in that application. Concerns of the landlords around the condition of the buildings on the area will vanish once the crofter has bought (Bowman v Guthrie 1997 SLCR 40).

Terms and conditions of purchase

[97] The terms and conditions of the purchase, including the consideration payable to the landlords are to be determined by the court in terms of section 13 and section 14 of the 1993 Act.
