In granting the application the court should consider imposing terms and conditions as set out, namely: the purchase to be subject to the existing 175 year shooting lease and a new 21 year brown trout fishing lease in Loch BB at £1 per annum granted; mineral rights reserved and a clawback security granted in the usual way; rent for the deemed croft (grazing rights in the common grazings) fixed by the court; no servitudes reserved for estate purposes; crofter to produce the title plan; and mutual fences to be mutually maintained. Reserved timber should be valued at the agreed valuation of £8,500. Any access rights required by the landlords would be granted in the sporting lease and not reserved in the conveyance.

[98] The experts for each party have proposed adjusted fair rents in terms of their joint minute and evidence. The landlords have suggested that the fair rent should be higher, taking into account a hypothetical tenant carrying out a forestry scheme on the croft. There is no basis for assessment in this manner. It is also not supported by the landlords’ position that it does not wish any forestry on the croft in case that affects the proposed windfarm development. It should be assessed in line with Borland v Crofters on the Lochend Estate (Applications RN SLC/137/17, SLC/138/17, SLC/139/17, SLC/140/17 – 7 June 2019) and fixed by the court in terms of section 14(2) of the 1993 Act.

[99] The landlord’s view is that, if the court does not agree, in any event the assessed rent should be no greater than the landlords’ expert and no lower than the crofter’s expert values is not sound. These are to assist the court but the court is the expert and should fix the rent. The only minimum figure the court requires to consider is the minimum level of £30 (Anderton v Crofters having rights in crofts on the Vaila Estate (Application RN SLC/68/22 – 6 February 2024)).

[100] A timetable should be laid down by the court for the grant of conveyancing and associated deeds to avoid any delay (such as was experienced in Rodenhurst v Thrumster Estate Limited (supra) .

[101] Expenses should be reserved pending the court’s decision.

Application to purchase - arguments led by the landlords

[102] There will be substantial hardship to the landlords if the order is granted, arising from two consequences. The first is to risk a proposed windfarm development situated primarily on the common grazing but with a possible turbine requirement on the croft (on the southern apportionment) from either going ahead only on a restricted basis or not going ahead at all. The second is the restriction of access to and use of retained land on the western side of the landlords’ estate, in particular Loch BB. Substantial hardship need not be financial: it can be emotional.

Windfarm development

[103] The crofter’s sole ground of opposition to the landlords’ position is that there can be no substantial hardship because the windfarm development is merely speculative. That was not supported by the evidence. An exclusivity agreement has been entered into and a first draft option and lease provided to the landlords. The extent of the area covered by the exclusivity agreement (which includes both crofter’s apportionments and designated wild land) is entirely understandable when the requirement for wind protection zones and restrictions on development within the vicinity of the turbines is factored in. A site inspection of the topography would assist the court in understanding why the exclusivity agreement covers the area it does.

[104] There is a constraint on the number of turbines within the common grazing due to the designated wild land. It is possible that a 10 turbine development may not be feasible but an 11 turbine development will be. Even in a 10 turbine development the wind protection zone and non-development areas will include the land the crofter seeks to purchase. The income to the estate of the proposed development is likely to be at least £16 million over the 37 year period of the lease.

[105] The estate when acquired by the landlords was in a run-down condition. It is still running at a loss. There is a stark contrast between the income of the estate without the development and the income of the estate should it go ahead. That increased income stream would benefit the crofters on the estate. The crofter has demonstrated opposition to any windfarm development and therefore there is no basis for concluding that he will co-operate in progressing a windfarm should he acquire ownership of the croft. If the crofter’s application succeeds there is a real danger to the progress of a windfarm development. The landlords’ evidence on this point should be preferred as being credible and reliable when compared to the crofter. The crofter’s position that the windfarm development is merely speculative cannot be sustained.

[106] If the court considers that there is a degree of contingency or uncertainty in the evidence as to the effect of making the order then the court should consider that ‘substantial hardship’ can be contrasted conceptually with an insubstantial degree of hardship. The policy of the 1993 Act appears intended to exclude minor or trivial hardship only. The factors on which the court heard evidence including the sums involved in achieving planning, the constrained area for development and the crofter’s hostile (or at best unpredictable) attitude to the development means that a finding of substantial hardship is appropriate even if viewed as a loss of opportunity.

[107] Loss of opportunity is a recognised form of loss (Kyle v P & J Stormonth Darling WS 1992 SC 57). English law recognises this as real loss within the law of damages (Chaplin v Hicks 1911 2 KB 786). The crofter would have to satisfy the court that there is only a very small chance the opportunity to progress the windfarm would be lost in order to say there would be no hardship caused. In the absence of that there is the degree of materiality that brings the case within the realm of a substantial degree of hardship.

Southern apportionment

[108] The landlords do not seek to advance any argument that substantial detriment will be caused by being unable to enforce the duty of cultivation (Malone v Pattinson (Application RN SLC/39/17 – 10 October 2018). Rather the southern apportionment should be excluded on the basis that this area is not sufficiently adjacent or contiguous to any other part of the croft. The cases of Gillies v Countess of Sutherland Trs (supra) and Ross v Trustees of Miss N Barr (supra) are specifically referred to in respect of the principles of adjacency.

[109] The evidence of Mr Oxley was that he has never seen stock on the southern apportionment. The crofter concedes that, to the extent he uses it at all, it is used differently from other parts of the croft. Some of the photos lodged in evidence were taken after Mr Oxley’s statement. To the extent it is worked at all, it is not worked in the same way as the rest of the croft.

Use of Loch BB

[110] The Franklins gave evidence of their use of and access to Loch BB and its importance to their family and enjoyment of the estate. If the purchase were to proceed then they have justifiable concerns from the past actions of the crofter that they would be prevented from accessing Loch BB in the future.

[111] In the event that the court was minded to make the purchase order then this should be subject to such terms and conditions as the court thinks appropriate in terms of section 13 of the 1993 Act having regard to the location and layout of the croft and also existing title conditions (as the same are defined in section 122 of the Title Conditions (Scotland) Act 2003).

[112] Mineral rights are reserved in terms of section 13(1)(a) of the 1993 Act. The landlords should have all appropriate ancillary rights consistent with Anderson v Williamson 1997 SLCR 23. The landlords and those authorised by them should have the right to mine including a right to enter the surface.

[113] The value of the reserved timber is agreed at £8,500. There should be a 10 year claw back security under sections 13(4) and 14(3) of the 1993 Act. Rent for the deemed croft consisting of grazing rights in the common grazing should be set by the court.

[114] The areas subject to the landlords’ application to resume should be excluded (referencing the court’s comments in Davie v The Trustees of the Countess of Sutherland’s No.3 Settlement SLC 2005 SLCR 137 at p162). Servitudes should be granted for drainage, water, electricity and services required for normal estate management or in connection with the resumed land. Mutual fences should be mutually maintained per the approach in Grant v Countess of Seafield’s Trs 1979 SLT (Land Ct) 7 and Nevis Estates Ltd v Cameron 2011 SLCR 117. The crofter should produce the title plan.

[115] Unhindered rights of access for current estate business and any future business reasonably in contemplation, including access for sporting rights, access to Loch BB and Loch Amat (which otherwise would be landlocked in each case) and access to and service rights for buildings and sites subject of the landlords’ application to resume should be granted (Inverness Seafield Development Co Ltd v Mackintosh 2001 SC 406 at [13] and [14]).

[116] Pedestrian and vehicle access to the area for the purposes of allowing the developer to exercise rights contained in the exclusivity agreement should be granted. The estate should have all rights to allow for the development of a windfarm project. Not all rights re capable of being created as title conditions which is why the purchase order should be refused: title conditions alone will not meet a developer’s requirements. However, certain specific title conditions should be created in order to prevent competing or restricting development or activity. The parties will agree the precise wording, which failing the court should.

[117] The price should be determined under section 14(2) of the 1993 Act. Certain reserved rights in terms sufficient to support potential windfarm development and for any area resumed under the landlords’ application to resume should be granted.

[118] The landlords wish to make clear within the context of the right to buy application they have an esto plea in law that if [not [sic]] granted then the rent should be reviewed (Lawson v Lord Strathcona 1992 SLCR 67 and Agnew: Crofting Law at p85).

Application for resumption - arguments for landlords

[119] Acknowledging that the “reasonable purpose” test has regard to the good of the croft, the good of the estate, the public interest and the good of the crofting community, many and varied purposes have previously been determined as reasonable by the court. The landlords’ proposed redevelopment of the two ruinous buildings on the area subject of the application is a reasonable purpose in satisfaction of the test under section 20 of the 1993 Act.

[120] There is a weighing of factors to be undertaken. The court is permitted to take account of the factors identified at sections 20(1AA) and 20(1AC) of the 1993 Act when assessing the public interest test. While it is anticipated that the crofter will raise concerns over the presence of wildlife as falling with the factor identified within section 20(1AC)(a)(iv) of the 1993 Act, the joint position taken by the parties’ respective experts is both that planning permission for redevelopment would be granted and any planning permission would include measures to be taken for the appropriate protection of statutorily protected species.

[121] There are a number of factors supporting the resumption being for a reasonable purpose, including that the area to be resumed is modest, the landlords’ intended redevelopment for affordable holiday accommodation would provide employment, income for the estate and economic activity for the wider community and provide a solution to the dangers and risks posed by the ruinous state of the current buildings on the area to be resumed. Such redevelopment cannot take place until this area is resumed as proposed.

[122] The concerns of the crofter raised in regard to environmental and wildlife protection matters apply alike for his stated intended use of the buildings. The crofter has however provided no detailed proposals or information on any wildlife mitigation measures or works required. It is appropriate for the court to apply the same standard to both proposals when assessing reasonable purpose. It would be unusual for the court to reject the landlords’ proposal in comparison with the tentative or speculative proposal of the crofter. The quote for works produced by the crofter do not correspond with his stated intentions. A failure to address the state and condition of the buildings would not support the tour business proposal of the crofter. The objections put forward by the crofter to the landlords’ proposals relate more to matters for the assessment of the planning authority rather than to relevant considerations on whether or not the purpose is reasonable.

[123] An argument has been made by the crofter that the resumption should not be granted as no planning consent has been granted for the landlords’ proposed development. The experts have agreed that planning permission would be granted for the landlords’ proposed scheme of development and that such planning permission would include all necessary mitigation measures. The experts appointed by each of the landlords and crofter have jointly agreed that planning will be granted for the landlords’ proposal.

[124] Reliance is made on Practice Note (No. 1) Resumption Application of the court (“Practice Note 1”)). The current situation can be distinguished such that Practice Note 1 does not apply: in this case there is no intention to erect houses on bare land. Even if the court was to disagree with this, Lands Improvements Holdings Landmatch SARL v Cole (supra) is authority for the case that the practice note should not be treated as creating a rule in addition to the legislation. If the court holds that planning permission would be a requirement for any resumption then the application could be continued to allow this to be obtained. Rule 16 and Rule 1(1) [of The Rules of the Scottish Land Court Order 2014, SSI 2014 No 229] would permit this course of action. Indeed this would be an appropriate way to proceed where the obtaining of planning permission would incur significant costs and there is opposition from the crofter to any redevelopment taking place. To decide otherwise would mean every landlord would require to expend time and money with no guarantee the resumption would be granted.

[125] Compensation should be determined in terms of sections 20 and 21 of the 1993 Act. Section 21(2) provides that the share payable by the crofter is half the difference between the open market value and the crofting value. The crofting value will be the proportion of the current passing rent attributable to the resumed area multiplied by 15. The experts appointed by each of the landlords and crofter have agreed a valuation of £55,000 to £60,000 per site. The landlords are agreeable to a mid range valuation of £57,500 as representing the open market value. The landlords are prepared to concede that the likely apportioned crofting value is so negligible as to apply a nil value.

Application for resumption - arguments led by the crofter

[126] The landlords are seeking resumption of buildings which form part of the croft, are crofter’s improvements and are used by the crofter as an integral part of the croft. Specifically, they are used for storage, stock shelter, quad bike security and as a nature habitat for wildlife including two breeding barn owls. Such resumption is for the purpose of conversion to holiday lets. This is not a reasonable purpose having relation to the statutory test, namely having relation to the good of the croft, or of the estate or to the public interest or to the interests of the crofting community in the locality of the croft.

[127] The application was made only in response to the crofter’s application to purchase. The application is premature in any event as planning permission has not been applied for or granted. It is therefore contrary to Practice Note 1 of the court. The landlords’ invitation to the court to make any resumption order subject to planning within 6 months is at odds with the practice of granting resumption orders and with the crofter’s application to purchase.

[128] In considering the relevant tests, the fact the purpose for which a landlord seeks to resume the land is one of those referred to does not ipso facto mean that it is a reasonable purpose in all the circumstances requiring the application to be granted automatically (Mackay’s Trs v Colthart 1959 SLCR 43). Even where ex facie reasonable the landlord must lead evidence to meet any objections to the application (Clegg v MacPherson 1963 SLCR App 108; Secretary for State for Air v Macdonald 1962 SLCR App 30; Countess of Sutherland v Shareholder in Doll Common Grazings 1970 SLCR App 85; South Uist Estates Ltd v MacDonald 1983 SLCR 86). The crofter has set out many valid objections: the landlords have failed to lead evidence to meet these.

[129] The crofter’s plan is to repair and improve the buildings. This is long standing, well thought out and costed and predates the landlords’ interest in them. The landlords in contrast have not applied for planning permission nor costed their proposed development as part of their existing letting business or ascertained any likely return on investment. They have not explored alternative locations on the estate. Their original plan to renovate the buildings has changed to demolition and rebuild. Their current letting business has occupancy rates of only 10% and expert evidence is that there is no obvious demand for tourist accommodation in the area.

[130] In each of Buckworth v Ross 1925 SLCR 94 sets out similar circumstances: there the resumption was refused. In Walker v McEwan 1946 SLCR 14 the resumption was refused as it would “have detrimental effects on the working and amenity of the holding” and the same is the case here. If, as is the case here, the proposed resumption will be in the interests of the general public as providing employment, Mackay’s Trustees v Colthart 1959 SLCR 43 is authority that evidence of urgent demand in the area for work of the nature contemplated must be offered up. No evidence was led as to the demand for employment in holiday lets in the area. Evidence would also have to be shown that the landlords had considered other areas less suitable for sheep. No evidence was led to show other areas had been considered.

[131] The application in Lord Brocket’s Trustees v Hodgeson 1961 SLCR 25 was refused as it would result in the creation of “an island” on the croft and no demand for additional council houses had been established. The landlords’ proposal here would create such an island and no evidence of additional short term holiday letting demand had been led.

[132] In Secretary of State for Air v Macdonald 1962 SLCR App 90 the application for resumption was refused on the basis that the landlords had other vacant land that could be used. This was raised by the crofter as an objection which the landlords in that case failed to answer. The same is the case here. Grimersta Estate Ltd v MacLeod 1972 SLCR (App) 128 held that the benefit in granting the resumption for a dwellinghouse was outweighed by the damage done to the croft. This is the case here.

[133] Shaw v Cummings 1987 SLCR 157 reiterates the approach in the foregoing four cases. Portman Trustees v Macrae 1971 SLT (Land Ct) 6 should be followed as preferring the crofter’s proposed development proposals to the landlords’ alternatives. The instant case is similar to Beardsall v Bell 1975 SLT (Land Ct) 2, Dunbeath Estate Ltd v Gunn (No 1) 1988 SLCR 52 and Fountain International Ltd v MacDonald 1991 SLCR 84: in those cases, resumption was refused where the land was important for sheltering stock.

[134] The court should consider the matters provided for section 20(1AC) of the 1993 Act. There is no decided case law on the matter but the matters apply here.

[135] The application is contrary to the Practice Note 1 as planning permission has not been applied for or granted. The suggestion that Practice Note 1 does not apply to this situation is incorrect. The overriding principle is that the court requires to be satisfied not only that the resumption is for a reasonable purpose in terms of section 20 but also that the purpose will actually be carried out. The examples given by Practice Note 1 are merely indicative of certain scenarios to assist applicants and do not detract from that principle.

[136] In the time since submitting their application to resume, the landlords have taken no steps to instruct architects or apply for full planning permission required for their proposed development. It is irrelevant whether the resumed land is for use by the landlords as opposed to being conveyed to the crofter or another third party. It is the landlords who must satisfy the court in all respects that the resumption should be granted (South Uist) Estates Limited v MacDonald 1983 SLCR 86).

[137] Whilst the court stated in Lands Improvement Holdings Landmatch SARL v Cole (Application RN SLC/39/14) that practice notes were for guidance and not law and could not import conditions as absolute requirements they did say that the practice note’s purpose was “to give guidance as to what the court looked for as evidence that the purpose for which resumption was sought was realistic, credible and feasible.” There would have to be circumstances to justify departure from a practice note. The landlords’ argument to justify departure, namely that Practice Note 1 “created a rule in addition to the legislation, especially where the circumstances are not apt for the Practice Note to be applied”, does not apply here. It is apt for Practice Note 1 to be applied because planning permission is required in this instance for the development proposed. The landlords have things the wrong way round in asking the court to grant resumption so that they could instruct an architect and apply for planning. This is on a par with the situation in Land Improvements.

[138] The court has no power to recall any order once made. It is imperative that resumption of croft land should not be lightly authorised for purposes which may soon fail (Secretary of State for Scotland v Shareholders of Lealt & Culnacnock Common Grazings 1982 SLT (Land Ct) 20). This is the case here. Land Improvement cites a number of other cases, all of which are authority that resumptions do not require proof of reasonable purpose in the abstract but require proof of a relevant purpose for which it is reasonable to grant in all the circumstances relevant to the interests specified in the statutory provisions.

[139] There is no basis to make any order conditional on planning permission such as is sometimes done in windfarm resumptions. In those cases they are supported by tenants and not conditional on finding a developer. Agreements are already in place subject to authorisation of resumption. Further, as the application is conjoined with the crofter’s application to purchase the court could not logically order the purchase of the croft subject to a resumption which might fail.

[140] All questions of expenses should be reserved pending the court’s decision and then addressed in the usual way with written submissions following thereon.

Discussion and decision

[141] There appears to be no dispute as between the parties on the relevant and applicable legal principles which were set out in and summarised by Lord McGhie in Nevis Estates Limited and others v Cameron 2011 SLCR 83 at paras [19] - [25] and which we have applied to the facts in hand. Nevis concerned competing applications to purchase and resume without necessarily imposing any strict order of priority. The statutory tests for each are not mirror images and there is a public interest consideration in any application to resume which arguably takes priority over a purchase application (Nevis, supra).

[142] The matters for determination are: (first) whether the landlords have made out a sufficient case in support of their application for resumption and (second) whether the landlords are able to satisfy the court that substantial hardship will be caused should the crofter’s application to purchase be successful. The evidence led by each side related to the various matters of potential relevance to each of the issues before us. In each application the onus lies on the landlords: in the case of the application for partial resumption, that the test in section 20(1) of the 1993 Act has been met so as to allow resumption and in the case of the purchase application, the landlords must satisfy us that the test in section 13(2) of the 1993 Act has been met (Macaskill v Basil Baird & Sons Ltd and Another (supra)). The crofter led evidence to counter the landlords’ case and to support their position in respect of the inclusion of the southern apportionment and, by consequence, Loch BB.

[143] We have set out our position in respect of the landlords’ application to resume first.

Application to resume

[144] The landlords’ proposals have evolved since the application for resumption was lodged with the court. The original proposal was redevelopment of the two buildings on the resumption area and the current proposal is the demolition of the two existing buildings and erection of two new buildings in their place. The stated purpose for the resumption is two‑fold: to make safe what the landlords consider to be derelict and unsafe buildings and to take an opportunity to expand their existing holiday lettings business with two additional properties. In doing so, their existing staff of two would be increased, thus offering local employment.

[145] The crofter set out a number of objections to the proposal. In summary these are that the resumption will take land and buildings presently used for croft purposes out of the croft, resident wildlife will be disturbed, historic buildings will be demolished and the crofter will be unable to implement his own, longer term plans for the buildings and croft.

[146] In deciding whether the landlords proposals are for a reasonable purpose we have considered the limbs of the test set out in section 20(1) of the 1993 Act based on the evidence placed before us, together with the case authorities cited by the parties in their submissions.

Good of the croft

[147] We took particular account of the evidence of the crofter and Dr Ross regarding the routine use of the buildings for shelter for the flock and for storing hay. This was supported by the evidence of Mr McGillivray, albeit Mr McGillivray had only visited last autumn. Mr Franklin had also observed use for storage though some time before. By Mrs Franklin’s own admission she had visited the buildings very infrequently and not gone inside. While Mr Oxley had not noted the buildings being used for storage or any vehicles his evidence was that he had visited the buildings for a specific reason (a possible hide) and, after no agreement was reached on this, had no reason to visit again. In our inspection we observed that the two buildings are derelict and in a poor state, however we did see that they were both being used to store small amounts of hay, presumably for supplementary feed.

[148] Notwithstanding the evidence of Mr Ross and Mr McGillivray, we saw no evidence of a fank or sheep handling in the area on the day of the inspection. It is level ground but appeared that it could hold water and we questioned if this was a good place to site a fank. We did not consider this to be a material point.

[149] The partial resumption area is surrounded by working croft land. Clearly, the use proposed by the landlords will result in additional visitors to the area, likely on a short term basis. The crofter and Dr Ross both expressed concerns around the potential impact on the land, the wildlife and the crofting business posed by short term visitors taking holiday lettings. We heard their concerns over the potential risks including security and biohazard concerns. It does not automatically follow that all visitors will behave in an irresponsible manner. However additional short term visitors must increase the risks of harm to amenity and security and the potential adverse impact on the croft when compared to maintaining the buildings for their current use or redevelopment for use by a family living and working there permanently.

[150] We take note of the position of the landlords that the crofter’s own plans for the renovation of the buildings are not advanced. This is the landlords’ application however and the onus is on the landlords to satisfy the court that the tests have been met with regard to their own plans (Macaskill v Basil Baird & Sons Ltd and Another (supra)). There is evidence that the crofter has made use of the buildings to support crofting on the land over the years. With regard to any plans for redevelopment on the crofter’s part, we consider it to be a reasonable position for the crofter to take that further investment will only be made after the crofter has acquired ownership of the land in question.

[151] Taking account of the evidence presented we do not consider that the landlords’ proposals will confer any good on the croft. The resumption will take land and buildings out of crofting tenure. The croft will lose access to and use of the two buildings and land. Loss of the buildings means loss of storage and shelter. The croft will lose the opportunity to develop the buildings for future use for renovation for a family. The nesting habitat of the owls will be lost. There will be an increased risk of disturbance to the land and stock by an increase in traffic and visitors. Two historical buildings will be demolished and replaced. This may or may not have an impact on the fledgling tour business but we consider it reasonable to assume that the visual impact of the historical buildings, even where dilapidated, is likely to be greater than bare land or new buildings. Income from that business is intended to supplement and be reinvested into the croft business for the good of the croft.

[152] The disadvantages are not outweighed by the potential opportunity to use the compensation paid for new facilities. Any new facilities will need a suitable alternative site to be identified and planning and technical consents to be obtained. Construction will need to take place. During that time the existing shelter and storage would be lost.

Good of the estate

[153] The landlords propose to demolish, rebuild and use the new buildings as holiday lettings to supplement their existing lettings business. No quotes or costings have been obtained for the proposed demolition and build works. By their own evidence the landlords have not considered any other sites within the estate. There is no defined nor ascertainable plan around delivery of the landlords’ proposals and no business plan has been prepared for the intended lettings, including any additional employees needed to assist.

[154] Despite Mrs Franklin’s view that there is some demand for tourism in the area, this was not the view of either expert. Ms Acheson expressed concerns around the viability of the estate achieving a return on the necessary capital expenditure. The evidence of the landlords is that the estate is already loss making. Even without the benefit of costings and a business plan, it is clear that the proposals would involve significant capital expenditure by the landlords - both for the required demolition as well as a rebuild - without any evidence of a viable resulting income stream in return.

[155] Taking all of the evidence into account we do not consider that the landlords have demonstrated that the resumption would be for the good of the estate.

Interests of the crofting community in the locality of the croft and the public interest

[156] While separate matters for consideration, they can be considered together with regard to the intention of the landlords to offer affordable holidays in the new properties. In doing so, the landlords would utilise local supplies and labour, both for the redevelopment works and the resulting business. The existing estate staff of two would be increased to service the additional lettings. The landlords’ proposals might be said to contribute to the public interest if the stated aim of offering reasonably priced holiday lettings is achieved and the demand for these is there. The new lettings could benefit the local community with increased economic activity from the tourists staying at the cottages. It is also reasonable to assume that awareness around crofting would be raised given that the lettings would be adjacent to the working croft.

[157] Such supply and employment prospects and resulting economic activity in the wider community are, however, entirely dependent on viable development proposals and a viable holiday letting business. We require to be confident that the stated purpose of the resumption is realisticand achievable (Secretary of State for Scotland v Shareholders of Lealt & Culnacnock Common Grazings (supra); Lands Improvement Holdings Landmatch SARL v Cole (supra)). We take account of the view of both experts that there is no obvious demand for tourism. Our concern is that the landlords’ plans would not in fact come to fruition as not being economically viable. No evidence was provided to support any urgent demand for employment in the area (similar to Mackay’s Trustees v Colthart 1959 SLCR 43). As such we find the proposals would not serve the interests of the community or public interest in this regard.

Public interest

[158] Further consideration of the public interest may be made. When assessing public interest, the court may have regard to the factors set out in sections 20(1AA) and 20(1AC) of the 1993 Act.

[159] Section 20(1AC) states:

“The matters mentioned in subsection (1AA)(a) above are—

(a) the sustainability of—

(i)  crofting in the locality of the croft or such other area in which crofting is carried on as appears to the Land Court to be relevant;

(ii) the crofting community in that locality or the communities in such an area;

(iii) the landscape of that locality or such an area;

(iv) the environment of that locality or such an area;

(b) the social and cultural benefits associated with crofting.”

[160] To the crofter, the buildings belonging to him have historical importance, having been built by his ancestors. This historical importance was echoed by Mr McGillivray’s evidence. Dr Ross’s evidence around the nature of the tour business demonstrates there is a public interest in crofting. We think it reasonable to assume this interest would include the historical nature of the buildings on the croft as relevant to the overall picture of crofting and its place in society. We heard evidence of the environmentally friendly agriculture practised by Mr Ross and that this places him well to maximise government support for the croft. We heard evidence of his commitment to wildlife for the benefit of the environment on the croft and the sustainable crofting practices. On that basis we therefore consider sustainability and environmental factors to be a specific factor that we may take into consideration here.

[161] In this regard, we were invited by the landlords to take account of the likely mitigation requirements of any planning consent. Where the purpose of resumption is for development, even where a planning permission subsists, section 20(1AA)(b)) allows the court to consider “the effect such development would have on the croft, the estate and the crofting community in the locality of the croft”. This illustrates the separate and additional function of the court over and above that of the planning authority who may have granted planning consent. In any event, here, no application for detailed planning permission has been made by the landlords and the conditions around drainage, services, foundations and wildlife mitigation measures are not known.

[162] Arguably, the environmental impact from the loss of nesting for two breeding owls and scrapes for waders could be said to be detrimental to the public interest. Ms Acheson’s view is that the wildlife species present would not stop planning being granted but would mean that the overall process took longer and would incur additional cost in the form of surveys and mitigation measures. Based on the evidence of Mr Swann, the proposals for redevelopment carry risks to the local resident wildlife, notwithstanding likely planning mitigation measures. Mr Swann favoured the status quo, which failing, the crofter’s proposals to redevelop over the landlords’ proposals to demolish. He considered the crofter’s proposed plans to be more beneficial for and supportive of biodiversity and local wildlife. On balance we would concur.

[163] Having considered the position overall we do not consider that the landlords have made a case that their proposals are for some reasonable purpose having relation to the public interest.

Practice Note (No. 1) resumption applications

[164] Acknowledging that any required planning consent for redevelopment had not been obtained, a request was made to us by the landlords to consider granting the resumption conditional on the landlords achieving planning permission. We were referred to the terms of Practice Note 1 by both parties.

[165] Practice Note 1 states:

“Before authorising resumption, the Court require to be satisfied not only that the resumption is for a reasonable purpose in terms of Section 20 but also that the purpose for which resumption is sought will actually be carried out. The Court may therefore, in cases where local authority planning permission for a development is required, require evidence that this has been granted …

… In an application where resumption is sought of a bare land site for sale either to the crofter or to a third party for any purposes involving development under the Planning Acts (including as a site for a dwellinghouse) the Court will require in addition to evidence of an agreed sale as detailed supra at least an indication that outline planning permission has been or will be granted. Normally the Court will expect to have sight of the actual grant of outline planning permission but the Court will be prepared to accept as an alternative a letter from the local authority indicating that planning permission will be granted. In the event of such an application being lodged where no planning permission has been obtained the Court will normally sist the application until such time as evidence of the grant of planning permission can be exhibited to the Court. … In all the above three categories the Court have indicated that evidence of an agreed sale will be required.”

[166] The status of practice notes and their application to this case was addressed by both parties in their submissions. Reference was made by the crofter to the fact that, in this case, the circumstances are not identical to the examples in Practice Note 1, in other words this was not resumption of a bare land site nor, though for “development under the Planning Acts (including as a site for a dwellinghouse)”, resumption for the purposes of sale either to the crofter or a third party.

[167] Practice Note 1 was issued in 1992 and revised in 1994. It predates the changes made to section 20 of the 1993 Act in 2010. It is guidance and should not be treated as creating a rule in addition to the legislation (Lands Improvement Holdings Landmatch SARL v Cole (supra)). Even where the facts of a case mirror the example given in any practice note issued by the court, application is always at the court’s discretion based on its assessment of whether the statutory test has been satisfied on the evidence led.

[168] We have considered the evidence put before us in relation to planning for the proposed use. The position of the experts in the joint minute was:

“…

Redevelopment under permitted development regulations is possible but unlikely in practice as you would have to keep development within the existing footprint of the buildings, which wouldn’t be desirable as a modern dwelling.

Therefore the most likely route to redevelopment will be to extend the existing building or perhaps demolish and build a new dwelling on the sites. We both agree that planning permission should be forthcoming on the basis of the existing footprint.”

[169] At the time of the preparation of the joint minute both experts were unaware of the change in the landlords’ plans from redevelopment to demolition and rebuild.

[170] Copies of correspondence with the relevant planning authority were lodged by each of the landlords and the crofter. Copy correspondence from Galbraith to the landlords advising on planning was also produced. All of the correspondence was predicated on the original proposal, namely renovation of the existing buildings rather than a demolition and rebuild. The landlords had submitted an application for planning permission in principle for the proposed renovation in May 2021 whereupon the planning authority responded to advise that an application for full planning permission was required for their proposals.

[171] The landlords’ position was that planning consent was not required at all if the resumption was successful in terms of the Town and County Planning (General Permitted Development) (Scotland) Order 1992 which permits certain types of development without a planning permission being required. Under schedule 1, class 18B, this includes a change of use from an agricultural building to a dwelling.

[172] Correspondence between the agent for the crofter and the planning authority from February 2024 (again referring to a proposed renovation rather than demolition and rebuild) asked for confirmation that no application for full planning permission had been made by the landlords and whether the provisions of schedule 1, class 18B might apply. The response from the planning department was short and merely reiterated that advice had already been given that planning permission was required for the proposed redevelopment. We heard no evidence or submissions around any correspondence with the planning authority in respect of the now proposed demolition and rebuild.

[173] The position of the landlords was that they did not wish to incur what may be significant cost in pursuing planning consents if the resumption was to be refused. We understand this concern given the potential costs involved. However, in order to make a reasonable assessment of likely costs for the overall project, the planning requirements need to be factored in. The business plan for any scheme for development would take account of associated costs such as planning and other consents. Advice on the planning requirements would clarify the detail of the proposal and requirements for planning such as associated surveys and the like.

[174] The court cannot comment on detailed planning matters. We have considered the views of the experts on planning and the lack of any detailed proposals on the part of the landlords, both as to the revised scheme of redevelopment and for the lettings business, to be significant factors. The views of the experts and the correspondence with the planning authority all relate to a different proposal. It is not clear whether what is proposed by the landlords will qualify as permitted development. Taking account of the uncertainties and qualified views, we are not persuaded to allow a resumption conditional on a 6 month (or any other) period.

[175] Taking all of the foregoing into account, the court is unable to find that the resumption is truly “for some reasonable purpose having relation to the good of the croft or of the estate or to the public interest or the interests of the crofting community in the locality of the croft”.As a result we decline to approve the application for resumption.

Application to purchase

[176] In terms of section 12(1) of the 1993 Act the right to purchase arises following on from a crofter’s failed attempt to negotiate. Evidence of at least one meeting and correspondence between the parties following the landlords’ purchase of the estate prior to the application to purchase being made was produced to us. Communications between the crofter and landlords over the course of 2017 through to 20 October 2020 did not advance to any agreement. Ultimately the landlords communicated their intention to seek resumption of part of the croft in November 2020. There was a clear failure to progress matters by agreement. As such no question was raised over the competency of the crofter’s application to purchase (Macdonald v South Uist Estates Ltd 2012 SLCR 150).

[177] The landlords’ case was based around substantial hardship being caused to the landlords in terms of section 13(2)(a) of the 1993 Act should the order be granted. No arguments were advanced in respect of any substantial detriment to the interests of sound management of the estate in terms of section 13(2)(b). For the sake of completeness, in the absence of any clear position being taken or any evidence led specifically in respect of the size of the application subjects when compared to the rest of the estate, we have discounted this for the purposes of whether substantial hardship is caused in this regard.

[178] The landlords’ case for substantial hardship stems from two aspects. The first is the loss of or a constraint on the opportunity of a windfarm development proceeding with a consequential loss of a significant financial return. The second aspect is a loss of the landlords’ access to and use of the western side of the estate, specifically Loch BB. The crofter’s position is that there is no evidence of any relevant substantial hardship arising in either or both aspects.

First aspect – loss of windfarm development

[179] As the loss of the potential development is a critical factor in the landlords’ case for substantial hardship we have carefully considered the status of the prospective windfarm development in light of the evidence presented to us. We have assessed the status of what would be the usual suite of documents entered into between parties relative to developments of this nature. We have considered the potential impact any purchase order may have on what is being proposed (in particular the viability of the scheme if the southern apportionment is included) based on the evidence led. Our assessment is set out in the following paragraphs.

[180] The signed exclusivity agreement between the landlords and Brookfield was produced to us. The heads of terms were not exhibited to us. We were referred to the draft option agreement and lease issued to the landlords by Brookfield’s in-house counsel. Neither contained any detail of the prospective development nor payments. Commercial terms were redacted in both. We heard that these have not yet been negotiated.

[181] The plan forming part of the exclusivity agreement was produced and a copy is annexed as schedule part 1E. Per the key on the plan, the Property (as defined therein) is shown outlined in red. This red line area includes the crofter’s two apportionments. There are two areas hatched in blue and labelled “Crofting Land excluding Common Grazing Land” on the key which we were advised are Brian Ross and Derek Matheson’s apportioned areas. The agreement refers specifically to these apportioned areas and the common grazings, excluding from its ambit (in the preamble), viz “the hatched areas which denote various crofts and apportionments which are not the subject of this Exclusivity Agreement at this time”.

[182] A particular concern of the crofter was that, despite bringing the extent of his croft land to the attention of the developer, his apportionments were not specifically excluded from the ambit of the exclusivity agreement the way the other crofters’ apportionments were. In addition, in the absence of any plans showing the location and extent of the proposed option site or wind protection zone, there was no confidence that the proposals would not directly affect him. The draft option agreement and lease issued have not taken account of the fact that the southern apportionment (included in the exclusivity agreement plan) is tenanted by him.

[183] The option agreement states:

“10.1 The Developer acknowledges that the Option Site comprises the Common Grazings and that exercise of the Option is subject to the Land Court granting either: (a) a Resumption Order; or (b) approval of a Scheme for Development over such parts of the Option Site as are required by the Developer and as are affected by crofting control, in terms acceptable to the Developer.

10.2 The Landowner warrants that other than the Common Grazings no part of the Option Site comprises land affected by Crofting Legislation and in particular no part of the Option Site comprises land occupied by individual crofter tenants.”

[184] Our primary source of information on the project is the evidence of Mr Franklin and the documentation exhibited. Mr Franklin was a credible witness and we have no reason to doubt his honest impression of the likelihood of the proposed development proceeding, however his evidence only takes us so far. No evidence was produced or led from any representative of Brookfield or OnPower on any matter pertaining to the prospective development nor the ongoing onward sale.

[185] The only concluded document produced was an exclusivity agreement with Brookfield. Per its terms this is terminable by the developer on one month’s notice at any time. The exclusivity agreement allows the developer access for preliminary investigations and surveys and works in order to assess the suitability of the location for a development. It contains obligations on the landlords to refrain from negotiations or discussions with any other prospective windfarm developers (including controls around access and on advertising or marketing the property for any other such development). It does not contain any obligations on the parties to progress the project documentation (the option and lease) nor any timetable. The draft option and lease are in draft form and have not been negotiated. Per Mr Franklin’s evidence, there is no timetable for negotiation or conclusion of these documents in the heads of terms either.

[186] While there is an obligation on the landlords, as land owner, to take successors bound by the exclusivity agreement, there is no corresponding obligation on the developer. Mr Franklin acknowledged that replacement heads of terms will therefore be required with the new owner, OnPower. Given the ongoing sale, we presume that, unless all surveys and works required have already been completed, the exclusivity agreement will need to be reconstituted and resigned. Fresh drafts of option agreement and lease may require to be issued. No evidence was presented that OnPower will take on and pursue the project, whether on the same commercial terms proposed by Brookfield or on other terms.

[187] There is no planning consent, nor indeed any live application. In the absence of a planning consent, the option site, wind protection zone, installed capacity, turbine numbers and locations (and ancillary rights such as access routes, construction areas etc) are still to be identified and will likely only be at the point of service of the option notice and step through to lease. The status of ancillary project documents such as the grid connection offer is not known: Mr Franklin had not seen the offer referred to and it was not produced to us. We have no evidence around the conditions attached to that offer, the status of these nor whether the offer can be utilised by Brookfield for a different development, nor by OnPower following the sale. This is all fairly standard for a project of this nature where it is still at an early and speculative stage.

[188] The landlords’ concerns are that the project will not be able to proceed if the purchase application is successful. They will no longer be in control of the land and able to grant any rights required. Particular concerns were expressed that the development may not proceed if an 11th turbine on the southern apportionment could not be offered.

[189] We do understand that a developer investing large sums in a project will require sufficient comfort that all necessary rights can be obtained. There are two aspects to this. The first is the 11th turbine. Other than the impression of Mr Franklin from his discussions with Brookfield’s agent, we heard no direct evidence that the viability of the entire project may be in jeopardy if an 11th turbine on the southern apportionment cannot be offered. The original proposal did not include an 11th turbine. The possibility of an 11th turbine was first raised by Mr Franklin with Brookfield’s agent. It was not part of the original approach. There have been no discussions with OnPower about their views or approach to this or any requirement they might have for an 11th turbine – nor indeed on the original development size and location.

[190] The second is more general around the rights required. Ultimately, whether or not an 11th turbine on the southern apportionment is a requirement of viability, the landlords and developer will have to include the crofters in the negotiations. The development originally proposed by Brookfield was for 10 turbines located on the common grazings plus rights over any areas required for a wind protection zone and temporary or permanent access routes and compounds and the like. The precise location of these has not been identified. The rights of Mr Ross on his croft land, as tenant, include the right to plant trees and build. As far as this may have any effect on a wind protection zone, these rights will have to be accommodated in any proposed development whether Mr Ross is a tenant or an owner. Going forward, all the crofters, including Mr Ross, will need to be involved in the negotiations to acquire the necessary rights on the common grazings for the 10 turbines. That was all acknowledged by the landlords. In other words cooperation of Mr Ross will be needed whether or not the purchase application proceeds (and whether or not an 11th turbine is needed).

[191] While productions lodged showed that Mr Ross may have voiced some opposition to a prospective windfarm development in the past, his evidence was that he was not against windfarm development per se. He simply wished to ensure that his interest in the croft was acknowledged and taken account of by the developer. He would make a decision once he understood the proposed terms and conditions, including the areas of ground likely to be affected and once any concerns around his return and community benefit had been addressed. He would be prepared to have a discussion with a developer over an additional turbine on the southern apportionment and was aware of the benefits to and potential restrictions on him as occupier of the croft and co-occupier of the common grazings if a development would go ahead. We accept this as a reasonable position to take in the circumstances.

[192] We heard that the value of the project is in excess of £16 million though no supporting evidence of this was produced to us. As discussed above, we saw no conclusive evidence that the entire development would not proceed if an 11th turbine could not be offered. If the development was to include an 11th turbine, the financial impact to the landlords of the purchase application proceeding would be restricted to a 50% loss of the rental income that would have been attributable to that turbine. Depending on the timings of development it is possible that there would be no loss to the landlords at all. Standard clawback provisions included in the terms of purchase could provide for recovery of the full or (on a reducing scale) at least part of this sum. When comparing the position of the landlords with the order having been granted and it not, the landlords will still benefit financially from any deal struck.

[193] In summary, we consider that what was produced to us illustrates a project that is very much in its initial stages and may or may not proceed. We have no direct evidence as to whether the development is, in fact, viable or will proceed only if an additional 11th turbine is included. Fraser v MacKintosh 1995 SLCR 91 (followed by Waugh v Thrumster Estate Ltd (South Yarrows)(supra)) is authority that:

“the determination of the question as to whether a landlord would be caused a substantial degree of hardship by the making of an order for acquisition must involve a comparison of the position of the landlord in the absence of such an order with the position in which he would find himself following upon such an order.”

We are not persuaded that a comparison of the position of the crofter as tenant when compared to his position as owner would make any material difference to the position of the windfarm proceeding given its current speculative status or, indeed, whether the proposal was more advanced. Whether or not an 11th turbine is required, the co-operation and consent of Mr Ross will be needed for the turbines on the common grazing, the siting of any wind protection zone and the grant of any rights, whether temporary or permanent. There is no evidence of any material financial impact to the landlords should the purchase application proceed when compared to it not proceeding. We therefore find that the relative positions do not show a substantial detriment or hardship to the landlords arising from the order being granted in respect of the first aspect set out.

Second aspect: southern apportionment and Loch BB

[194] The second aspect of substantial hardship advanced by the landlords is their loss of access to and use of the western side of the estate should the purchase application proceed. Submissions primarily related to a loss of access to Loch BB.

[195] The extent of the croft subject to the right to purchase was also a matter of dispute between the parties. The parties were not in agreement on whether the purchase should include all apportionments (in particular the southern apportionment) and also the alveus of all lochs surrounding the croft (namely Loch BB and Loch Amat), in so far as owned by the landlords, as a pertinent of the purchase subjects. With regard to the inclusion of the southern apportionment, we asked for and received further submissions, specifically by reference to the case of Kennedy v Smith (supra) which had not previously been referred to by either party. We were referred to a number of cases and textbooks by Mr Inkster relating to the inclusion of the lochs as a pertinent, which authorities we have included in the authorities list.

Southern apportionment

[196] There is no argument being made by the landlords around an inability to enforce the duty of cultivation causing substantial detriment should the southern apportionment be included in any purchase order. The landlords’ position is that the southern apportionment is not worked by the crofter jointly in conjunction with his croft nor, by fact of being an apportionment, is it sufficiently contiguous or adjacent to the croft. The status of both western and southern apportionments, are in turn, relevant to the position of Loch Amat and Loch BB, namely whether these might be included in any purchase order as pertinents of the croft.

[197] Though we were not referred to the case of Kennedy v Smith SLC/81/15 by either party, we did consider this was a case which merited consideration here. We therefore asked the parties for submissions, in writing, which we received on 10 July 2025. Following this, the parties asked for the opportunity to provide further submissions and these were received, again in writing, on 21 July 2025. A summary of each set of submissions received is set out in the following paragraphs.

Original submissions for the crofter

[198] Mr Inkster acted for the landlord in Kennedy v Smith (supra). Kennedy can be distinguished from this case as it dealt with a standalone apportionment which was a deemed croft. Here the southern apportionment is (like the other three apportionments) linked to the croft with registration number C179 (R2126). In Kennedy the court held that the applicant had no right to apply to acquire his apportionment on the basis that section 3(5) apportionments are excluded altogether (paras [54] and [55]; section 3(5)(b) of the 1993 Act).

[199] Here all apportionments (including the southern apportionment), having (1) been apportioned under section 52(4) of the Act and (2) all adjacent or contiguous to another part of the croft, are included in the definition of croft land (para [55] of Kennedy v Smith and section 3(4)(b) 1993 Act). All apportionments (including the southern apportionment) are capable of being acquired as this is a section 3(4)(b) situation and not section 3(5)(b).

Original submissions for the landlords

[200] An initial matter to be raised is that there are three crofts registered separately. The crofter’s position that “the croft” should be found to be a single unit is not one which is open to the court. A distinction should be made between the three registered crofts and a distinction should be made between the apportionments and the in-bye ground. Each tenancy could be assigned separately.

[201] The crofter acknowledges that R2126 (C179) is the only one of the three with which the two apportionments are associated. The northern apportionment is contiguous with R2126 within the meaning of section 12(3). The southern apportionment is not and is therefore not croft land within the meaning of section 12(3) of the 1993 Act. It should be excluded from any purchase order granted.

[202] All of the authorities cited are exercises in statutory interpretation: here section 12(3) itself. Kennedy v Smith reaffirmed the decisions in Bowman v Guthrie (1997 SLCR 40) and MacMillan v Mackenzie (1995 SLT 7) that a standalone apportionment (a deemed croft) was not croft land within the definition of section 12(3). As a result an application to purchase the apportionment was incompetent. While the latter two cases were made by reference to earlier legislation, the statutory provisions were similar to that which is under consideration here. The court in Kennedy recognised that nothing in the Crofting Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 or subsequent decisions of the court changed the position from the earlier cases. There are limits on the court giving deeming provisions their full effect, particularly where there is clear statutory provision to different effect (Kennedy v Smith at [59]).

[203] Kennedy v Smith was decided in relation to a section 3(5) deemed croft. In the present case the court is dealing with section 3(4)(b). Kennedy v Smith may have a bearing in the present case as section 12(3) applies to exclude both, unless the apportionment meets the test under section 12(3)(i).

[204] In terms of section 12(3), the apportionment must be:

(a) Apportioned under section 52(4) and

(b) Adjacent to any other part of the croft or

(c) Contiguous to any other part of the croft or

(d) Consist of arable machair.

Point (a) above is met in this instance and point (d) is not applicable. The points in dispute are (b) and (c).

[205] If the crofter cannot establish contiguity or adjacency in relation to the southern apportionment, then it must be excluded from any purchase order (Bowman v Guthrie). The intention of section 12(3) was to exclude common grazings from the right to buy subject to limited exceptions (Kennedy, supra). Use of the words “close to” by the court in Kennedy [at paragraph 56] are a reminder that physical proximity is a requirement of adjacency as well as of contiguity.

[206] The reference to “another part of the croft” can only mean the in-bye croft to which the apportionment pertains (Kennedy v Smith at [55]). Applying Kennedy the croft which the apportionment relates to is the one to which the grazing shares were attached, and out of which shares the apportionment was made ie R2126. It is axiomatic that an apportionment does not (and cannot) pertain to another apportionment. The crofter cannot use the northern apportionment as a “bridge” between the southern apportionment and the in-bye ground to render it contiguous or adjacent.

[207] Each apportionment must be assessed against the statutory criteria on the basis of its own characteristics (Kennedy v Smith). Here, that is by assessing the southern apportionment’s relationship to the in-bye ground of R2126 only. To “anchor” the purchase of the southern apportionment, upon the purchase of another apportionment is not permitted by section 12(3).

[208] If the area of the northern apportionment was un-apportioned, the crofter could not submit that the southern apportionment is contiguous or adjacent to the relevant croft in-bye ground. The common occurrence of separation by a roadway in Gillies v Countess of Sutherland’s Trustees may be the reason for the relaxation of the absolute statutory requirement of the apportionment being contiguous by the allowance of adjacency. Here, the southern apportionment is plainly not contiguous.

[209] The crofter would have to rely on the southern apportionment being treated as adjacent. The court in Gillies, identified three criteria with regard to adjacency:

(i)  Physical proximity;

(ii) Access from the croft to the apportioned area; and

(iii) Ready convenience of joint working of the croft and the apportioned area.

[210] These are all objective criteria. Such objective approach is consistent with the wider statutory framework around crofting, which assumes an objective approach. Gillies did not refer to the actual use of the apportionment nor would these features be affected if the crofter or the method of cultivation changed. Adjacency cannot be separated from consideration of the physical proximity of the apportioned area to the in-bye ground.

[211] The criteria all look at physical features relating to the croft and the apportionment from slightly different angles. It is not self-evident how the angle of (ii) is distinct from (iii). Ease of access seems likely to be the principal factor in the ready convenience of joint working. It may be possible to distinguish physical features of the access itself as factor (ii), and other matters, which not physical, impact on the ability to utilise the access as conveniently or easily as factor (iii).

[212] If factor (i) is not present, factors (ii) and (iii) are unlikely to exist. As such criteria (ii) and (iii) will normally operate to defeat adjacency. In relation to factor (ii) one might have an area of ground which was physically proximate but could only be accessed in practical terms by taking a circuitous, far longer, route. That would constitute a physical limitation, which would cause the apportionment to fail the adjacency test. For factor (iii), an access may be appropriate in physical terms but have some designated or restricted status, meaning that the apportionment is just not readily convenient to use jointly with the croft. Again the test of adjacency would fail to be met.

[213] With regard to physical proximity, in Gillies the apportionment was located between 20 and 90 metres from the in-bye ground. Here, the southern apportionment is located in the region of 900 metres from the in-bye ground. There is a significant difference in altitude between the croft and the apportionments of R2126.

[214] With regard to access from the croft, an access track which runs up the hill through the northern apportionment (referred as “Robins Hill Track” by the crofter). This stops short of the southern apportionment itself.

[215] With regard to ease of joint working we have reservations about reliance on Ross v Trustees of Miss S N Barr. It is not a proper application of Gillies. Section 12(3) is concerned with objective matters in regard to the apportionment as opposed to subjective matters relating to one tenant’s particular cultivation. Ross was a divisional authority only and was taken on the basis of what the court identified as “special circumstances” set out within the decision. It is difficult to gain much from the case beyond authority for the uncontroversial proposition that 1200 metres by road was too great a distance to consider an apportionment adjacent. Any attempt to rely on the case for any other principle, risks going beyond what the statutory provisions properly permit.

[216] Section 12(3) should not be construed to create a system by which the same apportionment might be rendered adjacent by the practice of one crofter and non-adjacent by the practice of another. Such an approach would lead to arbitrary and incoherent results and be a departure from the approach in the statute to the right to buy. The approach of Gillies should be preferred and applied to the facts in the present case.

[217] Even if the application of adjacency in Trustees of Barr did permit subjective assessment of the tenant’s crofting practices then adjacency of the southern apportionment would not be established. The evidence of Mr Oxley regarding use should be preferred over the crofter, namely that stock do not use the southern apportionment. The evidence of use from the crofter is not a sufficient type or level of use to meet the requirements of section 12(3) even taking the most generous (to the crofter) interpretation of either Gillies and/or Trustees of Barr.

[218] The southern apportionment should be excluded on the basis that it does not meet the definition of “croft land” under section 12(3).

Further submissions for the crofter in response

[219] There is no ingenuity or logic involved in an argument that tries to defy clear and well established statute and case law. The crofter has a proper statutory basis for the exercise of a right to buy in relation to the southern apportionment. The southern apportionment is clearly contiguous (or adjacent) to R2126 (C179) within the meaning of section 12(3), is croft land within the meaning of that section and should be included in any purchase order made by the court.

[220] It is agreed that in Kennedy v Smith, the court reaffirmed the logic of the decisions in Bowman v Guthrie and MacMillan v Mackenzie that a standalone apportionment (treated as a deemed croft) was not croft land within the definition of section 12(3), and as a result an application to purchase it was incompetent. It is also agreed that the case of Kennedy v Smith was decided in relation to a section 3(5) deemed croft and that in the present case the court is dealing with section 3(4)(b).

[221] The interpretation put on section 12(3) by the landlords is deeply flawed. A correct interpretation of section 12(3) must begin with section 3(4). In terms of section 3(4) all four apportionments, including both the northern apportionment and the southern apportionment, are “deemed to form part of the croft”. Then, by section 12(3), an apportionment to be “croft land” for the purposes of a purchase order requires to be “adjacent or contiguous to any other part of the croft”.

[222] This addresses the point made by the landlords that in Kennedy v Smith the court referred to the apportionment having to be adjacent or contiguous “to another part of the croft”. Here, the southern apportionment is contiguous to the northern apportionment. The northern apportionment is “another part of the croft” due to the deeming provisions in section 3(4). It is axiomatic that an apportionment does pertain to another apportionment where the deeming provision in section 3(4) applies and the apportionments are adjacent or contiguous to another part of the croft.

[223] The northern apportionment is a “bridge” as a result of the deeming provision. Even if the northern apportionment had not been granted and was still common grazings, any arguments by the landlords could still be defeated by the fact that in law adjacent does not mean joined onto. Section 12(3) in conjunction with section 3(4) creates an “anchor” whereby the purchases of the northern and southern apportionments are intrinsically linked.

[224] Even if the court considered that the northern apportionment could be ignored when considering the adjacency of the southern apportionment to the in-bye croft ground (which it cannot), the landlords’ submissions in that regard can be refuted. It is clear that the southern apportionment meets the terms of all three criteria laid down in Gillies v Countess of Sutherland’s Trustees.

[225] None of the hypothetical factors that are put forward by the landlords apply and are all irrelevant in any event. As the court in Gillies observed “each case must depend upon its own circumstances”. The court must therefore consider the actual circumstances based upon the facts before them and not hypothetical ones put forward by the landlords.

[226] In considering physical proximity, in Gillies the court considered the degree of proximity that would justify “adjacent” (citing Wellington v Lower Hutt [1904] AC 773 where a distance of 6 miles satisfied legislation relating to the costs of a bridge). There was no existing apportionment between the two. Here there is. Even discounting that, but taking the overall facts into consideration and applying Gillies, the court easily find that the southern apportionment was adjacent to the in-bye croft land for the purposes of granting a purchase order.

[227] With regard to access, the terminus of Robin's Hill Track from the main road through the northern apportionment is at the entrance to the southern apportionment. Access beyond this via foot, quad bike or tractor. It would not stop short 900m or so from entering the northern apportionment if only built to serve the northern apportionment.

[228] Ross v Trustees of Miss S N Barr should not be discounted with regard to ease of joint working. It follows the decision in Gillies where “each case must depend upon its own circumstances”. In Ross the “special circumstances” that applied there were taken into consideration when coming to a decision. Even if the court was to ignore the deeming provisions in section 3(4) we have “special circumstances” here: the southern apportionment is contiguous to the northern apportionment which, in turn, is contiguous to the in-bye croft land. This is greater reason to include the southern apportionment than the circumstances in Gillies or Ross.

[229] Joint working is clear through the existence of the northern apportionment. Contrary to the landlords’ submissions the southern apportionment is actively used in conjunction with the northern apportionment. In any event, section 12(3) does not specify use that must be made of an apportionment for it to be included within the definition of “croft land” for inclusion within a purchase order granted by the court.

[230] The southern apportionment clearly does meet the definition of “croft land” under section 12(3).

Further submissions for the landlords in response

[231] The principles from Kennedy v Smith are applicable in the present case, recognising that Kennedy was a section 3(5) situation and here is an apportionment pertaining to a croft. The decision in Kennedy cited the decisions in MacMillan v MacKenzie and Bowman v Guthrie, which did not relate to standalone deemed crofts. The general principle that apportionment ground cannot be purchased unless it is squarely within the categories explicitly permitted by section 12(3) is equally applicable in section 3(4) cases and section 3(5) cases.

[232] The crofter refers to four apportionments in his submissions when the application refers to three. When considering any apportionment under section 12(3) the court must consider: (i) To which specific croft does this apportionment pertain? (ii) Is the apportionment contiguous to any other part of that croft? (iii) If not contiguous, is the apportionment adjacent to any other part of that croft? The southern apportionment cannot be considered contiguous or adjacent. Our argument and the steps applies to any area apportioned under section 52(4).

[233] It cannot be the case that a decision taken in a section 3(5) context cannot be relevant in a section 3(4)(b) situation. The crofter’s failure to distinguish between in-bye ground and which of the apportionments are linked to which specific crofts has affected the presentation of evidence. No evidence was led which specifically connected the working of the southern apportionment with R2126, as opposed to the other crofts, even though such a distinction is required. This will not be an isolated case. The statutory provisions in section 12(3) require an apportionment to be considered in relation to the croft with which it is linked. In treating the three crofts and relative apportionments as a single unit the crofter invites the court to judicially innovate on the wording of the legislation. R2124 and R2125 cannot be considered in assessing the position of apportionments pertaining to R2126

[234] The crofter rests on the proposition that another apportionment is capable of being “another part of the croft” under section 12(3) in such a way that it renders the southern apportionment contiguous or adjacent to the croft within the meaning of section 12(3). This is the fundamental divide between the parties’ positions. It is not possible to use one apportionment to “bridge” to another in this way.

[235] The southern apportionment pertains to the in-bye croft ground and not to another apportionment. It is not contiguous nor is it adjacent within the meaning of section 12(3).

Discussion and decision on the apportionments

[236] We agree with the position put by the landlords that the northern apportionment, the southern apportionment and the western apportionment require to be assessed as pertaining to R2126 only. If that tenancy was assigned these apportionments would be assigned as part of R2126. If the tenancies of R2124 or R2125 were assigned, these apportionments would not be included. For the avoidance of any doubt, we believe that the reference in the crofter’s submissions to four apportionments reflects that the western apportionment is in two parts (“Area 4” and “Area 5” on plan B3(ii)) and the Crofting Register plans shows the three apportionments as four ‘Areas’ rather than to any other apportionment.

[237] In terms of section 3(4):

“For the purposes of this Act—

…

(b) any land comprising any part of a common grazing which has been apportioned for the exclusive use of a crofter under section 52(4) of this Act, and,

…

shall be deemed to form part of the croft.”

It is accepted by the parties that the three apportionments have been apportioned under section 52(4) of the 1993 Act for the purposes of section 3(4) of the 1993 Act.

[238] Section 12(1) permits the acquisition by the crofter “of croft land tenanted by him”. In terms of the relevant parts of section 12(3):

“croft land includes any land being part of a croft, other than … (b) any land, comprising any part of a common grazing, unless the land has been apportioned under s52(4) of this Act and - (i) is adjacent or contiguous to any other part of the croft …”

[239] There are two questions in dispute between the parties: (1) What meaning does “any other part of the croft” have here?
