title: Alastair Mac Lachlan Applicant against Jennifer Lamont or Mac Lachlan Respondent and Hugh Mac Donald Landlord [2025] SLC 7
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2025] SLC 7,
Case reference: SLC/50/23 & SLC/102/23

OPINION OF THE COURT

Court members: Lord Duthie,
Mr Smith

Alastair MacLachlan
Applicant
against
Jennifer Lamont or MacLachlan
Respondent
and
Hugh MacDonald
Landlord

Subjects: Ormerhaven, 3 Gott, Isle of Tiree

Applicant: Colquhoun, advocate; MacLeod and MacCallum

Respondent: Personally present

Landlord: Vennard, solicitor; E Thornton & Co

13 June 2025

Introduction

[1] These are two applications, the first (SLC/50/23) at the instance of Alastair MacLachlan (“AM”), the second (SLC/102/23) at the instance of Jennifer Lamont (“JL”). AM and JL were formerly husband and wife. In his application, AM seeks declarator that he is the cottar of the dwelling house known as and forming Ormerhaven, 3 Gott, Isle of Tiree; and an order requiring the landlord to grant a conveyance in his favour of the site of Ormerhaven in terms of section 12(2) of the Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993. JL opposes AM’s application. In her own application, JL seeks a determination that she and not AM is the cottar and corresponding orders. The Court fixed concurrent diets of preliminary proof before answer, restricted to the question of whether either party is a cottar. The proof was heard over two days on 1 and 2 April 2025, in Tiree.

AM’s application

[2] AM avers that in 2002 he was given permission by Donald MacIntyre (“DM”), then owner occupier of the croft 3 Gott, Isle of Tiree, to rebuild the ruined cottar house Ormerhaven on his croft; that AM carried out those works; that he has occupied Ormerhaven with the permission and knowledge of DM from 2002 until DM’s death in 2020 and with the knowledge and consent of DM’s executor subsequently; that ownership of the croft was transferred to the current landlord in February 2023; that he and JL occupied only as a holiday home prior to 2017; that he has lived there permanently without the interested party since 2017; and that he is a “cottar” as defined by section 12(5) of the Act.

JL’s Application

[3] JL avers that she and not DM was given permission by DM to rebuild and occupy Ormerhaven; and that she and not DM is the cottar as defined by section 12(5) of the Act.

Cottars in Scots Law

[4] Section 12(5) of the Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993 defines “cottar” as being:

“the occupier of a dwelling-house situated in the crofting counties with or without land who pays no rent, or the tenant from year to year of a dwelling-house situated as aforesaid who resides therein and who pays therefor an annual rent not exceeding £6, whether with or without garden ground but without arable or pasture land”.

[5] This case concerns the first of these two classes of cottar, the non-tenant cottar. A non-tenant cottar’s status is based on occupation and the knowledge and consent of the proprietor. The occupation founded on must be with the knowledge and consent of the proprietor. A squatter does not acquire cottar status until the landlord consents: MacInnes v Lady Strathcona 1926 SLCR 39 at 45. Non-tenant cottars enjoy two rights, (first) the right in terms of section 36 of the Act to be compensated for permanent improvements on removal if certain conditions are met; and (second) the right, in terms of section 12(2) of the Act, to buy the subjects he or she occupies as a cottar.

[6] When determining whether someone is a non-tenant cottar the Court is not concerned with how possession was acquired, rather, the present attributes of the purported cottar. Thus, a person may start out occupying property as a squatter and subsequently become a cottar: Sutherland v Earl of Ronaldsay 1920 SLCR 17 at 19-20. By the same token, a cottar who voluntarily ceases to occupy the subjects ceases to qualify as a cottar. The occupation founded on must be broadly residential in character: occupation of a cottage without living there may not be sufficient: see MacInnes v Lady Strathcona 1926 SLCR 39.

Evidence for AM

[7] AM’s Evidence: AM adopted his witness statement which had been lodged in advance of the proof diet. He has resided at the cottage full time as a cottar since late 2017/ early 2018. JL has never occupied the cottage full time – it was only ever a holiday home to her. Parties’ connection to the cottage dates back to 2000 when he and JL met with DM during a family holiday to Tiree. Mr McIntyre showed AM, JL and their children the ruined cottage and said that they could take the cottage on as a project and have it if they wished. AM and JL confirmed that they would be pleased to do so. The offer by DM was to them both jointly. AM then prepared the necessary plans for a planning application which are all notated as being for both AM and JL. AM enjoyed a close relationship with DM with whom he shared a number of interests, particularly boats and boat building. Planning permission was granted in 2003 and building commenced. AM carried out most of the works himself, mostly during holiday periods and in his spare time. He was self-employed throughout this period as a landscape contractor and a farmer at High Milburn Farmhouse on the mainland. JL was employed by Dumbarton Assessor's Department as a valuation surveyor and has never worked or lived full time on Tiree. During the reconstruction of Ormerhaven, AM and JL would visit Tiree with their family during school holidays and in addition he would carry out building whenever it was feasible to take time away from his business. When the property was nearing completion DM asked if he wished to formalise an agreement through solicitors, however, he thought this would be insulting to DM to do so and this was not taken forward. The certificate of completion was granted in 2007. Thereafter Ormerhaven was used for family holidays. Ormerhaven was only occupied by their family and friends, DM having made clear he did not want the property to be let out.

[8] When AM and JL separated in 2017, he moved initially from the family farm to his sister’s property and JL remained in the family home at High Milburn Farmhouse on the mainland. He continued to visit Tiree occasionally. He then decided he would like to live permanently in Tiree. He advised DM’s wife, Margaret MacIntyre (“MM”) of their separation and his wish to live in Tiree in late 2017. MM responded “this is your house, and you will always be welcome here”. AM felt it only polite to ask permission to occupy the house on a permanent basis given that it had only previously been used as a holiday home. AM took full time occupation of Ormerhaven in late 2017/ early 2018 as his main and permanent residence. He ran his business from Ormerhaven, working as a self-employed builder and landscape contractor on the Tiree. He was responsible for all outgoings in respect of Ormerhaven, including council tax and utility bills. DM and MM, who lived a few hundred yards away, visited on a regular basis. It was clear to them that he was occupying the property on his own and on a permanent basis. At no point did they challenge or question his right to do so. It was well known in the area that he and JL had separated and that AM was living at Ormerhaven on his own on a full time, permanent basis. AM is actively involved in the local community. He is an active member of the Tiree Maritime Trust and a committee member of Tiree Art Enterprises.

[9] Following their separation, AM and JL agreed that JL could continue to visit the property as a holiday home for three separate weeks in the year, at Christmas, Easter and July. During these times he would vacate the cottage. During the first year of this informal agreement, JL adhered to the agreed times. However, thereafter JL started to change times and visit other than at agreed times, with him remaining in the property during these subsequent visits.

[10] In January 2020, AM’s solicitor wrote to JL’s solicitor requesting that she adhere to the agreed three times for visits. On 8 August 2020, having returned from a hospital appointment, AM returned to the cottage to find JL sitting in the dining room which he believed was inappropriate for what was his home and in breach of the COVID regulations then in force. He therefore added an additional door lock to stop visits outwith the agreed times and to maintain the security of his home.

[11] We found to AM to be a credible witness who gave straightforward answers to questions. We consider he was doing his best to assist the Court and his evidence generally more coherent and plausible than JL’s evidence where they differed. We have no reason to doubt the reliability of his evidence.

Dr John Holliday:

[12]  Holliday adopted his witness statement. He is a friend of AM, with whom he shares an interest in Gaelic and Tiree wooden boats. He speaks to AM’s involvement in the Tiree community (including the Tiree Maritime Trust and cultural events), to his living at Ormerhaven as his permanent residence; and to his having been a good neighbour to DM and MM. Dr Holliday was not cross examined. We have no reason to doubt Dr Holliday’s evidence which provides some, albeit extremely slight, support to AM’s evidence, and we accept that evidence, quantum valeat.

Ewan MacKinnon:

[13] Mr MacKinnon adopted his witness statement. He is a Tiree crofter who knows AM and knew DM and MM well. He speaks to AM’s renovating Ormerhaven; to AM taking occupation of Ormerhaven on a full time basis in around 2017 or 2018 following his separation from JL; and to AM then immersing himself in the local community. Under cross examination he confirmed he had no knowledge of arrangements between parties and DM in 2003. His evidence was not otherwise challenged. We have no difficulty accepting Mr MacKinnon’s evidence, quantum valeat.

Evidence for JL

[14] JL’s Evidence: JL adopted her witness statement, lodged in advance of the proof diet. In or before 2001, DM, the then tenant of the croft 3 Gott, offered to “return” to JL the cottar’s interest in the ruined cottage Ormerhaven, which had previously been given to his father by JL’s grandfather. DM purchased the croft in 2003. JL and DM then agreed that Ormerhaven would be rebuilt by JL and used by her as a family holiday home. This verbal agreement was between DM and JL. AM was not a party to the agreement.

[15] The renovation works were funded by extending the mortgage on JL and MA’s family home at Alexandria. The works were completed in 2010. Thereafter JL has occupied the house as cottar, with AM and their children, with DM’s knowledge and consent. She owns furnishings and equipment in the house. No rent was ever paid or requested. JL complied with the terms of her agreement with DM. She has never been served notice to quit. She has not abandoned Ormerhaven.

[16] Following their separation in April 2017, JL allowed AM to occupy Ormerhaven temporarily until he could find alternative accommodation. She, and not he, remained the cottar. She allowed AM only temporary occupation, jointly with her and their children. She advised DM of this when she applied in 2018 to purchase Ormerhaven. She met DM and MM at their home in Gott and DM agreed to the purchase. However, DM’s health was declining, and it was decided to pause the sale.

[17] JL last stayed in Ormerhaven at New Year 2020. Thereafter, Covid restrictions prevented her visiting. Then in May 2021 she was diagnosed with and treated for cancer, further restricting her ability to travel. During her absence AM changed the locks. AM has refused to provide her with keys to the new locks. She is now being refused access to Ormerhaven by AM. Her solicitor advised her not to change the locks as this would be viewed dimly by the Sheriff dealing with parties’ divorce proceedings.

[18] JL has experienced aggressive behaviour and threats of harassment from AM. Her car was damaged while it was parked outside Ormerhaven. Because of this behaviour she was offered the key to a house neighbouring Ormerhaven where she stays when on Tiree.

[19] After DM’s death in 2020 his wife MM was appointed executor of his estate. MM knew that Mr MacLachlan occupied the house only as her husband on a temporary basis and that Ormerhaven “belongs” to JL. In 2021, JL reminded MM of her application to buy Ormerhaven. However, MM was then herself declining. Her niece held power of attorney and began to deal with MM’s affairs. JL was told by the family that the purchase of Ormerhaven would be dealt with once the crofts were transferred into the ownership of DM’s nephew, Hugh MacDonald (“HM”).

[20] JL subsequently learned that AM was seeking either to buy Ormerhaven or be paid compensation for the improvement works. At that point DM’s estate had not been settled. Once the ownership of the croft was transferred, JL instructed her solicitor, at HM’s invitation, to submit an offer to purchase Ormerhaven. She then learned of AM’s application to this Court. Negotiations of the site purchase are currently suspended, pending resolution of these proceedings.

[21] We found JL in some respects to be a reasonably credible witness, although we did consider on occasion she had a tendency, no doubt inadvertently, to give a spin to her narrative of events which supported the legal analysis of events most supportive of the outcome she is trying to achieve. Further, we consider that her (no doubt sincerely held) belief that she and not AM had cottar’s rights coloured her account of events. We are doubtful that in 2002/2003 DM would have expressly used the words “as cottar” or “cottar’s rights” when agreeing the basis of JL and AM’s occupation, or that the 1993 Act was at the forefront of anyone’s minds in respect of Ormerhaven. There is no contemporaneous documentation to support her narrative of discussions with DM, which we would have expected to exist had DM taken the trouble to seek to confer valuable rights on JL alone, as opposed to on JL and AM jointly. Moreover, if JL genuinely believed in 2020 she and not AM had cottar’s rights, given that she was being advised by solicitors, we find her three year delay in seeking to vindicate such rights inexplicable. We infer that the notion of cottar’s rights is something which has occurred to her only recently. We do not suggest JL was seeking to mislead the Court; however, to the extent that her evidence differs from that of AM, we prefer the evidence of AM as inherently more plausible.

Grant MacKinnon’s evidence:

[22] Mr MacKinnon (“GM”) adopted his brief written statement as his evidence. He was not cross examined. He lives on the neighbouring croft at 2 Gott. He moved there in 2001 and met JL thereafter. He was aware of the family connection between JL and DM. DM informed him that JL’s grandfather had allowed his parents and him to live in Ormerhaven. Ormerhaven then fell into disrepair. DM was “more than happy” to pass the property back to JL. He considered JL to be cottar of her old family home. Although not doubting his honesty, we did not find GM’s evidence of material assistance. What do not consider his impression of arrangements between DM, AM and JL to be reliable evidence.

Malina MacIntyre’s evidence:

[23] Ms MacIntyre adopted her handwritten witness statement as her evidence. She was not cross examined. Her grandfather was the tenant of 3 Gott. On his death in 1956 her mother handed the tenancy over to her cousin DM. Ormerhaven belonged to Captain Hector Lamont, a distant cousin, who gave the use of Ormerhaven to her great uncle Hugh MacIntyre. She recalls DM saying that Ormerhaven belonged to the Lamont family and was being kept for them. When JL returned to Tiree DM “handed back” Ormerhaven “to her as a Lamont”. JL was cottar, not AL. After DM died in January 2020, HM informed her that AM was threatening to sue MM, DM’s widow in respect of Ormerhaven. Again, while we do not doubt her honesty, we did not find Ms MacIntyre’s evidence to be of material assistance. We do not consider her impression of arrangements to be reliable evidence and we formed the impression that her evidence was based on what had been reported to her by JL.

Inspection

[24] On completion of the evidence but before hearing submissions and mindful that it might be relevant at a later stage of proceedings, the Court took the opportunity to inspect Ormerhaven which is located only a few miles from the hearing venue. The inspection was carried out in clear, sunny conditions, unaccompanied by parties or their representatives. The Court referred itself to the plan lodged as Production 3. The three areas marked blue on the plan could be easily identified. The house occupies most of the middle area with fences to the front (north-east) and the rear (south-west) of the house. The Court inferred that this would have been the original curtilage of the cottars house. The other two areas on either side of the middle area were overgrown grass and had the look of not being crofted by the neighbouring crofter. The land is reasonably level. The house is of sound construction with very thick walls of considerable age. The house has been modernised in a sympathetic way, consistent with the evidence we heard earlier in the day. We had no reason to inspect the interior and did not do so.

Submissions for AM

[25] Counsel adopted his detailed written submissions. Parties’ use and occupation of Ormerhaven may be divided into two periods; the first period is from 2002 to 2017; the second is from 2017 to the present day.

[26] During the first period, Ormerhaven was constructed and then used as a family holiday home. Neither party was then a cottar within the meaning of the Act. Both parties resided on the mainland. Although they visited the island regularly, Ormerhaven was never their home. Such occupation is not of the sort required to bring either party within the statutory definition of a cottar. DM appears to have wanted the agreement to remain informal, an attitude inconsistent with the intentional grant of cottar’s rights. In any event, his intention – and the colloquial use of the term ‘cottar’ - are irrelevant in law to the question of whether either party fall within the terms of section 12(5) of the Act.

[27] During the second period, Ormerhaven became AM’s full time residence. He occupies Ormerhaven with the knowledge and consent of the present and previous landlords. He sought their permission to live there full time and they were aware of his presence there on a permanent basis. He falls within the statutory definition of cottar and has done so since 2017. However, JL has never resided in the cottage. For a time after 2017 she would visit for three weeks in each year. That continued until a combination of the pandemic, illness and her failure to keep the terms of the agreement between parties ended her use of Ormerhaven. She lives on the mainland. She chose to spend lockdown at home on the mainland. She chose to convalesce there. On separating from AM, she chose to remain in residence on the mainland. When AM changed the locks, she did not object to the landlord, nor did she take action to recover possession. She acquiesced in AM’s occupation of Ormerhaven. Only after a gap of three years, during which period she did not visit, did she purport to assert cottar’s rights. She has continued to visit the island for holidays but stayed elsewhere.

[28] JL’s submission that her husband has occupied Ormerhaven as a guest of his wife since 2017 and that she has thereby maintained civil possession is entirely artificial considering (i) AM obtained the direct consent of the landlord for his permanent occupation; and (ii) JL’s later exclusion from the property. AM’s right to occupy the cottage is not parasitic on any right of JL. To JL, Ormerhaven is a place of recreation rather than work or residence. Her financial contribution to the building of the cottage was limited and she has never lived in it full time.

Submissions for JL

[29] JL also adopted her written submissions. She occupied Ormerhaven as a cottar for over 20 years by taking possession, furnishing it and living in it as a second home. DM knew when offering the cottar’s agreement that the property would not at that time be her primary residence. That, however, does not mean that she does not meet the statutory definition of non-rent paying cottar. She does not require to live in Ormerhaven as her main residence to meet the terms of her agreement with DM, nor to meet the statutory definition of a non-rent paying cottar. Following her separation from AM in 2017, she occupied Ormerhaven on occasions until 2020. During this period, when she was absent, a member of her family (i.e. AM) lived there, but only ever with her permission. This was all with the full, informed knowledge and consent of (i) the landowner, DM; (ii) following his death by his executor and widow, MM, then her niece (who held power of attorney) Heather Murphy; and (iii) finally by HM, DM’s nephew who succeeded to the ownership of 3 Gott. JL has complied with the conditions set by DM. This cottar’s agreement could be terminated by notice from the landowner, however, there has been no such termination and JL has not renounced the tenancy, notwithstanding her difficulties obtaining access to the property due to AM’s actions. She has not abandoned the property.

Decision

[30] For what it is worth, we prefer AM’s evidence that the offer made by DM, such as it was, was made to both AM and JL, although we accept that JL may genuinely have thought it was being made solely on her account, standing her family’s historic connection to Ormerhaven. However, that agreement did not result in the conferring of cottar’s rights within the meaning of the Act, rather, an informal and gratuitous licence to occupy. We are not persuaded that DM expressly used the words “as cottar” or “cottar’s rights” when agreeing the basis of JL and AM’s occupation, nor that the 1993 Act was then at the forefront of anyone’s minds in respect of Ormerhaven. However, even if DM did use those words, that is irrelevant for present purposes, standing the tenuous extent of both parties’ occupation of Ormerhaven prior to 2017. We find, on the evidence, that prior to 2017, neither party fell within the statutory definition of cottar. During this period, parties’ respective and combined occupation of Ormerhaven was insufficient in both extent and nature to be characterised as residential. During this period, their occupation of the subjects was occasional and sporadic. Moreover, during this period, Ormerhaven was only ever occupied as a holiday home rather than as a dwelling-house within the meaning of the Act. That is not to set up an absolute rule that it is impossible for cottar’s rights to exist in respect of a second home, rather, that the threshold is not met on the facts of this case. We consider there to be force in the submission that the 1993 Act and its statutory predecessors did not intend to confer a valuable benefit on holiday makers from the central belt of Scotland.

[31] Matters changed in 2017 following parties’ separation. We accept AM’s evidence that thereafter he resided full time in Ormerhaven with the express knowledge and consent of the landlords. Since then, he has fallen and remains within the statutory definition of cottar.

[32] Even if we are wrong in finding that JL never had cottar’s rights, she would have lost them in 2020 when, as a matter of fact, she ceased to occupy Ormerhaven and did nothing to vindicate any such rights for a period of approximately three years.

[33] We will fix a procedural hearing to discuss the terms of the interlocutor necessary to give effect to this decision and further procedure. All questions of expenses are reserved.
parties: Alastair Mac Lachlan Applicant against Jennifer Lamont or Mac Lachlan Respondent and Hugh Mac Donald Landlord

title: Gary Jack Appellant against The Crofting Commission Respondent [2025] SLC 6
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation:[2025] SLC 6,
Case reference:SLC/23/24 6 Naast
SLC/24/24 3 Naast

DECISION OF THE COURT

Court members:Lord Duthie,
Mr Tom Campbell

Gary Jack
Appellant
against
The Crofting Commission
Respondent

Subjects: 3 Naast, Poolewe and 6 Naast, Poolewe

The Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993

4 April 2025

Introduction

[1] The appellant is owner occupier of two crofts at Poolewe and a shareholder in respect of rights in the common grazing pertaining to 3 Naast and 6 Naast (Register of Crofts No R6542 and R6537). The common grazings is not currently used by any shareholder. There is no grazings committee.

[2] The appellant submitted two applications to the Crofting Commission under section 52(4) of the Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993 to apportion parts of the Naast Common Grazings extending, over the two applications, to 93 hectares or thereby for the stated purposes of tree planting, rewilding and the growing of bog myrtle.

[3] On 4 March 2024 the Commission refused the applications and issued written grounds for those decisions. The appellant appeals against those decisions. The Court appointed parties to lodge written submissions upon which the Court could determine the appeals, which were duly lodged. Representations were also lodged by Mark Williams of GBB Estates Limited, the owner of the common grazings.

Apportionment

[4] The Commission’s task when determining an application for apportionment is not some fine balancing exercise, rather, it is the exercise of a very broad discretion: Mackenzie v Crofter’s Commission 2011 SLCR 73 at [34]; Anderson v Crofter’s Commission 2014 SLCR 1 at [35]. In Matheson v The Crofters Commission (2012), the Court said this:

“… the Commission had a balancing act to carry out. It had to take account of the interests of the other shareholders. And it had to consider the future. Except where an apportionment is granted temporarily, the land is lost to communal use in perpetuity. As the Commission themselves put it in the Note of Decision (final page, second paragraph) ‘When considering applications for apportionment, as well as taking the aspirations of the applicant into account, the Commission must also safeguard the present and future interests of the other shareholders.’ That is an accurate statement of the task they had to perform. They had to balance those interests. There is no legal requirement to give one set of interests greater weight than the others”.

[5] Here the appellant, across the two applications, sought the apportionment — and therefore the removal from communal use — of a significant area of land, some 93 hectares or thereby.

The material before the Commission

[6] Prior to making its decisions in respect of the proposed apportionments, the Commission obtained and considered a report from the local Scottish Government Rural Payments and Inspections Directorate (SGRPID) office. That report states, in summary, that the common grazings is not currently used by any shareholder; that it has the potential to be used for grazing in future, having vegetative cover typical of wet heathland; that tree planting on land which has a depth of peat greater than 50cm is not recommended in respect that trees will not thrive on such land; that Scottish Forestry recommend against planting on deep peat due to risk of damage to peat soils and potential loss of carbon; and that it is not possible to establish the extent of deep peat without a peatland survey.

[7] The Commission obtained a desktop survey from Scottish Forestry prepared by a woodland officer who visited the proposed apportionment areas. He stated that the main constraint on tree planting would be deep peat and peat overlaying rock, and that the area would need further surveying to determine if the extent of the mineral soil within cultivation depth suitable for tree planting is enough to justify the cost and/or practicality of the deer fencing that would be required.

[8] The Commission received two objections to the application, one from a shareholder and the other from the owner of the common grazings.

[9] Scott Maclean, a shareholder in the common grazings raised the following concerns: (i) the significant area which would be lost from the common grazing should the apportionment be granted; (ii) the unsuitability of the grazings for tree planting, 35-40% of the area being deep peat; (iii) apportionment would block of an area of hill ground that has previously and could again support stock; (iv) apportionment would block access to the community burn which has been used by stock for water; and (v) such large scale proposals should be undertaken only by agreement with other shareholders and the owner of the common grazings.

[10] Mark Williams of GBB Estates Limited, the owner of the common grazings, raised the following concerns: (i) the proposed land is unsuitable for tree planting and the proposal unsupported by a peat survey; (ii) the fencing will cut off stag migration routes; (iii) the proposal would not promote rewilding but instead be hazardous for deer, raptors and other birds and be a fire hazard.

[11] The Commission had the benefit of a number of lengthy email exchanges between the objecting parties and the appellant on these issues. The appellant indicated, in summary, that (i) he had walked over the land and carried out some peat probing to identify the best area for planting; (ii) he is reluctant to incur the cost of a peat survey until he knows that the apportionment sought will be granted but will do so in due course; (iii) stag migration routes would not be affected as tree planting pockets would be fenced separately; and (iv) the proposed use of the land would assist rewilding.

The Commission’s decisions

[12] The grounds for the decision issued by the Commission to refuse the applications run to five pages. They state, in precis, that the Commission, having considered concerns expressed by the owner of the common grazings and comments by the Reporting Officer from the local SGRPID office, found that the interests of the appellant in the apportionments being granted were outweighed by the interests and future interests of the township in preserving the areas for township use. The Commission placed weight on the SGRPID report as evidence that there could be detriment to current and future shareholders’ stock accessing one of the main water supplies in the common grazings; and that it considered there was little objective information as to whether the area in question would be suitable for woodland creation or as to the feasibility (or otherwise) of the appellant’s plans.

The statutory grounds of appeal

[13] Section 52A(3) of the 1993 Act sets out six grounds upon which a party may appeal to the Court against a decision of the Commission, as follows:

“The grounds are that the Commission, in reaching their decision or as the case may be in determining as they did, in making their direction or in imposing the condition in question—

(a) erred on a point of law;

(b) made a finding as to a fact material to the decision, determination, direction or imposition but did not have sufficient evidence on which to base that finding;

(c) acted contrary to natural justice,

(d) took into account certain irrelevant or immaterial considerations;

(e) failed to take into account certain relevant or material considerations;

(f) exercised their discretion in an unreasonable manner.”

The appellant’s grounds of appeal

[14] The appellant’s written case founds on grounds a, b, d, e and f from section 52A(3) of the 1993 Act. His written submissions for both appeals set out the various challenges in that sequence. These submissions contain a number of refrains, with numerous criticisms being repeated under multiple grounds. For present purposes and in the interests of clarity and brevity we collate and deal with the various criticisms and statutory grounds in the following sequence:

The Commission wrongly took into account Scott Maclean’s objections (ground a — error of law; ground f — exercised discretion in an unreasonable manner).

The Commission issued a single grounds for decision document in respect of both applications (ground a; ground b — material finding without evidence; ground e — failure to consider material or relevant considerations)

Future shareholders’ stock access to water (ground b; ground d — irrelevant or immaterial considerations; ground e; ground f)

Suitability for woodland creation (ground b; ground e; ground f)

Peat constraints (ground b; ground d; ground e; ground f)

The reasons for objections by Mark Williams, owner of common grazings (ground d; ground e)

[15] In addition, the appellant’s grounds of appeal and written submissions contain a number of criticisms which amount to service complaints about the Commission’s handing of his application, including complaints as to the time taken to make a decision and criticisms as to the Commission’s lack of communication with him. Some of these are presented as falling within ground f. These criticisms may or may not be well founded, however, these are not matters for this forum. Taken at their highest, they do not vitiate the Commission’s decisions, nor do they engage ground f, still less any of the other statutory grounds of appeal. We set them aside for present purposes.

Decision and reasons

[16] For the reasons given below we refuse both appeals.

(i) Taking account of Scott Maclean’s objections (ground a — error of law).

The appellant’s submissions

[17] The Commission erred in taking account of Scott Maclean’s objections. Mr Maclean does not reside and has not within the past ten years resided on or within 32km of his croft. He is accordingly in breach of his residence duty. Moreover, he does not and has not cultivated or put to purposeful use his croft in the past seven years. It follows that there was no objection from any “legal” crofter.

The Commission’s submissions

[18] The Commission did not err. In carrying out the balancing exercise, the Commission will consider the comments of any shareholder in the common grazing. A shareholder is not disqualified from objecting to an apportionment because he is not ordinarily resident on the croft or is not cultivating the croft.

Decision regarding Scott Maclean’s evidence

[19] The Commission took into account Mr Maclean’s objections. It was entitled to do so. Doing so did not involve the unreasonable exercise of a discretion. As noted above, the Commission enjoys a broad discretion when determining apportionment applications. Any breaches by Mr Maclean of his obligations of residence or to cultivate his croft (neither of which are in issue here) do not divest him of the right to object to the proposed apportionments.

[20] In his written submissions the appellant sought to make some point out of the fact that in their Note of Opposition and Answers to the appeal, the Commission refers to Mr Maclean not being disqualified from “commenting”, and accordingly they treated him “as an objector not a commenter”. For completeness we will simply observe that this is a distinction without difference and that when the Commission’s reasons for decision document is read fairly and in context, the terms commenting and objecting should be treated as interchangeable.

(ii) Issuing a single grounds for decision document in respect of both applications (ground a — error of law; ground b — material finding without evidence; ground e — failure to consider material or relevant considerations)

The appellant’s submissions

[21] The Commission issued a single document as grounds for the decision in respect of both applications. This constitutes an error of law. In paragraph 3 of the grounds for decision document the Commission state “They are two separate applications as an apportionment can be granted in respect of a single grazing share only.” This indicates that there should have been two grounds for decision documents. Each application’s area has different issues. The single joint grounds for decision report did not address the different nature of the two different apportionments applied for. The Commission ought to have identified that the Allt Donn watercourse and its tributaries are mainly, although not exclusively, within the proposed apportionment for 3 Naast (share) and not 6 Naast (share).

The Commission’s submissions

[22] The Commission did not err, make a material finding without evidence, nor did it fail to consider material or relevant considerations. A single set of grounds for decision was issued because, from a practical point of view, the apportionments applied for were contiguous and to be fenced and managed as a single unit. In any event, even if the Commission ought to have identified that the Allt Donn watercourse and its tributaries are mainly, although not exclusively, within the proposed apportionment for 3 Naast (share) and not 6 Naast (share), the main reason for refusal of both applications was the same: the appellant’s interests in obtaining an apportionment were outweighed by the interests of the shareholders, including future shareholders, in retaining the land as common grazings available for communal use.

Decision regarding the issue of a single grounds for decisions document

[23] The point of distinction between the two applications identified by the appellant (location of the Allt Donn watercourse and its tributaries) was not material, still less determinative to the applications and further, was never likely to be material to the decisions reached by the Commission in either application. For the purposes of this appeal, we proceed on the basis that the Croft 6 application does not encroach on the Allt Donn: that, however, does not vitiate the decision in respect of that application. It would clearly have been better had the decision noted this expressly. However, none of statutory grounds of appeal are made out in respect of this criticism. Given the very significant extent of the areas sought to be resumed — which, as noted above, would result in the land being lost to present and future shareholders in perpetuity — and the relative dearth of available objective information as to whether the area in question would be suitable for woodland creation or as to the feasibility (or otherwise) of the appellant’s plans, it is unsurprising that the Commission concluded that the interests of the shareholders, including future shareholders, in retaining the land as common grazings outweighed those of the appellant in the apportionment being granted.

(iii) Future shareholders’ stock access to water (ground b; ground d — irrelevant or immaterial considerations; ground e; ground f)

The appellant’s submissions

[24] The appellant attacks the Commission’s finding that were the apportionments to be granted, “there could be detriment to the use of current and future shareholders stock accessing one of the main water supply in the common” (sic). In response to the SGRPID report’s finding that “there are lochs dotted in the commons, but whether livestock would use these in dry weathers is up for debate”, the appellant asserts “there is no debate, livestock will definitely seek out and drink from a fresh water loch in dry weather.” He contends that there are other burns and lochs on the common grazing, including one which he has never seen go dry.

[25] The Commission erred in stating that both apportionment sites block off the main water source, the Allt Donn burn. This is incorrect: the Croft 6 application does not block access to the Allt Donn burn, only the proposed apportionment in respect of Croft 3 does.

Decision regarding future shareholders’ stock access to water

[26] This ground of appeal appears to proceed on the premise that the Commission’s decisions to refuse the applications were based on a definitive finding anent future shareholders’ stock access to water. Not so: the Commission did not find it appropriate — or, standing the limited objective information before it, possible — to make a definitive finding regarding stock access to water. That is perhaps unsurprising: the evidence in the SGRPID Report is notably tentative (“there could be detriment to the use of current and future shareholders stock accessing one of the main water supply in the common” (sic) (emphasis added). The Commission states expressly that “the application contains very little in the way of objective information”. On the one hand, the SGRPID reports expresses reservations on the question. On the other hand, the appellant asserts the contrary. Faced with conflicting evidence, the Commission stated merely that “there could be detriment to the use of current and future shareholders stock accessing one of the main water supply in the common” (sic). (emphasis added). It follows that the Commission did not make any decision without evidence. Nor can it fairly be said that they failed to take into account relevant or material considerations or took into account irrelevant or material considerations: the conflicting considerations regarding stock access to water are all expressly noted in the grounds for decision document. Again, given the extent of the areas sought to be resumed and the relative dearth of available objective information as to the feasibility of the appellant’s plans, it is unsurprising the Commission reached the decision it did.

(iv) Suitability for woodland creation (ground b; ground e; ground f)

The appellant’s submissions

[27] The tree stumps on the Croft 6 apportionment demonstrate there was previously a woodland there. The Commissioned erred in not finding accordingly.

The Commission’s submissions

[28] Evidence of historic woodland, which is not admitted, is not evidence of current suitability for afforestation, nor would evidence of the current suitability of the land for afforestation be determinative of the application. The Commission has a range of factors to consider when exercising its discretion.

Decision regarding woodland creation

[29] The submissions of the Commission are to be preferred. The presence of tree stumps is not conclusive evidence of current suitability for afforestation and accordingly the Commission did not fail to take into account a material consideration. Neither did the Commission make any a finding without sufficient evidence. In fact, the Commission did not make any definitive finding as to the suitability of the proposed subjects of apportionment for tree planting. Rather, in the absence of a peat survey or other evidence from the appellant that the land is suitable for tree planting, it took the positive step of obtaining a desktop survey from Scottish Forestry prepared by a woodland officer who visited the proposed apportionment areas. As noted above that survey was inconclusive. The Commission found that “the application contains very little in the way of objective information in the lengthy submissions … in particular on whether the area in question would be suitable for woodland creation”. That was a conclusion which was open to the Commission on the available evidence and further, one that does not close the door to any future application which might be made, accompanied with adequate information as to the feasibility of what is being proposed. Again, given the extent of the areas sought to be resumed and the relative dearth of available objective information as to the feasibility of the appellant’s plans, it is unsurprising the Commission reached the decision it did.

Peat constraints (ground b; ground d; ground e; ground f)

Submissions for the appellant

[30] Had a peat survey been necessary the appellant would have obtained one. He did not say he would not obtain one, rather, only that it would not be worthwhile incurring the expense of such a report if he was not going to get the apportionments. A walk over survey carried out by Botanaeco clearly states that “around 60-70% of this is certainly free of peat (maybe more)”. The Commission’s implication that trees might not grow on the land in question is misfounded. The presence of tree stumps demonstrate that there was woodland on the site previously.

Submissions for the Commission

[31] The Commission made no finding regarding peat depth, nor did it make a finding without sufficient evidence. Rather, the Commission acknowledged in its grounds of decision that only a specialised peat depth survey could establish the peat depth over the proposed apportionment. The main reason for refusing the application was the current and future interests of shareholders, including potential future uses that could benefit all shareholders collectively. Had the appellant obtained such a peat depth survey and the results were favourable to his proposals, that would not have been determinative of the application.

Decision regarding peat constraints

[32] For similar reasons as those given above in respect of the substantially overlapping issue of suitability for woodland creation, we prefer the submissions of the Commission. The presence of tree stumps is not determinative of current suitability for afforestation. The Commission found that “the application contains very little in the way of objective information in the lengthy submissions … in particular on whether the area in question would be suitable for woodland creation”. That was a conclusion which was open to the Commission on the available evidence and further, one that does not close the door to any future application which might be made, accompanied with adequate supporting information.

[33] There was no failure to take into account a material consideration. Neither did the Commission make a finding without evidence. The Commission did not make any definitive finding. In the absence of a peat survey or other evidence from the appellant that the land is suitable for tree planting, it took the positive step of obtaining a desktop survey from Scottish Forestry prepared by a woodland officer who visited the proposed apportionment areas. As noted above that survey was inconclusive.

[34] The information from Botanaeco, referred to by the appellant, was before the Commission. The 60-70% figure referred to by the appellant derives from an email from Andy McMullen dated 19 January 2022, which makes clear that no conclusion was reached by him as to how much was suitable for tree planting, that being a matter beyond the author’s “botanical competence”. That figure, quantum valeat, is self-evidently based on the most superficial of investigations and is not to be treated with undue credulity, particularly when set against the information derived from SGRPID and Scottish Forestry. Again, given the extent of the areas sought to be resumed and the relative dearth of available objective information, it is unsurprising the Commission reached the decision it did.

Mark Williams’ reasons for objecting (ground d; ground e; ground f)

Submissions for the appellant

[35] The owner of the common grazings objected to the application purely for his own financial gain. Mr Williams has previously attempted to prevent the appellant from installing a mini hydro system on his croft as it meant he could not use the water from the river running through his croft for upgrading his own hydro system. Mr Williams has planted tens of thousands of trees in the area to make money from carbon credits. He has an incentive to prevent the apportionment of land that he could potentially plant trees on in the future.

Decision on Mark Williams’ reasons for objecting

[36] Even if what the appellant says is true (and this is disputed by Mr Williams), Mr Williams’ underlying reasons for objecting to the applications are not here relevant. As owner of the common grazings he was entitled to object to the proposed apportionments. Those objections are not rendered irrelevant or immaterial by any such underlying motive, nor are any such motives a relevant or material consideration of which the Commission failed to take account. Moreover, to the extent the Commission weighed Mr Williams in the balance, doing so is not on any view the unreasonable exercise of a discretion.

Disposal

[37] We refuse both appeals.
parties: Gary Jack Appellant against The Crofting Commission Respondent

title: Ronald Niall Campbell Applicant against Duncan John Campbell Respondent [2025] SLC 5
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2025] SLC 5,
Case reference: SLC/34/19

NOTE

Court members: Lord Duthie,
Mr J A Smith

Ronald Niall Campbell
Applicant
against
Duncan John Campbell
Respondent

Subjects: Croft “Strachurbeag”, Strachur

The Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993

14 March 2025

[1] The applicant is the former tenant of the whole croft Strachurbeag, Strachur. Following the making of this application the respondent agreed to make a voluntary sale of the croft to the applicant. On 27 June 2019 the respondent executed a disposition in favour of the applicant. The subjects conveyed are now registered in the Land Register under Title Number ARG27078. The consideration is stated on the disposition to be £237.90, which is the figure brought out, in terms of section 14(2) of the 1993 Act, of 15 times the annual rent for the croft (which was £15.86).

[2] The applicant avers that, in error, a small area of ground amounting to 0.0712 acres (0.028814 ha) or thereby was omitted from the relative disposition plan and accordingly the subjects conveyed to him. He inadvertently remains tenant of that area only. He accordingly amended the application to seek an order authorising acquisition of that smaller area which had not been conveyed to him.

[3] We are satisfied that it is appropriate to make the order now sought. The acquisition of the croft was ultimately uncontroversial. The amended application is in the nature of corrective conveyancing. None of the factors identified in Section 13(2) of the 1993 Act are here present.

[4] Since the consideration agreed between parties as narrated in the disposition already granted is the full consideration payable in terms of section 14(2), we infer that that sum was intended to be in consideration of the 0.0712 acres area also. No further consideration is payable: section 14(6).

[5] The applicant seeks the expenses of the application, averring that his solicitors have sent repeated correspondence to the respondent seeking a second voluntary conveyance but the respondent has “failed or delayed to convey the remaining tenanted croft land to the applicant”. In respect of proceedings up to and including the granting of the 2019 disposition, (which was intended to give effect to and extra judicial settlement), we consider the appropriate disposal is no expenses due to or by either party. In respect of subsequent proceedings, we see some force in the submission that the cost of proceedings might be said to have been caused by the respondent’s failure to engage with the applicant once the conveyancing error was noticed. Generally, expenses should be borne by the party that has caused them. However, here the need for the amended application was the error in the conveyancing plan in the 2019 disposition. In the absence of any indication to the contrary, we proceed on the basis that that error was on the part of both parties. In those circumstances the appropriate disposal in respect of those subsequent expenses is none due to or by either party.
parties: Ronald Niall Campbell Applicant against Duncan John Campbell Respondent

title: Zetland Estate Applicants against Crofters Having Rights in Various Crofts on Zetland Estate Respondents [2025] SLC 4
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2025] SLC 4,
Case reference: SLC/104/23

DECISION OF THE COURT

Court members: Lord Minginish,
Tom Campbell

Zetland Estate
Applicants
against
Crofters Having Rights in Various Crofts on Zetland Estate
Respondents

Subjects: Zetland Estate

The Crofters (Scotland) Act, 1993

Applicants: Peterson, solicitor; Tait & Peterson

Respondents: Inkster, solicitor; Inksters Solicitors

3 March 2025

Introduction

[1] Brian James Thompson is the owner‑occupier of the croft of Houlscarpa, Weisdale, Shetland, having purchased it from the original owner‑occupier, David James Arthur, in 1989. The disposition in his favour narrates that “the rights of peat‑cutting and common grazing in scattald or common grazing” belonging to Mr Arthur were being conveyed as parts and pertinents of the croft. These rights had been acquired by Mr Arthur when he bought the croft from the Marquis of Zetland in 1970, the disposition in his favour including

“the rights of peat-cutting and common grazing belonging to [the disponer] as hitherto exercised by the said disponee [i.e. Mr Arthur] and his predecessors in the tenancy of the said croft or holding”.

[2] In 1997 Mr Thompson applied for and was granted an apportionment in respect of his rights in the relevant scattald or common grazings but he has never acquired a heritable title thereto. That apportionment has been included in the list of crofts and croft land for which we are asked to fix fair rents in this application. However, our right to do so has been challenged by Mr Thompson’s solicitor, Mr Brian Inkster by way of motion which was heard by Lord Minginish and Mr Campbell by way of Webex hearing on 4 December 2024.

[3] Mr Inkster’s submission was that, the rights in the common grazings having been acquired along with the inbye croft land, any question of their being rentable was extinguished and could not be resurrected simply by the conversion of the original rights, which extended over the whole scattald, into an apportionment. Reference was made to what the court had said in reference by Crofters Commission under section 53 of the Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993 (Application SLC/121/11, order of 3 August, 2012) in answer to the question “If a grazing share is included as part of the purchase of croft land can a rent still be charged in respect of that share and, if so, does this alter the status of that share?”, viz:

“No. The thinking behind this question is not clear. Once a purchase has been completed there can be no question of continuing rent. In the usual case, the landlord must have had rights in the grazings in the grazing share to be able to provide it for his tenant as a pertinent of the croft. How that landlord acquired the rights does not appear to us to be of significance in this context, although it will almost invariably have arisen from his original ownership of the grazings. Once the former crofter holds the right as owner, no question of rent can arise.”

[4] Mr Inkster pointed out that the value of the grazing shares would have been taken into account when the purchase price of the croft was computed.

[5] All of that being so, this application, in so far as it related to Mr Thompson’s apportionment, was incompetent.

[6] The motion was opposed by Mr Eric Peterson, solicitor for the applicants, who submitted that the apportionment was rentable as a “deemed croft”. Moreover, it was in any event reasonable for it to be rented because the practical effect of this apportionment was that the landlords were being permanently deprived of 109 acres of his land.

Discussion

[7] We should first record that, having cleared it with Mr Inkster in the course of the hearing, Mr Smith has also been included in Lord Minginish’s and Mr Campbell’s subsequent deliberations and he is in agreement with the decision at which they have arrived.

[8] Had the question in this case been whether grazing rights in a common grazing remained rentable by the court after having been conveyed to an owner-occupier crofter as part of the title to the inbye croft, we would have answered it in the negative. Is the answer different when an apportionment has been granted? In our opinion it is. That is because the granting of an apportionment brings about two changes in the situation, one practical, the other legal. The practical result in this case is that Mr Thompson has the exclusive use of the apportionment area and has lost his rights over the rest of the common grazing. The legal change is brought about by subsection(s) (4) and (5) of section 3 of the Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993, which provide that:

“(4) For the purposes of this Act –

(a) any right in pasture or grazing land held or to be held by the tenant of a croft whether alone or in common with others, and

(b) any land comprising any part of a common grazing which has been apportioned for the exclusive use of a crofter under section 52(4) of this Act, and,

(c) any land held runrig which has been apportioned under section 52(8) of this Act,

shall be deemed to form part of the croft.

(5) For the purposes of this Act, where –

(a) a crofter has acquired his entire croft other than any such right or land as is referred to in subsection (4) above; or

(b) any person, not being a crofter, has obtained an apportionment of any land under section 52 of this Act,

then the person referred to in paragraphs (a) or (b) above shall be deemed to hold the right or land referred to therein in tenancy until held otherwise and that right or land shall be deemed to be a croft.”

[9] It seems to us that sub‑paragraph (a) of sub‑section (4) applies in this case. Since this provision was part of the original 1993 Act, when Mr Thompson acquired his apportionment in 1997 he should have realised, or, at least, could have found out, that the creation of a deemed croft with him as tenant would be the result.

[10] What the court said in the Crofters Commission reference does not bear on this question because the court was not there addressing the situation where an apportionment is granted subsequent to the acquisition of the croft.

[11] The suggestion that there is unfairness in an apportionment being rented when the grazing rights have already been paid for by the crofter is countered by the fact that an apportionment is a new creation involving the acquisition of enhanced rights by the crofter including not only the exclusive use of the apportionment area for grazing purposes but the right to pursue valuable diversification and development projects on that land, to the exclusion of his former fellow shareholders in the common grazings.

Decision

[12] We therefore refuse Mr Inkster’s motion. The apportionment will be rented as a croft.
parties: Zetland Estate Applicants against Crofters Having Rights in Various Crofts on Zetland Estate Respondents
